In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Hijr.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed in Mecca. This is also related from Qatadah and Mujahid. In Majma' al-Bayan (a Qur'anic commentary by al-Tabarsi), it is reported from al-Hasan that it is Meccan except for the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the magnificent Qur'an﴾, and His words: ﴿As We sent down upon the dividers, those who made the Qur'an into parts﴾. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti, in al-Itqan, mentioned that some scholars exempt only the first verse. Then he said: "I say: the exemption should also include the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And We certainly know those who go forward among you, and We know those who lag behind﴾, the verse, because of what al-Tirmidhi and others narrated about its occasion of revelation, that it concerned the rows in prayer." Based on this, the statement of Abu Hayyan, and the similar statement in the tafsir of al-Khazin, that it is Meccan without any disagreement, is apparent. The fact that it does not mention an exception is evidence of little investigation. It has ninety-nine verses. Al-Dani said: "Likewise al-Tabarsi (reported it) by consensus." It is said to contain five verses abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation) by the verse of the sword.

The link between it and what precedes it is that it opens in a manner similar to the opening of the previous surah, and it also contains a description of the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection and their wish that they had been Muslims. The first surah contained something similar. Also, the first surah mentioned a part of the state of the criminals in the Hereafter, and this surah mentions a part of what befell some of them in this world. Also, in each of the two surahs, He Most High mentioned what relates to the matter of the heavens and the earth. Also, He did something similar concerning Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Also, in each of them there is consolation for our Prophet (ﷺ), and other matters without number.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾ The discussion of it has already passed. ﴿Those﴾: many scholars have chosen that it refers to the surah, meaning: that magnificent surah. ﴿are the verses of the Book﴾: the complete Book, which deserves that the name "the Book" be applied to it absolutely, as the definite article indicates. That is, it is a portion of it, distinct and marked by a particular name. So what is meant is the whole Qur'an, or the whole of what had been sent down at that time. ﴿And a Qur'an﴾: of great rank, as the indefinite form indicates. ﴿clear﴾: making clear within its contents wisdom and rulings; or making clear the path of right guidance and error; or distinguishing between truth and falsehood, and lawful and unlawful; or manifest in its meanings; or making manifest its inimitability. So "clear" is either transitive or intransitive. In combining the two descriptions, "Book" and "Qur'an," there is a magnifying of the status of the Qur'an: by the first, it is pointed to as including the attributes of perfection of the entire genus of divine books, so that it is as if it were all of them; and by the second, it is pointed to as being distinguished from others, unique, unparalleled in its kind, beyond the scope of ordinary eloquence, a Qur'an with no crookedness.

The opening of Surat al-Naml is similar to this, except that here the description as "Qur'an" is placed after the description as "Book." This is because pointing to its distinction from all other books, after alerting to its containing the perfections of the others, is added in praise, lest one suppose at first that its distinction from others is due to its being independent with attributes specific to itself, without including the qualities of perfection of all the other noble books. There, the order is reversed, in view of the state in which the description as "Qur'an" precedes the description as "Book." This was said by some of the verifying scholars.

It is permitted that "the Book" means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It is mentioned that its being placed first here is in terms of existence, and its being placed later there is in terms of our knowledge, since we only know that this (the Book) is established from the Qur'an. It was objected that the attribution of "verses" to it creates a difficulty for this view, since there is no known basis for it containing verses.

Al-Zamakhshari made the reference here to what the surah contains, and "the Book" and what is conjoined to it refer to the surah. He mentioned there that "the Book" is either the Tablet, or the surah, or the Qur'an, and here he chose one of the possibilities mentioned there.

In al-Kashf (by al-Zamakhshari) he said: "Because 'the Book' used absolutely for other than the Tablet is more apparent, and interpreting it as the surah is more eloquent in emphasis, as is indicated by the style of His words: ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. And the referent of the demonstrative should match, for it refers to the verses of the surah." Then he said: "The choice of interpreting it so, avoiding the identity of the conjoined and the conjoined-to in meaning, is because the apparent sense of the attribution of 'verses' is that."

Since definiteness carries one kind of grandeur and indefiniteness another, and since the purpose was combination, he made "the Book" definite and "a Qur'an" indefinite here, and reversed this in al-Naml. He made the definite noun first in both places to add to the emphasis. And because in that place He followed it with speech about the particular (the special Qur'an), its being a Qur'an was placed first, because that is more indicative of the particular revelation sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) as a miracle.

It was objected to this explanation, which interprets it as the surah and not the whole Qur'an or what had been sent down at that time, that it is not immediately understood, whereas what is immediately understood upon absolute mention is what was mentioned. On this basis, the benefit of describing the verses with the attributes of perfection of what they are attributed to becomes apparent, rather than making it a reference to the surah. For the surah, in its attribute of that, is not at that level of fame such that one could dispense with stating the description explicitly. Moreover, it would be a reference to all its verses, and so one must make "those" a reference to each one of them individually, and there is in this much artificiality, as is not hidden.

Then al-Zamakhshari, after explaining the two conjoined items as the surah, pointed to the reason for the difference between them by his saying: "As if it were said: the Book that combines perfection and wondrous eloquence." He hinted that since it was made independent in perfection and wonder, its two aspects were intended, so one of them was conjoined to the other. Therefore the purpose of mentioning the essence in both places is the two descriptions. This is the benefit of choosing this style. For this reason, some who counted it among the figures of abstraction (tajrid, the rhetorical device of presenting an attribute as if it were a separate entity) listed it there. This was said in al-Kashf.

Al-Tibi, after quoting from al-Baghawi the explanation of the difference between the two conjoined items, that "the Book" is what is written, and "the Qur'an" is what is gathered, some of it to some of it, said: "If you say: the outcome returns to 'the Book and Qur'an' being two attributes of one described entity placed in its stead, what is that described entity and how is it to be estimated? If you estimate it as definite, it is in the nominative (raf'), (and Qur'an-in-clear is in the genitive) ... and if you go to say it is indefinite, the word 'Book' forbids that. I say: I estimate it as definite ('and a clear Qur'an') in the sense of definiteness, because its meaning, reaching in wonder to the limit of inimitability, is then bounded, indeed restricted," and so on to the end of what he said. It is a statement empty of verification, as is not hidden to its people. It was said: what is meant by "the Book" is the Torah and the Gospel, and by "the Qur'an" the Book sent down upon our Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir narrated this from Mujahid and Qatadah. The matter of conjunction on this view is quite apparent, except that this itself is not apparent, and the referent of the demonstrative on it is also obscure. In al-Bahr (by Abu Hayyan) it is said that the demonstrative on this view refers to the verses of the Book, and this, as you see, is (weak).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

Then, when He, glory be to Him, had explained the matter of the verses, to direct the addressees toward receiving well what they contain of rulings, narratives and admonitions, He, majestic is His glory, began to explain what they include. He said, mighty is His saying: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, [meaning] submitting to what faith in it is obligatory, ﴿they had been Muslims﴾, believers in that. It has been said: what is meant is their disbelief in the Book and the Qur'an, and in its being from Allah, exalted is He, and their wish to submit to His judgment and yield to His command. In this is an indication that their disbelief was only through denial. However, this is open to question. This wish will occur on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the sinners coming out of the Fire.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bayhaqi and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they discussed this verse and said: "This is when Allah gathers together the people of sins among the Muslims and the polytheists in the Fire, and the polytheists say: 'What you used to worship has not availed you.' Then Allah becomes angry on their behalf and brings them out by the grace of His mercy."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted with a sound chain from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Indeed, some people of my community will be punished for their sins, and they will remain in the Fire for as long as Allah wills them to remain. Then the people of polytheism will reproach them, saying: "We do not see that what you used to affirm has benefited you." So no monotheist will remain but that Allah will bring him out of the Fire.'" Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse.

Other than one [narrator] transmitted similar [reports] from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, each of them raising it to the Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayers and peace. The same has been related from many of the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih). As for al-Zamakhshari's saying: "That the saying of this is a door of wishing, a house of foolishness, whose sitter is its ugly belief," [it is rejected].

Al-Dahhak said: this [wish] is in this world, at the time of death, when the evil end of disbelief is revealed to them. From Ibn Mas'ud: the verse concerns the disbelievers of Quraysh, who wished for this on the day of Badr when they saw the victory of the Muslims. In another report from him and from some Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that this [wish] will be when their necks are struck and they are presented to the Fire.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that this wish from the disbelievers occurs in every state in which the disbeliever is punished and the Muslim is safe. "Rubba" (رُبَّ, "perhaps / how many a"), despite its frequent occurrence in the speech of the Arabs, does not occur in the Qur'an except in this verse. It is said in it: rubba with a damma on the ra' and a shadda on the ba' and with a fatha on it; and raba with a fatha on the ra'; and rubu with a damma on both; and rubat with a damma and a fatha on the ba' and the ta'; and rubt with a sukun on the ta'; and raba with a fatha on the three; and rabat with a fatha on the first two and a sukun on the ta' and a lightening of the ba'. These are seven. Also: rubbata with a damma and a fatha on the shadda'd ba'; rub with a damma and a sukun; and rab with a fatha and a sukun. These are seventeen languages, all of which Ibn Hisham related in al-Mughni except rubbata, and Abu Hayyan related eleven of them, including rubbata. If the joining of "ma" to it and its being unjoined from it are considered, the languages reach a number that is not hidden.

Ibn Fadalah, in al-Hawamil wa'l-Awamil, claimed that it is biliteral in origin, like qad, and that the fatha on the ba' when lightened without the ta' is a poetic necessity, and that the fatha on the ra' in every case is anomalous. It is a preposition (harf jarr), contrary to the Kufans, al-Akhfash in one of his two opinions, and Ibn al-Tarawah. They claimed that it is a declinable-less noun (ism mabni) like kam (how many), and they argued for its nominality by referring to it in his saying:

"If they kill you, your killing was not a shame upon you,
but perhaps a killing is a shame."

So rubba, according to them, is a subject (mubtada'), and 'ar (shame) is its predicate (khabar). It occurs, according to them, as a verbal noun, like rubba darbatin darabtu ("how many a blow have I struck"); as a time expression, like rubba yawma sirtu ("how many a day have I travelled"); and as a direct object, like rubba rajulin darabtu ("how many a man have I struck").

Al-Radi preferred its nominality, but its i'rab (grammatical case-marking) according to him is always raf' (nominative), on the basis that it is a subject with no predicate, just as he preferred that in their saying: aqallu rajulin yaqulu dhalika illa Zaydan ("few a man says that except Zayd"). He said: if it is made ineffective by ma, then it has no place of i'rab at that point, because it is like the negative particle entering a sentence. The Basrans refused this, saying: if it were a noun, it would be permissible for the verb to reach it through a preposition, so that one would say: bi-rubba rajulin 'alimun marartu ("I passed by a man, a scholar, how many"), and for a pronoun to refer back to it, and for it to be made a construct (mudaf) and the signs of the noun to be absent from it altogether.

They answered regarding the line: the known reading is [...] "ba'd" (some) instead of "rubba", and even if that narration is sound, then 'ar is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is a shame", as he stated in his saying: "Oh how many a battle, it is better than ease." The sentence is an attribute of the genitive (majrur) or its predicate, since it is in the position of a subject.

Its analogy with kam is rejected, as Abu 'Ali said: they did not separate between it and the genitive as they separated between kam and what it governs.

Regarding its meaning, there are several opinions:
First, that it is always for paucity (taqlil). This is the view of the majority; in al-Basit, al-Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Mazini, al-Farisi, al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Hisham, and a host of others are counted among them.
Second, that it is always for multiplicity (takthir). This is the view of the author of al-'Ayn, Ibn Darastawayh, and a group; and it has been transmitted from al-Khalil.
Third, which al-Jalal al-Suyuti chose in agreement with al-Farabi and a group, that it is for paucity mostly and for multiplicity rarely.
Fourth, the reverse of this, which was asserted in al-Tashil and chosen by Ibn Hisham in al-Mughni.
Fifth, that it is for both without one being predominant; Abu Hayyan transmitted this from some later scholars.
Sixth, that it was not established for either of them, but is a particle of affirmation that does not indicate multiplicity or paucity; rather, that is understood from outside. Abu Hayyan chose this.
Seventh, that it is for multiplicity in boasting and for paucity in other than that. This is the view of al-A'lam and Ibn al-Sayyid.
Eighth, that it is for an undefined number. This is the view of Ibn al-Badhash and Ibn Tahir, and it is obligatorily placed at the beginning in most cases, as in his saying:

"I am certain that a man who is imagined to be
trustworthy is a betrayer who makes the trustworthy seem a betrayer."

And his saying:

"Had the peoples known how I left them,
many a redeemer and praiser would be in the graves."

This may be, as al-Shimni said, a poetic necessity. Abu Hayyan said: what is meant is its being placed at the beginning of what it governs, so one does not say: laqitu rubba rajulin 'alimin ("I met how many a scholarly man").

They mentioned that it may be preceded by alla (ألا), as in his saying:

"Oh, how many one who is seized for the crime of another!
So do not be too quick to abandon one who was a sinner."

It is often introduced by ya at the beginning of a conditional's response, as in his saying: "If he is distressed today, then oh how many a youth [...]." And, not in the common usage, "Ya rubba kasiyatin" (Oh how many a clothed woman) in the hadith.

It does not govern anything but an indefinite noun. Some permitted its governing a definite noun with al (ال), citing his saying:

"How often the camel, the tethered one among them,
and the swift [horses] among which are the mahar."

The majority answered that the reading is with raf' (nominative), and even if the genitive is sound, then al is extra.

On whether its genitive must be described: al-Mubarrad, Ibn al-Sarraj, al-Farisi, most later scholars, and it is attributed to the Basrans, say it is obligatory, to treat it as the negative particle, since it occurs only at the beginning and nothing that operates on the following noun can precede it. The rule for the negative particle is that it enters a sentence, so the most analogical [position] is that its genitive be described by a clause for this reason. It may also be described by what functions as a clause, such as an adverbial phrase, a prepositional phrase, an active participle, or a passive participle. Ibn Hisham decided this in al-Mughni and al-Radi approved it.

Al-Akhfash, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Ibn Tahir, Ibn Kharuf and others said it is not obligatory, and that its implying paucity or multiplicity serves in place of the attribute. Ibn Malik chose this, and Abu Hayyan followed him, and he criticised the aforementioned argument in ways that are not hidden.

It governs a noun that is a construct (mudaf) to a pronoun of its genitive, conjoined with a conjunction (wa), as in rubba rajulin wa-akhihi ("how many a man and his brother"). Sibawayh does not allow this to be used as an analogy.

As for what al-Asma'i transmitted about rubba directly governing a noun construct to a pronoun, where he said to an Arab woman: "Does so-and-so have a father or a brother?" She said: "Rubba abihi, rubba akhihi" (how many a father of his, how many a brother of his), meaning rubba abin lahu, rubba akhin lahu ("how many a father of his, how many a brother of his"), considering the separation, since "ab" and "akh" are among the nouns that may be described by an attribute. So it is not analogized from this, by consensus.

It governs a singular masculine pronoun, which is explained by an indefinite accusative noun that agrees with the meaning the speaker intends, not separated from it. Its genitive has been heard in his saying:

"And how many a destruction, from which you rescued
[him] from his destruction."

This is on the intention of min (from), and it is anomalous.

The Kufans permitted agreement of the pronoun with the explanatory indefinite noun in the dual, plural and feminine, as in his saying:

"How many a youth I called to what
brings lasting praise, and they responded."

The soundest view is that this pronoun is definite but treated as indefinite. Ibn 'Usfur, following a group, chose that it is indefinite, and that its governing it is neither rare nor anomalous, contrary to Ibn Malik. He held that it is an extra particle in terms of i'rab, not meaning, and that the position of its genitive follows the governor, not the necessary accusative by the verb after it, or by a deleted governor, contrary to al-Zajjaj and his followers in their saying: "bi-dhalika" (by that), because it would entail the transitive verb reaching its object through an intermediary, which it does not need. Thus it is conjoined to its position just as it is conjoined to its form, as in his saying:

"And a camel like Sunayq in height and loftiness,
startled by the swift trotting of the noon heat, rising [...]."

It governs in the same way as the other prepositions. Al-Rummani and Ibn Tahir said it does not govern, like extra particles. The governing is through the governor which is the predicate of its genitive, or which acts in its position, or which explains it; this was said by Abu Hayyan. Ibn Hisham said: the view of the majority, that it governs its governor, if they mean the mentioned governor, is an error, since it governs by itself; or if the omitted [governor], it is estimated as hasala ("he attained") or the like, as a group stated, so in this there is an estimate of what the meaning of the speech is independent of, and it was not uttered at any time. Then, according to the governing, he said: its omission is a solecism (lahn), and it is rare for al-Khalil and Sibawayh, as in his saying:

"And a wilderness of desert, whose ostriches walk
like the walking of the Christians in light sandals of yarandaj."

That is: "they crossed it". Ibn Hisham rejects this, and their saying: "rubba rajulin qa'imin" (how many a standing man) and "rubba ibnatin khayrin min ibnin" (how many a girl better than a boy), and his saying:

"Oh, how many one whom you deceive, [while] he is your sincere advisor,
and a trustworthy one in the unseen, not trustworthy."

Al-Farisi and al-Jazuli said [it is] frequent, and Ibn al-Hajib decided on this.

Fourth: it is obligatory, as al-Basit transmitted from some of them. Fifth: it was transmitted from Ibn Abi al-Rabi' that its omission is obligatory if the attribute stands in its place, and otherwise both options are permitted, whether there is an indication or not. It is obligatory according to al-Mubarrad, al-Farisi and Ibn 'Usfur, and this is the well-known view, as Abu Hayyan said. The view of most is that it is past in meaning. Ibn al-Sarraj said: it comes as a circumstantial state (hal). Ibn Malik said: it comes in the future, and he chose this in al-Bahr, except that he said it is rare, and the occurrence of the past is more frequent. He cited for it the saying of Sulaym al-Qushayri:

"And one who takes refuge in cowardice from fear of death
will die; and a warrior, anxious, will return."

And the saying of Hind:

"Oh, how many a sayer tomorrow will say:
'Alas, mother of Mu'awiyah!'"

Like Ibn Malik, he took the verse as an instance of this. Most interpreted it as placing the present tense in the position of the past, on the pattern of "and the Trumpet was blown". Ibn Hisham criticised this, saying that it involves artificiality, since it entails that the future verb was used to express a past metaphorically referring to the future. Al-Shimni answered that there is no artificiality in it, because they said: this future state has been made equivalent to the realised past, so rubama, which is specific to the past, was used with it, and he turned to the present-tense wording because it is the speech of one whose reports are not doubted. The present tense, for him, is equivalent to the past; so it is future in actuality and past according to interpretation. He said: and this, as you see, [is weak].

It is reported from Abu Hayyan that he answered the verse of Hind by saying that it is from the category of describing with the future, not from the category of rubba's governing what follows it. It is like your saying: "rubba musi'in al-yawma yuhsinu ghadan" (how many a wrongdoer today will do good tomorrow), meaning: how many a man who is described by this description.

The Kufans, as in al-Mutawwal, interpreted the verse as having an estimate of kana ("was"), meaning rubbama kana yawaddu alladhina kafaru ("perhaps those who disbelieved used to wish"), so it was omitted because kana is very frequently used after rubama. Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that this is not one of the places where kana is implied.

In Jam' al-Jawami' and its commentary, it is mentioned that ma is added after rubba, so the usual is the cessation of its governing, and its being followed by the past verb in that case, because

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

The particle *rubba* (a particle used for fewness or for multiplicity) indicates multiplicity or fewness only with what has a known limit, whereas the future is unknown, as in his saying:

*How often I have climbed a mountain-peak,*
*while the northern winds lift up my garment!*

It may be followed by the imperfect (present-tense verb), as in ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, the verse. It may also be followed by a nominal clause, as in: *Many a camel, the carefully tended herd among them...* It may also be used without being neutralised (kuffa), as in:

*Many a blow with a polished sword,*
*between Busra and a wide-gaping spear-thrust!*

It has been said: when it is neutralised (*kuffa*), a verbal clause must follow it. This is the view of al-Farisi, and the beginning of this line is taken as meaning that *ma* is an indefinite noun described by a clause whose subject has been omitted, i.e. "many a thing is the camel..." The verb after it may also be omitted, as in his saying:

*So he, if he meets adversity, meets it praised;*
*and if he is made rich one day, then often (he is...)*

It may also be joined by *ma* without being neutralised, as in his saying:

*O Mawiyya, how many a raid, fierce as a branding with the iron!*

End of quotation. Some scholars explained the verse in a manner similar to al-Farisi's interpretation of the line. They said: *ma* is an indefinite noun described by the clause *yawaddu* (wishes) to its end, the returning pronoun is omitted, and the verb governed by *rubba* is omitted, i.e. "many a thing which those who disbelieved wish for has come to pass and been established." A similar usage is the saying of Ibn Abi al-Salt:

*Often souls grieve at a matter*
*which holds a release like the untying of a tether.*

They insisted that the governed element is omitted, because in that case *rubba* cannot govern *yawaddu* and it needs a verb to govern, as several scholars have affirmed. As for the view preferred by al-Radi, that *rubba* is a subject with no predicate, and the meaning is "the wish of those who disbelieved is few or many," there is no need for it. This interpretation, according to al-Samarqandi, is one of the two opinions of the Basrans. Al-'Allama al-Taftazani criticised it, saying that its artificiality and cutting off of the noble text (i.e., cutting off ﴿if they had been Muslims﴾ from what precedes it) are not hidden. The artificiality is that the meaning would be "few or many is their wish," not "few or many is a thing," unless it is intended as "many a thing they wish for, insofar as they wish for it." My own preferred view is that of Abu Hayyan, and likewise that of the author of *al-Lubb*: that *rubba* enters on both the past and the present tense, though its entry on the past is more common. Whoever surveys the poetry of the Arabs will find examples of its entry on the present tense where it is far-fetched to resort to interpretation, as is not hidden from a fair and diligent reader.

They differed about its function here. A large group held that it is for fewness, and this is the apparent sense of most reports, since they indicate that their wish occurs when the disobedient Muslims leave Hell and remain in it. Yes, some claimed that the truth is that what is in those reports refers to the intensity of their wish at that time, and that the wish itself is not specific to one time rather than another, but is established and continuous at every moment that passes over them.

The rationale of al-Zamakhshari for using the particle of fewness on this view is that it follows the usage of the Arabs in their saying, "Perhaps you will regret your action," and "Often a person regrets what he did." They do not doubt his regret, nor do they intend to diminish it. Rather, they mean: if the regret were doubtful or few, it would be incumbent upon you not to do this act, because sensible people guard against exposure to a suspected harm just as they guard against exposure to a certain harm, and against a little of it just as against a lot. Likewise, the meaning in the verse is: if they wished for Islam only once, it would be fitting for them to hasten to it, so how much more so when they wish for it at every hour. End of quotation.

The discussion on this, according to what has been said, is of the allusive metonymy (*kinaya ima'iyya*), and there is in this much exaggeration, which is not hidden. Ibn al-Munayyir said: There is no doubt that the Arabs often express a meaning by something that conveys the opposite of what is intended. Among this, and Allah knows best, is ﴿And you certainly know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾. What is intended by it is rebuking them for their harm to Musa, peace be upon him, despite their abundant knowledge of his mission and his sincere advice to them. Likewise his saying: *I often leave the foe with fingertips yellowed,* where he praises himself for doing that often, yet he expressed it with *qad*, which indicates fewness. The scholars of rhetoric (*'ulama' al-bayan*) differed in explaining this. Some explained it by what was mentioned from al-Zamakhshari, namely alerting to the greater by means of the lesser. Others explained it by saying that the purpose of such expressions is to notify that the meaning has reached its extreme, to the point that it nearly returns to its opposite, and that is the nature of everything that reaches its limit: it turns into its reverse. Al-Mutanabbi clearly expressed this in his saying:

*You were so generous that you nearly became miserly,*
*an obstacle to the ultimate; and out of joy there is weeping.*

Both explanations bring the speech to exaggeration by a kind of alerting to it. The main thing in this is the context of the speech, because when it requires, for example, a multiplicity, and an expression is inserted into it whose apparent wording suggests fewness, the hearer is alerted, since the intended meaning is exaggeration by one of the two methods mentioned. In *al-Kashf*, it is said: The basis in this matter is that borrowing one of two opposites for the other produces exaggeration through inversion, and it is not restricted to mockery and wit, contrary to what the apparent wording of the author of *al-Miftah* in one place suggests. He is the one who counted *al-mafaza* (the desert) among this type for the purpose of seeking good omen. Then its position may be restricted to an additional benefit, as al-Zamakhshari mentioned in this context. There is no allusive metonymy in this; rather, that is one of the benefits of this metaphor. If Allah the Exalted wills, a more thorough discussion of it will come in surah al-Takwir. End of quotation.

The truth is that there is no obstacle to saying that it is allusive metonymy, as is not hidden.

It has been said: the fewness is relative to the time of their losing their minds from astonishment, meaning that the terrors of the Resurrection will astound them, so they will be bewildered. If they then regain some consciousness, they will wish for it. The apparent practice of al-'Allama al-Taftazani in *al-Mutawwal* is to prefer this view. It is also permitted that it be a metaphor for multiplicity. Saying it is a metaphor for multiplicity is not needed according to the view reported from the author of *al-'Ayn* and those with him, as you have heard. Ibn al-Hajib mentioned that it has been transferred from fewness to certainty, just as *qad*, when it enters on the present tense, is transferred from fewness to certainty.

The object of *yawaddu* (wishes) is omitted, i.e., Islam, as indicated by ﴿if they had been Muslims﴾, on the basis that *law* (if only) here expresses wishing, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), i.e., "saying: if only they had been Muslims." Estimating the object as we have mentioned is what many have gone to. Al-Shihab said: its estimate should be "salvation," and it is not appropriate to estimate "Islam," because then it would become "they wish Islam, if only they had been Muslims," which is superfluous (*hashw*). There is in this an issue.

The author of *al-Fara'id* said: "that if only they had been..." to the end is treated as in the position of the object. This was objected to, on the grounds that this is not apparent, since that is not among the things that govern clauses, unless it means "they mentioned the wish," and it runs in the manner of a saying according to the view of some grammarians. The reference in reporting their wishing is like the reference in your saying: "He swore by Allah the Exalted that he will surely do it." If you had said "I will surely do it," that would be permitted. On this basis came His saying ﴿They swore to one another by Allah: we will surely attack him by night﴾, read with the nun and with the ya'. The use of the third person is more common, lest it be confused. The reason given, that it is for the sake of brevity in estimation, is not valid, as al-Kashf revealed.

Some people denied that *law* comes for wishing, saying it is not a separate category by itself; rather, it is the conditional *law* which has absorbed the meaning of wishing. According to the first view, which is the more correct one, there is no answer (*jawab*) for it according to the more correct view. This is explicitly stated by Ibn al-Da'i'  and Ibn Hisham al-Khadrawi. The report that the two said it requires an answer like the answer of the conditional is an error (*sahw*). Abu Hayyan mentioned that what appears is that it must have an answer, but it is obligatory to omit it, because it has absorbed the meaning of wishing, since whenever it is possible to reduce the rules and to treat the matter as a figurative usage, that is preferable to multiplying the rules and claiming homonymy, because the latter requires two settings, whereas figurative usage involves only one setting, which is the literal meaning.

It has been said that here it is a conditional of impossibility (*imtina'iyya shartiyya*), and the answer is omitted; its estimate is "they would have succeeded," and the object of *yawaddu* is what you know. Some claimed that it is a verbal noun (*masdariyya*) when it comes after something indicating wishing, so the verbal noun then is the object. This is, on the view that *ma* is an indefinite noun described by a clause, a substitute (*badal*) for it, as in *al-Bahr*.

Asim and Nafi' read *rubama* with a light ba' (*rubama*). From Abu 'Amr, both the light and the heavy readings are reported. Talha ibn Musarrif and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read *rubbatama* with an added ta'. I have expanded on this verse at length, especially regarding what concerns *rubba*, because I once had a discussion on this matter with one of the eminent scholars, and he showed great ignorance and gross stupidity. By the Lord of the Ka'ba, I found him the most ignorant of all the young students I had seen regarding *rubba*. Yes, he has counterparts among the eminent scholars, may Allah make them deaf and blind to their own affairs, and reduce them, and I do not multiply their likes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 3:

﴿Leave them﴾ i.e., abandon them, and the imperative (dhar) has largely been dispensed with by its past tense (taraka), though the form dhar occurs rarely. In a hadith: "Leave the Abyssinians alone as long as they leave you alone."

The intended sense of the command is to let them be with their desires, since counsel and warning have not benefited them. It is as if it were said: "Leave them to themselves, ﴿that they may eat and enjoy themselves﴾ with their worldly life." The placing of eating first indicates that their enjoyment is only of the sort that cattle have in food and drink. The verb and what is conjoined to it are in the jussive mood as an answer to the imperative. In al-Kashshaf it is pointed out that the intended meaning is an emphasis on abandoning them, to the point that it is as if he, peace be upon him, was commanded to tell them things that would only increase their regret. The scrupulous scholar, the author of al-Kashf, supported this, saying: the command is intended in terms of meaning, because he made their eating and enjoyment the desired goal of the command to abandon them. Desired goals, if it is correct to command them, are themselves commanded by the very command, and more emphatic than its explicit form. So when you say, "Stick to the door of the scholar; learn from him what will save you in the Hereafter," it is more forceful than your saying, "Stick to him and learn," because you made the command a means to the second, so it is more strongly desired. If it is not correct, it is taken as commanded figuratively, like your saying, "Submit and you will enter Paradise." In our case, since the goal of the command was made so by way of figurative extension, it becomes commanded, as I have guided you to. End of quotation, and it is of great value. He thought that the understanding of the command comes from an implied lam before the verb, which is part of the command. As for what is in al-Bahr, that if ﴿leave them﴾ is taken as a command to abandon their counsel, and his, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, preoccupation with them, the answer does not follow from it, because they eat and enjoy themselves whether or not he abandons their counsel. This is a standing still on the shore of verification, as will not be hidden from one who has plunged into the depths of meanings and extracted the pearls of secrets. He also inferred that it is a command to abandon fighting them, leaving their path free, and making peace with them. Then he said: For this reason it is correct that what is mentioned is the answer, because if he, peace be upon him, had occupied them with fighting, the swinging of swords and the waging of wars, neither eating nor enjoyment would have been pleasant to them. This is shown by the fact that the surah is Meccan, and that is, as you see, far-fetched.

Then the intended meaning, as has been said, is their continuing in what they are upon, not the introduction of what has been mentioned, or their enjoyment without anything disturbing their life; and enjoyment in this manner is a newly arising matter which may be suitably ordered upon leaving them to their own affairs. So reflect.

﴿And hope diverts them﴾ and occupies them with expectation: for long life, the attainment of aims, the soundness of conditions, and that they will meet only good in the final outcome and end, away from faith and obedience, or away from reflecting on what they are coming to. ﴿But soon they will know﴾ the evil of their conduct when they witness its recompense and the gravity of its consequence, or the reality of the situation which compelled them to wishful thinking.

The apparent meaning of the words of most scholars is that this knowledge is in the Hereafter. It has been said: the intended meaning is that they will soon know the outcome of their affair in this world, of humiliation, killing and captivity, and in the Hereafter, of everlasting punishment. This, as has been said, together with being a threat, is the most extreme of threats and warnings following one another. It is a reason for the command to abandon them, and it contains the establishing of proof and emphasis in warning, since the command to the opposite is not realized, as you know, except after repeated warning and the establishment of denial and rejection. "Whoever warns has given excuse." Likewise what follows from it, namely eating and what comes after. In the verse there is an indication that luxury, indulgence, and lack of preparation for the Hereafter and readiness for it are not the character of one who seeks salvation. It is reported from al-Hasan: "No servant prolongs hope except that he worsens his deeds."

Page 10
Ahmad in az-Zuhd, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I do not know it except as a raised (marfu') report: The righteousness of the first of this Ummah is by asceticism and certainty, and its last will perish by stinginess and hope."

In some reports from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "I only fear for you two things: long hope and following desire, for long hope makes one forget the Hereafter, and following desire turns away from the truth."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 4:

﴿And We did not destroy any town﴾ — that is, any town of the towns, by sinking it along with its unbelieving inhabitants as was done to some of them, or by emptying it of its inhabitants after destroying them, as was done to others. ﴿Except that it had﴾ in that matter ﴿a decree﴾ — a fixed term, written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) — ﴿known﴾, not forgotten, nor neglected, such that deviation from it through advancing or delaying could be imagined. This begins his explanation of the secret of delaying their punishment.

(And "a decree") is a subject (mubtada'), its predicate being the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), and the clause is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "town" (qaryah). It is not necessary that it precede, since its referent is indefinite, because it occurs after a negation, and that justifies the coming of the circumstantial qualifier, since it has the sense of a descriptive adjective, especially as it has been reinforced by the particle "min". The meaning is: We did not destroy any town of the towns in any state except in the state that it has a known decree, so that We do not destroy it before its term arrives and We do not neglect it, so that its violation would be possible. Or it is in the nominative case by the adverbial phrase, and the clause, as it is, is also a circumstantial qualifier, i.e., We did not destroy any town of the towns in any state except that there was for its destruction a fixed term that is not neglected.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the clause is a descriptive attribute of "town" (qaryah), and by analogy the waw should not intervene between them, as in His Exalted words: ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners﴾. It has only intervened to emphasize the adherence of the attribute to the thing described, as one says of the circumstantial qualifier: "Zayd came to me, upon him a garment," and "Zayd came to me, and upon him a garment." Abu al-Baqa' agreed with him on this, and al-Bahr criticized him, saying: we do not know of anyone among the grammarians who said it, and it is based on the view that what follows "illa" may be a descriptive attribute, while al-Akhfash and al-Farisi explicitly prohibited that. Ibn Malik said: making what follows "illa" a descriptive attribute of what precedes it is a view not known to any Basran or Kufan, so it should not be heeded, and he refuted the claim that the waw intervened to emphasize adherence.

It is related from Mundhir ibn Sa'id that this waw is the one that indicates that the state following it, in utterance, is in time before the state preceding the waw. Among its examples is His Exalted words: ﴿until, when they came to it and its gates were opened﴾. Al-Sakkaki excused this by saying that it is an error, and there is no fault in it. The author of al-Kashf was not satisfied with this and defended al-Zamakhshari, saying: this meaning has recurred from them in this book, so there is no error, as the author of al-Miftah excused. And if the insertion of the waw is established, as the Kufans hold, and analogy does not reject it, because it is established in the circumstantial qualifier and in what the preposition governs after it, as in: "I sold the sheep, a ewe and a dirham," and "kam" and "kam," then this indicates that metaphor is widespread in the waw generically, indeed in kind, so we do not rely on the particular transmission, and it is not establishing language by analogy, since the transmission from the masters of Kufa is established and supported by analogy. The meaning is: it is not far from the author of al-Ma'ani to prefer the Kufan view when the context requires it, just as they preferred the Tamimi view over the Hijazi in the matter of exception according to him. There is no doubt that the meaning with the attributive reading is more eloquent, and that this attribute adheres more closely to the thing described than in His words: ﴿except that there were warners for it﴾, because it is a rational necessity, whereas that is a customary one, established by God's Exalted practice. End of quotation. In ad-Durr al-Masun it is stated that Ibn Jinni had preceded al-Zamakhshari to what he said, and that is a sufficient authority.

Some of the verifiers said: the thing described is not the town mentioned, but rather a hidden town that stands as a substitute (badal) for the one mentioned, according to the preferred view. Thus it is like the attribute being for it: "We did not destroy any town of the towns except a town for which there is a known decree," as in His Exalted words: ﴿They have no food except from thorny plants (dari')﴾ ﴿which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾, for ﴿which neither nourishes﴾ and so on is a descriptive attribute, but not of the food mentioned, because it would only indicate that their food, which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger, is restricted to dari'; and that is not the intended meaning. Rather, it is for a food assumed after "illa," i.e., they have no food of any kind except food which neither nourishes, etc. So there is no separation between the described and the descriptor by "illa." As for the insertion of the waw, although analogy requires its absence, it is to signal the completeness of connection. End of quotation. It should not be concealed that he has not brought anything regarding the matter of the insertion that would ward off dispute and debate. What he mentioned about estimating the described thing after "illa" does answer the objection of separation. However, Abu Hayyan related from al-Akhfash that after prohibiting separation between the attribute and the described thing by "illa", he said: and like "ma ja'ani rajul illa rakib," its estimate is "illa rajul rakib," and in it there is ugliness, because you make the attribute like the noun; and perhaps the answer to this is easy.

Ibn Abi Abla read (illa laha) with the waw dropped, and this, it is said, supports the view that it is an insertion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 5:

When Glorified is He had explained that the nations that were destroyed, and for each of them and for others as well, there is a decreed term (kitab) that cannot be advanced or delayed, He, Mighty is He and Speaking, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term﴾ from among the destroyed nations and others. Here "min" (from) is extra (mazīdah), for the sake of comprehensiveness (istighrāq). It has been said that it is for partiality (tab'īd), but that is not the case. ﴿its term﴾ is what is written in its record (kitab), meaning its destruction does not come before the coming of its record, or no nation passes away before its appointed term passes. For "sabq" (outstripping), as al-Imam reported from al-Khalil, when it is applied to time, its meaning is passing beyond and leaving behind. So when you say "Zayd outstripped ʿAmr," it means that he passed beyond him and left him behind, and that ʿAmr fell short of him and did not reach him. When it is applied to a point in time, it is the reverse of that: when you say "So-and-so outstripped the year such-and-such," its meaning is that he passed away before its arrival and did not reach it. The secret of this, according to what is in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Suud's commentary), is that time is considered with respect to motion and direction, so what precedes it is realized before its realization. As for the temporal thing (zamani), what is considered in it is motion and direction toward what will come of time. Thus the one who outstrips is the one who got ahead toward the goal. Its being mentioned under the heading of "term" is in view of what it requires of outstripping, just as its being mentioned under the heading of "record" is in view of what it necessitates of destruction. ﴿Nor can they delay﴾, meaning, nor can they lag behind.

The form of the verb (istif'āl, as in yasta'khirūn) indicates their inability to do that despite their seeking it. The choice of the present tense (muḍāriʿ) for the two verbs after the mention of the destruction in the past tense (māḍī) is because the purpose is to explain the continuance of these two (outstripping and delaying) among past and remaining nations, and the Noble Book has parallels to this. Attributing these two to the nation after attributing the destruction to the town is because outstripping and lagging is the condition of the nation without the town, along with the generality of the nation for the people of those towns and others whose punishments were postponed until the Hereafter. The negation of their outstripping is mentioned in a context of emphasis on the certainty of their punishment, either in view of the precedence of outstripping in existence, or in view of the fact that the aim is to explain the secret of delaying their punishment despite their deserving it. The verb is given in the masculine plural form out of regard for the meaning of (ummah) together with the predominance of the masculine, just as its wording was observed first, along with regard for the rhyme (fawasil). For this reason the prepositional phrase is omitted, and the sentence clarifies what preceded it, and for this reason it is separated. The meaning is that the delay of their punishment until the Day of Ambiguity (or Day of Affection, yawm al-widad), as indicated, is only for the delay of their appointed term, determined according to what it requires of wisdoms. Among the parts of that is what God Most High knew of the faith of some who will emerge from among them, as stated by Shaykh al-Islam. He used the verse as evidence that everyone who dies or is killed, it is only by his term that he dies, and al-Imam has clarified this.

**[Page 12]**

﴿And they say﴾: this begins the explanation of their disbelief in the one to whom the Book was revealed, which includes their denial of it and a statement of what their condition will lead to. The speakers are the people of Makkah. Muqatil said: the verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Umayyah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. They are the ones who said to him (ﷺ): ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed﴾, meaning the Qur'an. They addressed him, upon him be blessings and peace, in this way, although they were disbelievers who did not believe that anything was revealed, out of mockery, derision, and to indicate the falsehood of their own claim: ﴿Indeed, you are a madman﴾. They mean: O you who claims such a great matter that breaks the normal course of things, by this claim your madness is established in the most complete form. This is like a man saying to someone who hears from him a statement he finds unlikely: "You are mad." It was also said that their statement was due to what appeared in him, upon him be blessings and peace, of a state resembling a swoon (al-ghashy) when the revelation of the Qur'an came down upon him. The first explanation, as it has been said, is the more suitable to the context. Some scholars held that what is spoken is only the emphatic clause, not the address; the address, however, is part of the speech of Allah the Exalted, to absolve him, upon him be blessings and peace, of what they attributed to him from the very beginning. This has been objected to on the ground that it does not fit the word of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾, etc., since, as will come, God willing, it is a rebuttal of their denial and mockery. It may be answered that on this view that verse is a rebuttal of what they meant implicitly within their stated words. However, the apparent meaning is that the whole is their speech.

Pharaoh, may the curse of Allah be upon him, preceded them in a similar statement, saying concerning Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾. The placing of the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur) before the deputy of the agent (nāʾib al-fāʿil, the grammatical substitute for the subject in the passive) is, as has been said, because their denial is directed at the revealed matter being a Reminder from Allah the Exalted, not at the one upon whom it was revealed being the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), after accepting that what descended was from Him, the Exalted. This is as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ For there the denial is directed at the one upon whom it was revealed being the Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace.

The use of the verb in the passive form (ṣīghat al-majhūl) is to create the impression that this is not an action that has an agent, or to direct the denial at the revelation descending upon him rather than at its being attributed to an agent. Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read *nazala ʿalayhi al-dhikr* with the verb lightened (*nazala* instead of *nuzzila*) in the active voice, and *al-dhikr* in the nominative as the agent. It is also read: *Yā ayyuhā alladhī ulqiya ʿalayhi al-dhikr* (O you upon whom the Reminder has been cast). Abu Hayyan said: this reading should be taken as an explanation, since it differs from the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-Mushaf, the written consonantal text).

**"Law ma ta'tinaa"** (لَوْ ما تَأْتِينا): The word **(لَوْما)**, like **(لَوْلا)**, is used in one of two meanings: (1) the prevention of something due to the existence of something else, or (2) reproach (*takhdid*, urging or rebuke). When the second meaning is intended, it is followed only by a verb, either explicit or implied. When the first meaning is intended, it is followed only by a noun, either explicit or implied in the view of the **Basrans** (the grammarians of Basra).

Among the examples is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

*Lawma al-haya' wa lawma al-din 'ibtukuma bi-ba'di ma fikuma idh 'ibtuma 'awari*

("Were it not for shame and were it not for religion, I would have blamed you both for some of what is in you, since you blamed me for my faults.")

Some scholars hold that the **mim** in **(lawma)** is a substitute for the **lam** in **(lawla)**. Similar examples are *istawla* and *istawma* (both meaning "to overcome"), and *khalaltuhu* and *khalamtuhu*, so that *fa-huwa khilli* and *khilmi* mean "he is my friend." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that **law** is combined with **la** and **ma** for two meanings, while **hal** is combined only with **la** alone for *tahdid*. Abu Hayyan preferred simplicity (*al-basatah*, i.e., treating them as simple, uncompounded particles) in both cases and held that the **mim** is not a substitute for the **lam**. Al-Maliqi said that **(law ma)** occurs only for *tahdid*, but this is refuted by the preceding verse of poetry. Whatever the case, the meaning here is *tahdid*, i.e., "Why do you not bring to us **﴿the angels﴾** who would bear witness for you and support you in warning (the people)," as in His saying, relating their words: ﴿Why has no angel been sent down to him so that he might be a warner along with him?﴾ (25:7). Or (the meaning is) that they would punish you for denying (us), as the angels used to come to the nations who denied their messengers.

**﴿if you are of the truthful﴾** in your claim that God's power to do this is beyond doubt, and likewise that you need them to carry out your mission, since we would not believe you in this grave matter without them. Or (the meaning is): if you are among those truthful messengers whose denying nations were punished.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 8:

﴿Why do We not send down the angels?﴾ With the nun (ن), on the basis that the verb is built for the divine pronoun (ḍamīr al-jalāla) from tanzīl (sending down). This is the reading of Ḥafṣ, al-Akhawān (Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī), and Ibn Muṣarrif. Abū Bakr, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read (tunazzalu l-malā'ikatu) with a ḍamma on the tā' and a fatḥa on the nūn and zāy, in the passive voice (mabnīyan lil-maf'ūl), with al-malā'ikatu in the nominative as the deputy of the subject (al-niyāba ʿan al-fā'il). The two Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ) and the rest of the Seven read (tanazzalu l-malā'ikatu) with a fatḥa on the tā' and zāy, the original being (tatanazzalu) with two tā's, one of which was dropped for lightness (takhfīfan), with al-malā'ikatu in the nominative as the subject (al-fā'iliyya). Keeping the verb on its apparent meaning is preferable to making it mean the triliteral tanzil (tanzil al-thulāthī). Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read (mā nazala), in the past tense, lightened, in the active voice, with al-malā'ikatu in the nominative as the subject. Al-Bayḍāwī built his commentary on the reading of the verb as (yunazzilu) with a yāʾ at the beginning, in the active voice, its subject being the pronoun of Allah, exalted is He, and (wal-malā'ikata) in the accusative as its object. It was objected to him that none of the ten readers read this way, nor is this reading found even among the irregular readings (al-shawādh), and this contradicts what he followed in his commentary; perhaps may Allah have mercy on him, he erred. This statement comes from Him, glorified is He, addressed to His Prophet ﷺ as a reply to them concerning their spoken claim and a rejection of their false suggestion, which issued from pure partisanship and obstinacy; and because of the great need for a response to this, its rebuttal was placed before what is the answer to its first part, namely,

[Page 13]

His words, may He be glorified: ﴿Indeed, it is We who send down⦈ etc. The deviation from the expected form of their speech, which would have been a request such as "what do you bring them with?", signifies that they have erred in their proposal. It also indicates that the angels, because of their lofty rank, are too exalted to be described by mere "coming," which includes moving from one of two equal places to another, but rather that the fitting description for them is descent from their exalted station, and that this descent occurs by way of sending down from the presence of the Lord, the Majestic. So said Shaykh al-Islam.

It has been said: perhaps this is an answer to what might occur to the noble mind of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, when they asked him to bring the angels, namely a question about sending down out of desire for their Islam. In that case the reason for mentioning "sending down" would be apparent, though it is not apparent, as is not hidden.

﴿Except with truth⦈, i.e., except a sending down accompanied by the aspect which wisdom requires. The bāʾ (ب) here denotes accompaniment (mulābasah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of an adjective to a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar); it is an exception of the type called istithnāʾ mufarragh (exception from an unspecified general context). It was also permitted to treat it as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to either the subject or the object. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the bāʾ denotes causation, connected to nunazzil (we send down), and to this view Ibn ʿAtiyya's statement below points, God willing. The first is preferable. According to what has been said, the requirement of legislative and creational wisdom is that the angels who are sent down should appear in human form; but sending them down in that manner would cause confusion, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them about what they are confusing⦈. This is an indication of the negation of the purpose being achieved and of the absence of benefit in that. His words, the Exalted: ﴿And they would not have been given respite⦈ indicate the occurrence of harm and the realization of the opposite of what is sought. It seems to be coordinated (ʿaṭf) with an implied element required by the preceding discourse, as if it were said: We do not send down the angels to them except in the forms of men, because that is what wisdom requires, so confusion occurs and they do not benefit. And if We had sent them down, they would not have been given respite, i.e., they would be harmed by their descent, because We would destroy them without fail and not delay them, since Our custom with the nations before them has been that whenever We brought them a sign they proposed, the punishment followed it if they did not believe, and We knew this about them. The intent is to negate that their proposal to bring the angels has any proper basis, by indicating that it would not benefit them at first and by stating explicitly that it would harm them afterward. It has also been said that the coordinated element is implied as "they will not believe," as if it were said: We do not send down the angels except in the forms of men, because wisdom requires that; so they do not believe, and they would not have been given respite. There is something in the soul concerning this and what precedes it.

Some of the verifiers said: the meaning is, We do not send down the angels except accompanied by the aspect which makes the sending down fitting, of what wisdom requires and divine custom follows. What they proposed, sending down for the sake of testifying before them, while they themselves and their status in reality are such that it hardly falls within soundness and wisdom at all. For that kind of sending down belongs to the category of revelation, which is hardly granted except to the noble prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, and to some individuals among all believers. How then could it be granted to such ignoble disbelievers? What does fall within wisdom in their case, in general, is sending down for punishment and annihilation, as was done to their counterparts among the earlier nations. And if that were done, they would be utterly uprooted and would not be delayed, as was the practice with all the denying, mocking nations. Yet despite their deserving that, the pen of decree has run to postpone their punishment until the Day of Resurrection, as summarized in the verses before. And the barrier of wisdom has stood between them and their annihilation, because knowledge is connected to their increase in punishment and to the faith of some of their descendants. Placing the faith of some of them within the thread of wisdom is refused by their persistence in disbelief and obstinacy. So ﴿they would not⦈ etc. is the answer to an implied condition, i.e., "and if We had sent them down, they would not⦈ etc.

It has been objected that what better fits His words, ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man⦈, is that the aspect which makes sending down fitting for a purpose like theirs is that they appear in the forms of men. But that is not part of sending down by revelation, which hardly applies to them at all, so his statement is not complete. There is discussion in this, as is not hidden. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Mujahid that the truth here is interpreted as messengership and punishment. The verse was given a reading along the lines of this interpretation, and it was said: the meaning is, We do not send down the angels except with messengership and punishment; and if We had sent them down to them, they would not have been given respite, because sending them down with messengership is hardly applicable to them, so it is necessarily sending down with punishment. Al-Mawardi mentioned restricting it to messengership. It was narrated from al-Hasan that it is restricted to punishment. In the same sense is what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: that the meaning is, We do not send down the angels except with the truth which is death, in which there is no advancing or delay.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the truth is what is required and what is due of revelation and the benefits which God the Exalted intends for His servants. The meaning is: We do not send down the angels except with a due truth of revelation and benefit, not in response to your proposal. Also, if We sent them down, you would not be given respite after that with punishment, because Our custom is to destroy the nations that propose, once We bring them what they proposed. In this there is what there is.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is, except a descent accompanied by wisdom and benefit; and there is no wisdom in their coming to you in plain sight, which you witness and which bears witness for you to the truth of the Prophet ﷺ, because at that point you would be believers out of compulsion. This is based on the premise that sending down is in their true forms, and from this the author of the aforementioned saying first took his view. Al-Baydawi made what contradicts wisdom the sending down of them in the forms of men, saying: there is no wisdom in their coming to you in forms you witness, for it would only increase you in confusion.

Some said: what is intended is that the sending down of the angels occurs only with truth and with the attainment of benefit by their sending down; and God the Exalted knew from the state of these disbelievers that if He sent the angels down to them, they would remain persistent in their disbelief, so their sending down would be in vain and false and not true. Some of the verifiers pursued the three views by saying that, even with the failure of each of these in its terrible consequence, it does not follow from supposing that any of these occurred that punishment is hastened, which is what His words, the Exalted, ﴿And they would not have been given respite⦈ indicate. Some people went to great lengths to justify the necessity in some of these views. Some preferred that the intended meaning of the truth is destruction, and the sentence after it is an answer to an implied question: as if it were said, "We do not send down the angels except with destruction, since that is what is due to such stubborn people," and it was said, "Let it be so." It was then answered that if We did that, they would not have been given respite, i.e., while they had been given respite, as was summarized earlier in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves and let hope distract them; they will soon know⦈. The essence of the answer then, as it has been said, is that what they asked for, bringing the angels so that they might bear witness to the truth of the Prophet ﷺ, is not something that will be granted to them, because what Our wisdom requires and Our custom has followed with people like them is nothing but sending down for destruction, not for witnessing, for wisdom does not require it and custom has not followed it in that. For if the angels were in their true forms, faith in the unseen would not occur and choice, which is the basis of obligation, would not be realized; and if they were in human form, confusion would occur, so its existence would be like its non-existence, and infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow. And it is prevented from sending down with destruction, as was done with their counterparts among the obstinate, since We have made them respited. So if We sent down the angels and destroyed them, that would return as a contradiction to what We have decreed, according to what We know of the wisdoms in it.

It has also been said, regarding the interpretation of the verse on the assumption that their proposal was for bringing the angels to punish them: the meaning is, We do not send down the angels for punishment except with a sending down accompanied by what wisdom requires; and if We had sent them down as they proposed, that would not be accompanied by what it requires, because wisdom required postponing their punishment until the Day of Resurrection. And since attributing the sending down of them for punishment to a lack of agreement with wisdom carries some implication that they did not deserve punishment, He turned away from what the apparent wording would require to what the noble text stands upon. So it is as if it were said: if We sent them down, they would not have been given respite, and that is not in accordance with wisdom. So reflect upon all of that, and may God the Exalted take charge of your guidance.

This is the word ﴿idhan⦈ (إذًا). In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is a response and a conditional consequence, because the speech is a response to them and a consequent to an implied condition, i.e., "and if We had sent down⦈. Sibawayh explicitly stated that it has this meaning. However, al-Shalawbin took that to mean constancy and strained to justify it, while Abu ʿAli took it to mean the usual case, and it may become purely responsive according to him. It is a simple particle according to the majority of grammarians. Some people held that it is a noun of time, its original form being the temporal idhā, to which tanwīn was attached as a substitute for the sentence it is annexed to, and it was transferred to the conditional function, so the sense of connection and causation remained in it. Al-Khalil held that it is a particle composed of idh and in, and the particle's rule came to predominate over it; the hamza's vowel was transferred to the dhāl and then the hamza was deleted, and this transfer was made obligatory, so the meaning is: if the speaker says, "I will visit you," and you say, "idhan, I will visit you," I say: my visiting then is established. This is not said in this way.

Abu ʿAli ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Majid al-Zaydi went to the view that it (idhan) is compounded of idha and in, and that both together give what each of them gives individually: so it gives the connective force of idha and the accusative force of in. Then the hamza of in was deleted, then the alif of idha was deleted to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. Apparently, if a condition were implied in the sentence, it would be merely for emphasis. They cited as an example of this the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾ etc. It is reported from al-Kafiyaji that he said in such cases: "idhan here is not the well-known word; rather it is the conditional idha, whose clause that it is attached to has been deleted, and tanwin has been substituted for it, as in yawmi'idhin (on that day)." He had a precedent in this, for al-Zarkashi said in al-Burhan, after mentioning it: "idha has two meanings." Some later scholars added a third meaning for it, namely that it is compounded of idha, which is a adverb of past time, and a clause following it, actually or implicitly, but it was deleted for lightness and tanwin was substituted for it, as in their saying hinaʾidhin (at that time). This is not the one that puts the imperfect into the subjunctive, because that one is specific to the imperfect, whereas this one is not; rather it enters upon the past, as in ﴿idhan la-amsaktum﴾ ("then you would have held back"), and upon the noun, as in ﴿wa-innakum idhan la-min al-muqarrabin﴾ ("and indeed you would then be among those brought near"). Then he said: "The grammarians have not mentioned this meaning, but it is analogous to what they said about idhh." In al-Tadhkira of Abu Hayyan, it is mentioned to me by ʿAlam al-Din that the judge Taqi al-Din ibn Razin used to hold that the tanwin of idhan is a substitute for the deleted clause, and that this is not the view of a grammarian. Al-Juwayni said: "I think it is permissible that you say to someone who says, 'I will come to you then (idhan)': 'I will honour you' with the raf', meaning 'if you come to me, I will honour you', so the clause 'you come to me' was deleted, tanwin was substituted, and the alif fell away to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. The naṣb on which the grammarians agreed is for putting it to a meaning other than this one, and that does not negate the raf' when this meaning is intended." Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti mentioned that the consensus in the Qur'an on writing it with an alif and pausing on it is evidence that it is a tanwinned noun and not a particle whose last letter is a nun, especially when it does not serve as a naṣb-particle for the imperfect. So the correct view is to affirm this meaning for it, as our shaykh al-Kafiyaji and those before him from whom it was transmitted inclined to. On this basis, it is better to read it in the verse according to what has been mentioned. We mentioned some of this discussion earlier, so recall it. Then, He the Exalted refuted their denial of the revelation and their mockery of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and consoled him
صفحة 16
(peace be upon him) with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder﴾, meaning: We, by the greatness of Our majesty and the loftiness of Our side, sent down that which they denied, and denied its descent upon you, and said about you what they said because of your claim to it, and We made it its sender, since the verb was constructed in the passive, as a hint that it is a matter with no source and an act with no doer. ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾, meaning: from everything that would harm it, such as distortion, addition, omission, and other things, to the extent that if a dignified shaykh changed a single dot, the children would correct him and say: "The correct reading is such-and-such." This includes the mockery of those mockers and their denial of it, as a primary inclusion. The meaning of its being guarded from that is that it is not affected by it and that it is protected from it. Al-Hasan said: its guarding is by preserving its law until the Day of Resurrection. More than one scholar permitted that its guarding be understood as its inimitability at every time, as the nominal sentence indicates, guarding it from every addition, omission, distortion and alteration. Allah the Exalted did not preserve any other book in this way; rather He entrusted the guarding of the earlier books to the rabbis and scholars, and so what happened to them happened. He Himself undertook the guarding of the Qur'an, so it has remained guarded, first and last. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to this in al-Kashshaf, then asked, in substance, that since the speech was directed at refuting them, and the answer was complete with the first part, what is the benefit of the appended second part? It is only fitting if the speech was aimed at establishing the guarding of the Reminder, first and last. He answered that it was introduced for a sound purpose, and the meaning mentioned was incorporated into it. As for whether it is evidence that it was sent down from Allah the Exalted as a sign, the first part, although it is a refutation, would be like a mere claim; so it was said: "Were it not that the Reminder is from Us, it would not have remained guarded against addition and omission, as other speech is not, because its composition, being inimitable, cannot admit any addition or any omission without impairing its inimitability," as stated in al-Kashf. In this there is an indication of the reason for the conjunction, which is evident.

You know that inimitability is not a cause of its being preserved against the dropping of some surahs, because that does not impair inimitability, as is clear. Rather the preferred view is that the preservation of the Qur'an and its continuance as it was revealed, until the command of Allah the Exalted comes with inimitability and other things that Allah, mighty and majestic, wills. Among that is the success of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, in collecting it, as you learned at the beginning of the book. The judge cited the verse to refute the view of some of the Imamiyya, who are of no account, that the Qur'an has been subject to addition and omission. Al-Imam refuted this by saying that it amounts to establishing a thing by itself, since those who hold that could say: this verse is among the additions, and the claim of inimitability in this amount needs a proof. Those who hold that the verbal speech is created also cited it, and it is evident in that. It is strange what he transmitted from his companions when he said: "Our companions said regarding this verse that it is evidence that the basmala is a verse of every surah, because Allah the Exalted promised to guard the Qur'an, and guarding has no meaning except that it remain protected from addition and omission. So if the basmala were not a verse of the Qur'an, it would not be protected from alteration nor guarded from addition. And if it were possible to suspect the Companions of adding, it would be possible to suspect them of omitting, and that would remove the Qur'an from being a proof." By my life, calling such a thing "nonsense" is more fitting than calling it "argument." Nor is hidden the eloquence in the composition of the two sentences, indicating the perfection of majesty and grandeur and the magnificence of the revelation's status; both contain several forms of emphasis. ("Nahnu") is not a pronoun of separation, since it did not occur between two nouns; rather it is either a subject or an emphasis for the subject of inna. From what we have established it is known that the pronoun in ("lahu") refers to the Reminder, and this is the view of Mujahid, Qatada and most scholars, and it is the evident one. Al-Farra' permitted, and a few adopted, that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: "And indeed We are guardians for the Prophet to whom the Reminder was sent, from the scheming of the mockers," like His saying: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. The reliance, however, is on the first. This answer was delayed, although it is a refutation of the beginning of their false speech, for the reason we pointed out earlier, and for its connection with what follows it from His saying, the Exalted:

صفحة 17

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, We sent﴾ i.e., messengers, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas. It was not mentioned because the indication of it is evident. ﴿before you﴾ is connected either to "sent" or to a deleted element that occurs as a qualifier (naʿt) of its deleted object, i.e., messengers existing before you. ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ i.e., their groups, as al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said, and al-Zajjaj went to this view. Wa-kadha (and likewise) ashyaʿ is the plural of shiʿah, and firqah (group) is a company agreed upon a path and a creed, derived from shaʿa (transitive) meaning "followed," because some of them follow and pursue others. The term shiʿah is also applied to helpers and supporters. The origin of this, as has been said, is from al-shiyaʿ (with kasra and fatha), the small pieces of firewood with which larger ones are kindled.
