The connection to the second usage is clear, and to the first usage is that the follower, insofar as he is a follower, is lesser than the one he follows. Its idafah (construct) to "the former" is, according to al-Farra, an idafah of the described to its descriptor, and according to the Basrans, a deletion of the described, i.e., the sects of the former nations. The prepositional phrase is connected to "sent."

The meaning of sending messengers into the sects is making each of them a messenger among a group of them, so that they follow him in everything he brings and leaves of the matters of the religion. It seems that if it were said "ila" (to) in place of "fi" (in), the intention of this meaning would not be apparent. It has been said: he deviated from ʿan (from) to ila (to) only to inform of greater establishment. Some have claimed that the prepositional phrase is connected to a deleted element that is a qualifier of the implied object or a circumstantial clause, but its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 11:

﴿Never came to them a messenger﴾ is a narration of a past state, as al-Zamakhshari said, because mā (ما) does not enter upon an imperfect verb except that it is in the position of the state (ḥāl), nor upon a perfect verb except that it is close to the state (ḥāl). This is the view of most scholars. Some of them said: the more common usage is that mā enters upon the imperfect verb with the meaning of the present (ḥāl), and it may also enter upon it with the meaning of the future (istiqbāl). He cited the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

My sons perished and left me with grief at bedtime and a tear that does not cease.

And the verse of al-A'sha praising the Prophet (ﷺ):

He has gifts whose bounty never ceases, and today's giving does not prevent him from giving tomorrow.

And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for me that I should change it of my own accord﴾. Perhaps this is the preferred view, although mā here is for narration. The intended meaning is the negation of each messenger coming to his own particular group, not the negation of every messenger coming to each of those groups all together, or in turn; that is, no messenger came to a group from among those groups who was specifically sent to it. ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾, as these disbelievers do. The clause, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is in the accusative position as a state (ḥāl) of the pronoun of the object in ya'tihim, if by "coming" is meant its occurrence; or in the nominative or genitive position as an attribute of "messenger" according to its wording or its position, since it is the subject. It has been objected to making it an attribute according to its wording, that it would lead to an additional min of universal negation in an affirmative context because of illa (إلا), and to the estimation of the governing element for the attribute after it. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative as an exception, although the preferred reading is the nominative as a substitute. This, as you see, is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that this is the manner of the ignorant nations toward the messengers (peace be upon them) before him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 12:

Since the Messenger was accompanied by a Book from Allah, the Exalted, the mention of their mockery of the Messenger included their mockery of the Book. For this reason, He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like the threading that We threaded into the hearts of those mockers of their messengers and of what they brought, ﴿We cause it to enter﴾, i.e., We make it enter. It is said: "I threaded (salaktu) the thread into the needle, and the spear into the one who was stabbed," meaning: I caused to enter. It has been read as (naslukuhu), as "salaka," and as "aslaka," with one meaning, as Abu 'Ubayda mentioned. The pronoun, according to a group, including al-Hasan, as reported by al-Ghaznawi, refers to the Reminder (al-dhikr), ﴿into the hearts of the criminals﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah, or the category of criminals, so that they enter into it primarily. The sense of likeness is that its being accompanied by mockery is unacceptable, given what wisdom requires. The summary of this is that He, exalted is He, casts the Qur'an into the hearts of the criminals while it is mocked and not accepted, because they are among the forsaken, having no entitlement to accept the truth, just as He, glorified be He, cast the books of the Messengers, peace be upon them, into the hearts of their factions, mocked and not accepted for that reason. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is because the thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihi) is prior in existence, namely the threading that occurred among the factions of the earlier peoples.

﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ *They do not believe in it.* The pronoun refers to the Reminder (*al-dhikr*) as well. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) relating to the object of ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ *We cause it to enter*, meaning: not believing in it. This clause is either a past-tense circumstance (*muqaddarah*) or a simultaneous one (*muqaranah*), in the sense that disbelief follows the sending-in immediately without any pause, so the two occur at one time by customary usage. It is also possible that the clause is an explanation (*bayan*) of the preceding clause, in which case it has no grammatical place (*mahall min al-i'rab*). In *al-Kashf* (Zamakhshari's commentary), it is said: "This is the more apt view, because the method of obscurity followed by explanation, especially in this context, enhances the position of the speech." In *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), it is stated that the pronoun in ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ has been made to refer to the mockery (*al-istihza'*) understood from ﴿يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ *they mock*, so the explanatory reading is fixed, unless the pronoun in (*bihi*) is also made to refer to it, with the *ba'* (preposition) being of accompaniment (*li'l-mulabasah*), meaning: the mockery enters their hearts while they are not believers, by way of the mockery's accompaniment. Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn 'Atiyyah al-Andalusi) has also gone to the permissibility of returning both pronouns to the mockery, except that he made the *ba'* causal (*li'l-sababiyyah*). So too did al-Fadil al-Jalabi. It is not hidden that, after this, the refutation is unnecessary. Al-Baydawi went to the view that the first pronoun refers to the mockery and the pronoun in (*bihi*) refers to the Reminder. Distinguishing between successive pronouns that refer to different things, when the evidence indicates it, is not an innovation in the Qur'an. On this basis, it is also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial phrase relating to (*al-mujrimin*) *the guilty*, and it is not required that it be a circumstance of the pronoun, so that its reference to the Reminder becomes necessary. It has been mentioned that its referring back to the mockery does not contradict its being explanatory; rather, it strengthens it, since non-belief in the Reminder is more fitting to the entrenchment of mockery in their hearts. Taking the verse as evidence that God creates falsehood in their hearts contains a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) in their saying that this is ugly and therefore cannot proceed from Him, glory be to Him. It seems that God have mercy on him (Alusi) thought that what al-Zamakhshari did, in making both pronouns refer to the Reminder, was out of regard for his school, so he did what he did. It is not hidden that he did not hit the mark, and he overlooked their saying: "When evidence is subject to possibility, the argument based on it is invalidated."

In *al-Kashf*, after a discussion, it is said that the return of the pronoun to the mockery or to disbelief, along with what it contains of disharmony in the structure of the text, is not denied by the Mu'tazilah except as one denies the causing of the Reminder to enter in the attribute of denial and interpretation, as in interpretation. It seems they overlooked what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned in *al-Shu'ara'* (the chapter of the Poets), where he answered the question of ascribing the causing-to-enter of the Reminder with that attribute to Himself, exalted is He, by saying that what is meant is that it is firmly fixed in their hearts as something denied, to the utmost degree of firmness, like something they were created with. The meaning here is summarized as: He casts it into their hearts as something denied, not that the denial is His act, glory be to Him.

Yes, Ibn Abi Hatim related from Anas and al-Hasan the interpretation of the pronoun in ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ as referring to *shirk* (association of partners with God). He and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd that he said about the verse: "They are as God the Exalted said: He has led them astray and prevented them from faith. But this is a matter, and what we are discussing is another."

Some objected to the pronoun's referring to (*al-dhikr*) the Reminder on the grounds that the *nun* of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*, the plural of majesty) is not suitable for that, since it is only fitting when the act of the one who is magnified is his own act, one whose effect appears strongly, and this is not the case here, for it is contested and disputed. The answer was that when the context is one of rebuke, it is fitting, and it does not follow that the majesty must be in terms of domination and overpowering; it may be in terms of gentleness and kindness. Al-Shihab (Shihab al-Din al-Khafaji) followed up on that by saying: "It is not hidden that in terms of domination and overpowering, it requires that this have an effect on their hearts, and that is not the case because of their non-belief in it. Likewise, in terms of gentleness and kindness, it requires that their being made to enter it into their hearts be a favour upon them. So what favour is it upon them that entails anger? Hence there is no basis for what was mentioned." You know that when what is meant is causing it to enter and establishing it in their hearts as something denied, that is unacceptable; so the attribution being in terms of domination and overpowering is something over which two rams should not butt heads. The clear and strong effect of this is their persistence in disbelief and their insistence on error, even if every sign came to them. It is not hidden what there is in (*kadhalika*) *thus* that suits the *nun* of majesty as well, and this has been pointed out more than once.

(*Qad khalat*) *Has passed away*: (*sunnat*) *the way* of (*al-awwalin*) *the former peoples*. The intended meaning is God's customary practice (*'adatullah*) with them, while the attribution is for the slightest connection, not in the sense that the attribution has the meaning of *fi* (in). The intended meaning of that custom, on the assumption that the pronoun in ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ refers to the mockery, is abandonment (*al-khudhlan*) and causing disbelief and mockery to enter their hearts: that His custom, glory be to Him and exalted is He, with the former peoples to whom He sent messengers, peace be upon them, was that He abandons them and causes disbelief and mockery to enter their hearts. On the assumption that the pronoun refers to the Reminder, the intended meaning is destruction. In line with this is al-Zamakhshari's statement: that is, their way which God established in their destruction when they denied His messengers and what was revealed to them. He mentioned that it is a warning to the people of Makkah for their denial. The first view was taken by al-Zajjaj. The Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) claimed that it is the most fitting to the outward meaning of the wording, and al-Tibi explained that, saying: "The definite article in (*al-mujrimin*) *the guilty* is for prior reference (*al-'ahd*), and what is meant by them are the deniers from among the people of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because they are those mentioned after the illustration of that causing-to-enter which We caused to enter into the hearts of those mockers who denied the earlier messengers; We cause it to enter into the hearts of these guilty ones. So you have a model in the earlier messengers with their denying peoples, and you are not unique in that, and the way of the former peoples has passed. The context requires confirmation and emphasis, so there is in this additional consolation for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. The warning is far-fetched, because no mention of the destruction of the nations has preceded it, and the choice of this is because it is closer to the Mu'tazilite school." (End of quotation.) In this there is an oversight of al-Zamakhshari's purpose, and the author of *al-Kashf* perceived this. God gives him good reward for what he said: "He meant that the position of (*qad khalat*) *has passed away* to its end is the position of the goal in *al-Shu'ara'*, namely His saying, exalted is He, there: ﴿حَتّى يَرَوُا الْعَذابَ الْأَلِيمَ﴾ *until they see the painful punishment*. For when they were compared to them, it was said: *They do not believe*, and those before them were destroyed without believing, so likewise these." From this it appears that the discourse on this view is highly coherent. As for the claim that the warning is far-fetched because no mention of the destruction of the nations has preceded, there is in it that the word *sunnah* (way), when attributed to what it is attributed to, indicates that most clearly. Furthermore, the intended purpose is not the warning as we have established. Some eminent scholars have also stated explicitly that the clause is a new independent sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), brought as a completion of the consolation and as an explicit mention of warning and threat. Furthermore, what al-Zamakhshari took as the meaning of *sunnah* is related from Qatadah. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others related from him that he said about the verse: "The events of God, exalted is He, concerning those who passed away from the nations have passed." From Ibn 'Abbas it is related that what is meant is their way in denial. Perhaps the attribution on this view is in its apparent sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 14:

﴿Even if We opened for them﴾, i.e., for these challengers and obstinate ones, ﴿a gate from the heaven﴾. Its apparent meaning is a gate of some kind, not one of the well-known gates of heaven, as has been said. ﴿And they continued therein﴾, i.e., in that gate, ﴿ascending﴾, ascending as much as We facilitate for them, so that they see what is in it of angels and wonders all the day long, gaining clarity about what they see, as the word ﴿ẓallū﴾ indicates, because one says "ẓalla yaʿmalu kadhā" when he does it during the day, when a person has a shadow. It has been permitted in al-Bahr that ẓalla means ṣāra (became), but despite being contrary to the original usage, there is no reason for it. In any case, the plural pronoun refers to the challengers, and this is the apparent view narrated from al-Hasan, and al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim adopted it. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it refers to the angels, and this is also narrated from Qatada.
Page 20
That is, the angels whose coming they had demanded would continue ascending in that gate while they see them in the most complete manner. Al-Aʿmash and Abu Ḥaywa read ﴿yaʿrijūn﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ, and this is the dialect of Hudhayl regarding ʿurūj, meaning ascent (ṣuʿūd).

﴿لَقالُوا﴾ (they would say), out of their extreme obstinacy, their excessive stubbornness in denial, and their evasion of accepting the truth: ﴿إنَّما سُكِّرَتْ أبْصارُنا﴾ (our eyes have only been dazzled), meaning they have been blocked and prevented from seeing in reality, and what we see is imagination with no reality behind it. Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated this from Mujahid. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah, and in that case it derives from sakr (with a fatha on the sin), while Abu Hayyan said it is with a kasra, meaning to block and to hold back. Ibn al-Sayyid said: sakr with a fatha is blocking a door or a river, and with a kasra it is the blockage itself, and its plural is sukur. Al-Raffa' said:

Our singing therein is the melodies of the sukur,
when singing is scarce, and the groaning of the water-wheels.

This meaning is supported by the recitation of Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan and Mujahid, "sukkirat absaruna" (سُكِرَتْ أبْصارُنا) with the kaf lightened and the verb in the passive voice, because the lightened transitive form sakira (سَكِرَ) is well known in the sense of blocking. From Amr ibn al-'Ala' it is narrated that the intended meaning is "ḥuyyirat" (were bewildered), in which case it derives from sukr (سُكْر) with a damma, the opposite of sahw (sobriety). They explained it as a state that comes between a person and his intellect, and it is most often used for intoxication by drink, though it may also come from anger or passionate love. For this reason the poet said:

Drunk with the drunkenness of passion and the drunkenness of wine,
how can a youth who is intoxicated by it sober up?

The doubling of the consonant in this sense is for transitivity (ta'diyah), because sakira, like fariḥa, is intransitive in its most common usage, though its transitivity has been reported, and so it is for intensification and emphasis. They meant by this that our eyes have been corrupted, and a defect has afflicted their perception, just as intoxication afflicts the intellect of the drunkard so that his comprehension is disturbed. In this case the expression contains a metaphor (isti'arah, a figure of speech in which a term is transferred to a non-literal meaning), and according to some scholars the first interpretation also contains one. This meaning is supported by the recitation of al-Zuhri, "sakirat" (سَكِرَتْ) with a fatha on the sin and a kasra on the kaf, lightened and with the verb in the active voice, because the triliteral intransitive form is well known in it, and because sakara in the sense of "blocked" is known with a fatha on the kaf.

Al-Zajjaj chose that the meaning is "they became still regarding the perception of realities," from sakirat al-rih (سَكِرَتِ الرِّيحُ), "the wind became calm," when it stilled, and it is said: "a night of stillness (laylah sakirah), with no wind in it." The doubling is for transitivity. There are other opinions close in meaning.

Abban ibn Taghlib recited "suḥirat absaruna" (سُحِرَتْ أبْصارُنا), "our eyes have been bewitched," and this reading was rejected because it opposes the consonantal text of the Mushaf, so it is taken as an explanation (of the meaning, not as recitation). ﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ قَوْمٌ مَسْحُورُونَ﴾ (rather, we are a people who have been bewitched): Muhammad (ﷺ) has bewitched us, as they said this whenever the other clear signs appeared.

The apparent meaning, according to al-Qutb, is that they first intended: "our eyes have been dazzled, not our intellects," so although we imagine these things with our eyes, we know with our intellects that the situation is otherwise. Then they turned away from restricting the matter to the eyes, and said: "rather, it has gone beyond that to our intellects." Al-Zamakhshari explained the restriction (qasr, the grammatical device of limiting a predication to one thing) as meaning that this is nothing but making us drunk. This was objected to on the grounds that innama (إنَّما, "only") restricts what is mentioned last, and in that case the meaning would be what came before. This objection rests on the premise that placing the intended element before the element restricted is obligatory and its reverse is impossible. The Muhaqqiq (al-Taftazani?) said in his commentary on al-Talkhis that it is permissible when the placing itself gives restriction, as in our saying: innama Zaydan darabtu (إنَّما زِيدًا ضَرَبْتُ), "it is only Zayd whom I struck," because it restricts the striking to Zayd. Abu al-Tayyib said:

His attributes did not add to his knowledge,
but they are a pleasure we mention.

That is, we only mention them for pleasure. However, this does not help in our case. Yes, it is reported from Arus al-Afrah (a commentary on the Miftah) that the ruling of the scholars of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) is not accepted without question, for your saying innama qumtu (إنَّما قُمْتُ, "I only stood") means only standing occurred, so it restricts the action and is not something else, and if the restriction of the agent were intended it would be separated. Then he cited a number of examples from the words of the commentators that show what they mentioned on this question. The apparent position is that al-Zamakhshari does not consider what they said to be consistent, and they had missed his intention here, as al-Shihab said. What he transmitted from Arus al-Afrah regarding innama qumtu, that it is for restricting the action, and if it were for restricting the agent it would be separated, is contradicted by what is in the Sharifi commentary on the Miftah: that when it is intended to restrict the action to the hidden agent, then if something of the action's related elements is mentioned after the verb, the agent must be separated and postponed, as in your saying innama daraba al-yawma ana (إنَّما ضَرَبَ اليَوْمَ أنا, "it was only I who struck today"), and as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

I am the defender, the protector of honor,
and only I, or someone like me, defends their noble lineage.

If nothing is mentioned, it may be obligatory by analogy to the rule, or not obligatory, in which case separation is permitted considering the meaning, and connection is permitted considering the wording, since there is no separating element in the wording. This is clear that innama qumtu restricts the agent even if separation is not obligatory. However, al-Sa'd in his commentary chose that separation is obligatory in all cases, and ruled that the apparent meaning of innama aqulu (إنَّما أقُولُ) is "I am nothing but one who stands," as al-Samarqandi transmitted. Abu Hayyan, together with a small group of grammarians, denied that innama at all indicates restriction, and this is not the view relied upon by the scholars who verify, but they said that it may come merely for emphasis. The full discussion of this matter is to be sought in its proper place.

Al-Shihab justified the change of direction (idrab, a turning away from the first statement to another) after saying: it makes the first (statement) as something left unmentioned, not as a negation; the second may be a change of direction, because this (being bewitched) did not actually happen in reality, but only through magic. Or it is with regard to what the sentence conveys of continuity, which the nominal sentence indicates, i.e. our being bewitched is not confined to this state; rather we remain continuously in it with respect to every sign that is shown to us.

In this verse there is a description of them as stubborn, and their conspiring together upon what they are in of denial and corruption, which is clear. This confirms what is understood from the first verse. Ibn al-Munir mentioned for its meaning an interpretation which, in my view, is very far-fetched. He said: The meaning, and God knows best, is the establishment of proof against the deniers: that God the Exalted has threaded the Qur'an into their hearts and made it enter their innermost hearts, just as He threaded it into the hearts of the believing and affirming ones. These denied it, and those affirmed it, each on knowledge and understanding, so that whoever perishes perishes by clear evidence, and whoever lives lives by clear evidence, and so that the unbelievers will have no argument against God the Exalted by claiming that they did not understand the aspect of its inimitability as the one who believed understood it. So God the Exalted informed them, while they were still in respite and capacity, that they had only disbelieved with knowledge, being obstinate, rebellious, and not excused. For this reason He, glorified is He, followed it with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ولَوْ فَتَحْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (and even if We opened to them...), and so on; that is, these understood the Qur'an and knew the aspects of its inimitability, and that entered their hearts and settled there, but they are a people whose disposition is obstinacy and whose manner is persistent hostility, so that even if He led them to the clearest paths and the most conducive to faith, they would say after the great clarification: "our eyes have only been dazzled, and we have been bewitched, and these are nothing but imaginings with no realities beneath them." Thus He, glorified is He, established against them by this that they have no excuse for their denial, through lack of hearing, awareness, reaching the hearts, and understanding as others among the affirmers understood, for that was available to them, and there was in them nothing but obstinacy and persistence, and nothing more. End of quote. So let it be pondered. And God the Exalted is the Guide to the right path.

[Page 21]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 16:

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of those who deny prophethood, and this was a branch of tawhid (the oneness of God), He mentioned His heavenly and earthly signs. So He, mighty is His saying, said: ﴿And We have certainly placed in the sky constellations﴾ etc. The Imam and others went to this in explaining the connection (al-rabt, the link between verses).

Ibn Atiyya said: When He, glorified is He, mentioned that if they saw the sought-after sign in the sky they would be obstinate and would remain in the misguidance they were in, He followed that with this verse, as if He, majestic is His affair, had said: "Indeed, in the sky there are signs set up, other than this one mentioned, and their disbelief in them and their turning away from them is persistence on their part and insolence." End of quote. The apparent meaning is that the placing (al-ja'l) means creating and originating (al-khalq wa'l-ibda'), so the prepositional phrase is connected to it. It is also permitted that it means making or appointing (al-tasyir), in which case it is connected to an omitted element, as a second object (maf'ul thani) of it, and "burujan" (constellations) is its first object. Al-buruj is the plural of burj (tower, constellation), which in lexical usage means a palace or a fortress, and Ibn Atiyya interpreted it here in this sense. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "We made palaces in the sky, in which are guards." He also reported from Abu Salih that the intended meaning of al-buruj is the great stars.

In al-Bahr (Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), it is reported from him that they are the wandering stars (al-kawakib al-sayyara, the planets). Many narrators reported from Mujahid and Qatada that they are the stars without restriction. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that this is interpreted as the twelve well-known constellations (al-buruj al-ithna 'ashara, the zodiac), which are six northern, three of the spring and three of the summer, and the first of them is Aries (al-Hamal). And six southern, three of the autumn and three of the winter, and the first of them is Libra (al-Mizan). The length of each constellation in their reckoning is thirty degrees, and its width is 'qif' (the astronomical measure) degrees, of which some are in the northern direction and the like in the southern direction. It seems that they were named so because each is like a fortress or palace for the star residing in it. In reality they are sections of the greatest sphere, which is the mahaddad (the limiting sphere), called in their language the falak al-atlas (the outermost sphere) and falak al-aflak (the sphere of spheres), and in the language of the Shari'a it is the reverse of this. For this reason, al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, names the falak al-atlas "falak al-buruj" (the sphere of the constellations). The well-known naming is that the eighth sphere, which is falak al-thawabit (the sphere of the fixed stars), is called by this name because of their observation of division in it. It seems that this is due to the appearance, in it, of the forms by which the sections are distinguished, even if each of them moves from what it was assigned to another of them, because of the proven self-motion (al-haraka al-dhatiyya) of the fixed stars in a direction opposite to the sequence. Although the early philosophers did not affirm it for them, because of the lack of perception of it, most did not affirm their rotation on their own axis, while al-Shaykh Abu 'Ali (Ibn Sina) and those who followed him among the verifiers affirmed it. They have explicitly stated that these forms, named by the known names, were imagined on the belt (al-mintaqa) and what is near it on both sides, from fixed stars organized by imaginary lines, which fell, at the time of the division, into those sections. This was reported in al-Kifaya from the general body of astrologers, and that they imagined for each section a form so that instruction and teaching could be achieved, by saying, for example: "al-Dabaran is the eye of the Lion."

This was followed by his saying: "This is not correct in my view, because if those forms were imaginary, they would have no effect on similar things in the lower world, whereas the matter is not so. Ptolemy said in the Thamara (the Fruit): The forms that are in the world of composition are obedient to the celestial forms, since they are in their essences upon those forms, so the imaginations perceived them as they are." There is a discussion in this. Then these constellations differ in their effects and properties, rather for each part of each of them, even if it is less than a tenth, there are effects differing from the effects of the other part, and all of that are effects of the wisdom of God, exalted is He, and His power, mighty and majestic is He. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in some of his books that the effects of the stars and their judgments are poured upon them from those constellations considered in the mahaddad.

In the third chapter of the seventy-first and three-hundredth section of his Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya), there is what says, among other things, that God, exalted is He, divided the falak al-atlas into twelve parts, which He named constellations, and He settled in each of them an angel. These angels are the imams of the world, and He assigned to each of them thirty treasuries, each of which contains various knowledges, from which they bestow upon whoever descends to them as much as his rank provides. These are the treasuries of which God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾. Among the people of the sciences of the ancients (ahl al-ta'alim), they are called the degrees of the sphere, and those who descend to them are the jawari (the moving stars) and the manazil (the lunar mansions), and their 'ayyuqat (the fixed stars that are the markers) are among the fixed stars. The knowledges obtained from those divine treasuries are what appears in the general elements (amm al-arkan) of influences, indeed what appears in the concave of the sphere of the fixed stars down to the earth, down to the end of what he said. May his secret be sanctified, he made the discourse on this subject lengthy, and it is far removed from the belief of the traditionists (al-muhaddithin), the transmitters of the religion, may mercy be upon them.

Then, indeed, in the difference of the properties of the constellations, as attested by experience, together with what the majority agreed upon regarding the simplicity of the sky, is the clearest proof of the existence of the Creator, the Chooser, majestic is His majesty.

﴿And We adorned it﴾, i.e., the sky, with what is in it of wandering stars and others, and they are numerous, and none knows their number except God, exalted is He. Indeed, what has been observed of them is a thousand and more, twenty. They arranged them in six degrees and named them magnitudes (aqdar), increasing by a sixth, until the diameter of what is in the first magnitude was six times that of what is in the sixth magnitude. They made each magnitude into three degrees. What is below the sixth they did not establish in the degrees; rather, if it is like a piece of cloud they call it "sahabi" (cloud-like), and otherwise "muzlim" (dark). It is mentioned in al-Kifaya that what is among them in the first magnitude, its body is one hundred and fifty-six times and a half a tenth of the earth. It came in some reports that the smallest of the stars is like a great mountain. Abu Hayyan preferred the return of the pronoun to the constellations, because they are the subject being spoken of and it is closer in wording. The majority hold to what we have mentioned, out of caution against the scattering of the pronoun. ﴿For the observers﴾, i.e., with their eyes looking at them, as one of them said, because this is appropriate to adornment. It is also permitted that adornment means arranging them in a wonderful order which entails good effects, so that by "the observers" is meant those who reflect and who derive guidance from that toward the power of the One who determined it and the wisdom of the One who arranged it, exalted is His affair.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 17:

﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ (rajim), driven away from the good things. The term al-rajm is applied to the throwing of rajam, which are stones, so the meaning of al-rajim here is one pelted with the stars. It is also applied to destruction and to a hideous killing. The meaning of guarding it from the devil is either preventing him from approaching it at all and from knowing anything of what is in it in general. Thus the exception in the words of the Exalted:

[p. 24]

"Except one who eavesdrops by stealth" (﴿إلا مَنِ اسْتَرَقَ السَّمْعَ﴾) is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil). But preventing them from entering it and mingling with its inhabitants in the manner of mingling with the people of the earth is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'). In either case, the position of "man" (من) is accusative as an exception. Abu al-Baqa' and al-Hawfi permitted that it be in the genitive position, as a substitute (badal) for "from every accursed devil" (﴿مِن كُلِّ شَيْطانٍ﴾), a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull), and that it dispenses with a connecting pronoun because of "illa" (except). It was objected that a substitution requires the sentence to be negative and not affirmative, and this sentence is affirmative.

It was answered that it has the sense of a negation, meaning: We did not enable every devil or the like to reach it. It was objected that interpreting an affirmative sentence as negative is not a regular practice when it does not involve "aba" (refused) or its derivatives, and it is not good usage; one does not say "the people died except Zayd" meaning "they did not live." Perhaps the proponent of substitution does not accept this. They have interpreted as negative His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they drank from it, except a few﴾ and His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The world is ruined except those who have knowledge," the hadith, and other examples which do not contain "aba" or any of its derivatives. However, fairness weakens this substitution, as is not hidden.

Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being the clause ﴿then a clear flaming fire pursued him﴾. He mentioned that the "fa" (then) is due to "man" being either a relative pronoun or a conditional. "Istiraq" is a form of "saraqa" (theft), which is taking something secretly. It is used metaphorically for snatching the small portion from the Higher Assembly, which is what is mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾. "Al-sam'" (hearing) here means what is heard. "Shihab" (flaming fire), according to al-Raghib, is a blazing flame from a kindled fire, and from an accidental phenomenon in the atmosphere; it is also applied to a star because of its brightness, like a flame of fire.

Its root is from "shuhba", which is a whiteness mixed with blackness, not pure whiteness, as the common people err in this, saying "a white horse" (faras ashhab) for the paper-white horse (al-qirtasi). "Mubin" (clear) means its matter is evident to those who see. The meaning of "atba'ahu" is "tabi'ahu" (followed him) according to al-Akhfash, like "radaftuhu" and "ardaftuhu," so the hamza in it is not for transitivity. It was said: "atba'a" is more specific than "taba'a," because al-Jawhari said: "I followed the people (tabi'tu al-qawm) with tabaʿan and tabaʿa when you walked behind them, or they passed by you and you went with them; and I caught up with the people (atba'tu al-qawm), in the form af'alta, when they had preceded you and you overtook them." He considered the distinction between them good. Since following may imply destruction or other things, the scholars differed on that. Al-Qurtubi related from Ibn Abbas that the shihab wounds and burns but does not kill, and from al-Hasan and a group that it kills; he claimed the former is more sound. More than one transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: The devils mount one another up to the lowest heaven to steal hearing from the angels, peace be upon them, and then they are struck by the stars, which never miss. Among them is one who is killed, and among them is one whose face or side or hand is burned, or wherever Allah wills. Among them is one who is stricken and becomes a ghoul, so people go astray in the deserts.

[p. 25]

Among what is not relied upon is what is narrated, that some of them fall into the sea and become crocodiles, and that some people criticized the matter of this eavesdropping and pelting, as the Imam said, in several respects.

First, the falling of the stars is mentioned in the books of the ancient philosophers, who mentioned that when the earth is heated by the sun, a dry vapour rises from it, and when it reaches the sphere of fire below the celestial sphere, it burns in it, and that flame is the shihab. It may remain blazing for a time if it is dense, and sometimes the smokes heat up in the cold air through succession, and are compressed while blazing. Also found in pre-Islamic poetry, Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:

"The caravan is overtaken by dust, and its wild ass swoops after the two of them like the swoop of a star."

And Aws ibn Hajar said:

"He swooped like a pearl-shaped star, followed by a rising dust cloud that you would think was a tent-rope."

And other examples.

Second, how is it possible for these devils to see thousands of their own kind eavesdropping and burning, and yet they return to their deed? For whoever has even a little intellect, when he sees the destruction of his own kind from engaging in something repeatedly, he refrains from it.

Third, it may be said: The thickness of the heaven is five hundred years. If these devils penetrate its body and pierce it, that is false, because there are no rifts in it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Look again: do you see any rifts?﴾ And if they cannot penetrate it, how can they hear the secrets of the angels, peace be upon them, despite this great distance?

Fourth, the angels, peace be upon them, only became aware of the future states either because they read them from the Preserved Tablet, or because they received them through revelation. In either case, why did they not keep silent about mentioning them, so that the devils could not gain access to them?

Fifth, the devils are created from fire, and fire does not burn fire but strengthens it. How, then, is it conceivable to repel them with these flames?

Sixth, you say that this casting is for the sake of prophethood. Why did it continue after the death of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him?

Seventh, these flames occur only near the earth, as evidenced by our observing their movements. Had they been near the celestial sphere, we would not have observed them, just as we do not observe the movements of the celestial spheres and stars. And if it is established that they occur near the earth, how can it be said that they prevent the devils from reaching the celestial sphere?

Eighth, if these devils could convey reports of the angels, peace be upon them, about unseen matters to the soothsayers (kahana), why did they not convey the secrets of the believers to the disbelievers, so that by means of their knowledge of their secrets they could harm them?

Ninth, why did Allah, exalted is He, not prevent them from ascending in the first place, so that there would be no need to repel them with these flames?

Some also said: Hearing only benefits them if they know the language of the angels. Why did Allah, glorified is He, not make them ignorant of their language, so that hearing would benefit them nothing? Also, if the air ends below the concave of the lunar sphere, no sound would arise there, since sound comes from the undulation of air, and the assumption is its absence. If the air does not end, there would be terrifying sounds below that from the undulation of air caused by the motion of the great bodies, and these would prevent hearing the voices of the angels, peace be upon them, in their discourses. It is hardly conceivable that their voices in discourse would overpower those immense sounds so that they could be heard above them. Also, in the lowest heaven there is only the moon, and we do not see it being pelted with these, nor the rest of the wandering planets, above "each in an orbit swimming" (﴿كُلٌّ في فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ﴾). The fixed stars are in the eighth sphere. Pelting anything of that sort would require tearing the heaven and splitting it so that the flame could reach the devil, and that is hardly conceivable.

The Imam answered the first objection, first, by saying that the shihab did not exist before the mission (ba'tha), and this is the view of Ibn Abbas. For it is related from him that he said: "The jinn used to ascend to the heaven and listen to the revelation. When they heard a word, they added things of their own to it. When the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was sent, they were prevented from their seats, and the stars had not been hurled before that. Iblis said to them: 'This is only because of a matter that has occurred.'" The hadith continues.

It is also narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "No star had been hurled since Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised, until the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was sent. Then they were hurled, and Quraysh saw what they had not seen before, so they began to set free their livestock and free their slaves, thinking that it was the end. This reached their chief, who said: 'Why are you doing this?' They said: 'Stars have been hurled.' He said: 'Consider: if they are known stars, then it is the time of the end of people; otherwise it is a matter that has occurred.' They looked, and they were not known, so they informed him. He said: 'There is a respite in the matter, and this is at the appearance of a prophet.'" The hadith continues.

The books of the ancients have been subjected to successive distortions, so perhaps later scholars attached this question to them, as an attack on this miracle. Likewise, the poems attributed to the people of pre-Islamic ignorance may be fabricated against them.

Second, and this is the truth: the shihab existed before the mission for other reasons, and we do not deny that. However, this does not exclude that after the mission it may occur more frequently, by the repelling and deterring of the devils. It is related that al-Zuhri was asked: "Was it hurled in the Jahiliyya?" He said: "Yes." It was asked: "What then of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And we used to sit in some of its seats to listen; but whoever listens now finds a watchful flame lying in wait for him﴾?" He said: "Its matter became more severe and intensified when the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was sent." It is in this manner that what is related from Ibn Abbas and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both, is to be understood, if it is authentic.

As for the second objection: when the decree comes, sight is blinded. When Allah, exalted is He, decrees for a group of them burning because of their rebellion and error, He brings about for them the motives mentioned above, which lead them to the act that results in their destruction.

As for the third objection: the distance between the earth and the heaven is five hundred years. As for the thickness of the sphere, it is not great.

As for the fourth objection: it is related from al-Zuhri, from Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was sitting among a group of his companions, a star was hurled and became bright. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'What did you used to say in the Jahiliyya when something like this happened?' They said: 'We used to say that a great one is born, or a great one dies.' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'It is not hurled for the death of anyone or for his life. But when our Lord, exalted is He, decrees the matter in the heaven, the bearers of the Throne glorify, then those in the heaven glorify, and those in each heaven glorify, until the glorification reaches this heaven. The people of the heaven ask the bearers of the Throne: "What has your Lord said?" They inform them, and the report continues to reach this heaven, where the jinn snatch it and throw it down. What they bring is true, but they add to it.'"

As for the fifth objection: fire may be stronger than another fire, and the stronger extinguishes what is below it.

As for the sixth objection: it continued because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed of the invalidity of soothsaying (kahana). Had this casting ceased, soothsaying would have returned, and that would undermine the Messenger's report of its invalidity, peace and blessings be upon him.

As for the seventh objection: according to our school, distance is not an obstacle to hearing. Perhaps He, glorified and exalted is He, has made it His custom that when they stand in those places they hear the speech of the angels, peace be upon them.

As for the eighth objection: perhaps Allah, exalted is He, enabled them to listen to the unseen matters from the angels and rendered them unable to convey the secrets of the believers to the disbelievers.

As for the ninth objection: He, mighty and majestic is He, does what He wills and decrees what He desires. In this way the first objection is answered, as it is said.

The second objection was answered by saying: We choose that the air and hearing cease according to Allah's creation, and this does not depend on the existence of air and its undulation. It may also be chosen that there is no cessation, and it is said that He, exalted is His majesty,

[p. 26]

...is able to prevent the air from being set in motion by the movement of those bodies. Likewise, He, glory be to Him, is able to make them hear those terrifying sounds, though they are hidden and even more hidden.

As for the third point: the claim that the fixed stars are in the eighth sphere (*al-falak al-thamin*, the sphere of the fixed stars) is the view of the philosophers, who argued for it on the basis that some of them are in it, so all of them must be. As for the first argument, it is that the fixed stars close to the ecliptic are eclipsed by the planets, so the eclipsed fixed stars must be above the eclipsing planets. As for the second, it is that they all move with a single slow motion, one degree every hundred years or so, according to the differing reports, so they must all be fixed in one sphere. This is a weak argument, because it does not follow from the fact that some fixed stars are above the planets that all of them are here. For it is not far-fetched that there is a sphere below the sphere of the Moon, which in its slowness equals the sphere of the fixed stars, and that the stars fixed near the two poles are fixed in this lower sphere. It is not far-fetched either that there are two spheres differing in smallness and largeness while being similar in motion. On this basis, there is nothing impossible in these stars being in the nearest heaven. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti and others have mentioned that some reports state that the stars are suspended by chains of light in the hands of angels in the nearest heaven, who move them wherever and however God the Exalted wills. However, the soundness of that is open to question. Moreover, what is mentioned in the question, that this would entail *al-kharq* (rupture of the heavens), is something that hardly needs to be said. Either it is based on the view that rupture and reunion are impossible in the outermost sphere (*al-falak al-muhaddad*) and others, but the corruption of that has been established and the possibility of rupture and reunion has been verified by what cannot be improved upon in other books of *kalam* (theology). Or it is based merely on the sense of remoteness, but that does not establish anything, because most possibilities seem remote while they nonetheless occur, and I do not think you doubt this. Indeed, it may be said: we do not commit to the claim that the star itself follows the devil and burns him. The *shihab* (meteor) is not an explicit text about the star, as you know from what has been said about its meaning. And even if it is said that the star itself falls and strikes the devil and then returns to its place, this is based on the apparent usage of *rujum* (missiles) for stars and the expression "he was struck by the star."

Likewise, we do not commit to the view that a flame detaches from the star like a brand taken from a fire and is thrown with it, as more than one has said, so that we would need to answer the question with what preceded. For it is permissible to say that this flame, called the *shihab*, has an effect by God's permission and burns with it whichever devils God wills. The use of *rujum* for stars and their saying "he was struck by the star" may be based on what appears to the observer, as in the words of God the Exalted about the sun: ﴿it sets in a muddy spring﴾.

The Imam [al-Razi] said: these meteors are not the fixed stars set in the sphere, and their being visible would involve a great reduction in their number, though no reduction at all has been observed. Furthermore, making them missiles entails a reduction in the adornment of the sky. Rather, they are another kind, distinct from them, which God creates and makes into missiles for the devils. This is not contradicted by the words of God the Exalted: ﴿And We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾, since it indicates that those lamps are the very missiles. For we say: every luminous body that appears in the upper atmosphere is a lamp for the people of the earth. However, some of these lamps remain forever, secure from change and corruption, and some are not so, and the meteor belongs to this latter category. With this, the difficulty is resolved. End of quotation. Whether to accept or reject between the two views is left to the penetrating insight of your mind. And in his earlier answers, may God the Exalted have mercy on him, there is what its weakness is not hidden. Likewise, this is evidence of his scant acquaintance with the sound and well-known reports. Do you not see his statement in answering the third of the nine questions: the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years, and as for the thickness of the sphere, it is not great? This contradicts what the Sharia has declared and what philosophy has guided to. As for its contradiction of the first, it is established that the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, just as the distance between the heaven and the earth is the same. As for its contradiction of the second: no philosopher has said that the distance between the heaven and the earth is the distance he mentioned. The spheres, according to them, differ in thickness, and they have specified the thickness of each in farsakhs, as mentioned in the books on celestial bodies and distances. They have mentioned about the thickness of the outermost sphere what testifies to the greatness of God, majestic is His majesty. But they have no definitive basis for that. Indeed, their saying "there is no superiority in celestial matters," although it is very much like rhetorical argument (*khatabiyyat*), contradicts it.

His statement in answering the sixth point: the reason it persisted is so that its cessation would not undermine the report of the Messenger (ﷺ) about the invalidity of soothsaying. This entails circularity (*dawr*), since it is evident that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was informed of that only because he knew that the expulsion preventing the realization of what soothsaying depends upon would persist. His statement in answering the fifth point: that fire may be stronger than another fire and extinguish it, indicates that the devils are pure fire. This is not so. Rather, the truth is that the fiery element predominates in them, and by composition they have acquired what pure fire does not have, even with this element dominating. This is evident.

Furthermore, know that it is possible that the eavesdropping (*istiraq al-sam'*) is from the angels who are near the heaven, not from the angels who are between each heaven and heaven, so that the matter of the thickness would not arise, and the difficulty of hearing with it would be removed. This is supported by what al-Bukhari narrated from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, from Aisha, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: The angels descend into the *inan*, which is the cloud, and they mention the matter that has been decreed in the heaven. The devils then eavesdrop, hear it, and convey it to the soothsayers, and they lie with the word a hundred lies of their own." This is not contradicted by what he also narrated from Ikrima, who said: "I heard Abu Hurayra say: The Prophet, may God the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said: When God the Exalted decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon smooth rock. When fear is removed from their hearts, they say: What has your Lord said? They say: The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great. Then the eavesdropper hears it." The report continues. For there is nothing in it more than the eavesdropper's hearing the word after the angels, peace be upon them, speak to one another. The non-contradiction of this with that is evident to one who listens attentively while being a witness. Moreover, there is nothing in the verses that is explicit that what we see of meteors occurs only to strike an eavesdropping devil. Rather, the most that they indicate is that when a devil eavesdrops, a meteor follows him and he is struck by a star. And where is this from that? Yes, in the report of al-Zuhri there is something that requires reflection. On this basis, it is possible that the occurrence of some of the meteors we see is due to the rising of vapour, as was mentioned earlier from the philosophers. Likewise, it is possible that the ascent of the devils for eavesdropping occurs, for example, once a year. The benefit of this in answering the second question is not hidden.

Among the people there is one who answered it by saying: it is not far-fetched that the eavesdroppers are a category of devils whose natures require ascent, like the ascent of vapours. Indeed, it is possible that those devils are vapours to which wicked souls are attached, in the manner the philosophers mentioned, that a soul may become attached to the bodies of comets, so that it disappears and appears by itself. There is a discussion of this.

Al-Imam reported from al-Jubba'i that he said in answer to that:

The condition that befalls them has no fixed place, otherwise they would not go there. They are only prevented from reaching the places of the angels, and those places vary. Perhaps they reach the place of the angels and are struck by the meteors; perhaps they reach another place and do not encounter the angels, so nothing strikes them. When they perished at some times and were saved at others, it is permissible that they go to a place where it is likely in their estimation that they will not be struck, just as it is permissible for one who travels by sea to take a route where he estimates that salvation is likely.

He then followed this with: One may say: if they ascend, either they reach the places of the angels or other places. If they reach the first, they are burned; if they reach the second, they achieve nothing at all. In either case the goal is not attained. So when this experience occurs, and it is established by induction that attaining the goal is certain, they must refrain. This differs from the situation of the traveller at sea, for most travellers there succeed in attaining their goal. Then he said: The closest answer is that we say: this event occurs only rarely, so perhaps it is not well known among the devils because it is rare. End of quotation.

You know that this can hardly be completed except with the claim that not every meteor we see burns a devil. With this claim the matter is easy, as is not hidden.

Al-Baydawi mentioned that the eavesdropping is their brief snatching from the inhabitants of the heavens, because of the affinity between them in substance, or by inference from the configurations and motions of the stars. He also mentioned, at the words of God the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing﴾, that hearing is conditioned upon their sharing in the attributes of essence, and the receiving of the outpouring of truth, and imprinting with the angelic form. Their souls are wicked, shadowy, evil by essence, and do not receive that. There is no hiding what is in this, for it is evident that eavesdropping requires affinity of substance, and complete hearing requires the aforementioned sharing. This does not accord with the principles of the Sharia. And that their receiving comes from celestial configurations is contrary to the plain sense of the text and the hadiths, and it also entails that the inhabitants of the heaven are the stars, and that the word "*man*" (whoever) includes human devils, the astrologers. This is as you see. He and others have mentioned from Ibn Abbas, may God the Exalted be pleased with them both, that the devils were not barred from the heavens. When Jesus, peace be upon him, was born, they were prevented from three heavens, and when the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, they were prevented from all the heavens. End of quotation.

Some people, taking hold of some apparent indications, went to the view that the prevention occurred at the time of the mission (*al-ba'thah*). And God the Exalted knows best. "A difficulty remains here," which the Imam mentioned together with its answer. He said: One may say: if you allow in general that the devil may ascend to the heaven and hear reports of the unseen from the angels, peace be upon them, then convey them to the soothsayers, it must remove the reports of unseen matters from being a miracle that indicates truthfulness, because every unseen matter about which the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, informs contains this possibility. And it cannot be said that God the Exalted informed that they were unable to do that after his birth (ﷺ), because we say: this miracle cannot be established except after certainty that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is a Messenger, and that the Qur'an is true. And certainty of this cannot be achieved except through the miracle. And that the informing of unseen matters is a miracle is not established except after refuting this possibility. In that case, circularity (*dawr*) is entailed, and it is impossible. It may be answered in this way: we establish that he (ﷺ) is a Messenger through the other miracles. Then, after knowing that this is established, we are certain that God the Exalted made the devils unable to snatch the unseen by this means, and at that point the informing of unseen matters becomes a miracle, and circularity is not entailed. End of quotation. So reflect. God the Exalted is the Guardian of success, and in His hand are the reins of verification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 19:

﴿And the earth — We have spread it out.﴾ (basatnaha) We spread it out. Al-Hasan said: God Most High took a clay (tinah) and said to it: "Spread out," and it spread out. It is narrated from Qatadah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities) is Makkah, and from it the earth was spread out (duhiyat) and expanded (busitat)." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "We spread it out upon the surface of the water." It has also been said: the meaning may be that We made it extended in the three dimensions: length, breadth and depth. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is its spreading and widening, so that benefit may be gained by those who dwell upon it, and this does not necessitate denying its sphericity, since a very great sphere, because of its immensity, is seen as a level plane. The word "al-ard" (the earth) is in the accusative by omission, by way of the rule of exegesis (ʿalā sharīṭat al-tafsīr), and in such a context this is preferable to the nominative as a beginning (ibtida'), because of its coordination (ʿaṭf) with the verbal clause, namely His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We have certainly created﴾ etc., and in order to agree with what follows it, namely His, Glorified is He, saying: ﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾, i.e., firmly fixed mountains (jibalan thawabit), the plural of rasiyah, which is the plural of ras (peak) according to what has been said. He has explained the wisdom of casting these into it in His saying, Glorified is He:

Page 29

﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When God Most High spread the earth upon the water, it inclined like a ship, so He anchored it with the heavy mountains so that it would not tilt with its inhabitants. The discussion of this has already preceded. Some have claimed that it is permissible for the intended meaning to be that God Most High did this so that the mountains would be indicators of the paths of the earth and its regions, so that people would not stray from the straight road and would not fall into error. Then he said: "This view is strongly possible." But you know that it is not permissible to resort to it in the presence of reports that contradict it, such as (the report about) the mountains.

﴿And We caused to grow therein﴾, i.e., in the earth. It may include the mountains, since they are counted among it, or it may be specific to other than them, since most plants and the finest of them are in it. It is permitted that the pronoun refers to the mountains and the earth, by way of treating them as the things mentioned (ta'wil bi'l-madhkurat), or to the earth in the sense of what is opposite the heaven, by way of the figure of istikhdam; its return to the mountains because of their proximity is also possible, while taking "growth" to mean the bringing forth of minerals is remote.

﴿from every thing weighed﴾, i.e., measured by a specific quantity required by wisdom. So it is a metaphor used for its necessary meaning, or a kinaya (metonymy), or it means "from everything pleasing and well-proportioned," from the expression "kalam mawzun" (balanced speech). Al-Murtada in his Durar cited for this meaning the verse of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

And a discourse which I find sweet, and which is of what souls desire, is weighed out in its weighing.

This usage has become widespread in the speech of non-Arabs and the muwallidun (later Arabic speakers), who say: "qiwam mawzun," meaning balanced and proportionate, or what has value and consideration among people in matters of blessing and benefit. Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning is what is literally weighed, such as gold, silver and others. "Min" (from) here, as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), is partitive (lil-tab'id). Al-Akhfash said: it is superfluous (za'idah), i.e., "every thing."

The Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 15, verse 20:

﴿And We have placed for you therein means of living (ma'ayish)﴾, meaning what you live by of food, drink, clothing and other things on which survival depends, and it is with a clear *ya'* (ي). Al-A'raj and Kharijah, on the authority of Nafi', read it with a *hamza*. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The preferred reading is to leave it without the *hamza*, because the *ya'* in this word is the middle radical ('ayn al-kalimah) of the root. The rule for such a word is that it should not be changed into a *hamza*. The change to *hamza* happens only when the letter is an augmentation, as in the *ya'* of *shama'il* and *khaba'ith*. However, since the *ya'* here resembles the *ya'* there in occurring after an augmented *alif* in the plural, it has been treated like it, contrary to the rule."

﴿and [We have placed for you] those whom you do not provide for (wa man lastum lahu biraziqin)﴾ is coordinated with *ma'ayish*, meaning: And We have placed for you those whose provision you do not supply, from among dependants, slaves, servants, animals and the like, by way of *taghlib* (the predominance of one term over another within a grouping), as al-Farra' and others said. He mentioned them with this description either to refute the assumption of some ignorant people that they gain their sustenance from them, or to affirm that God Most High provides for them and for you, together with the great favour contained in that. It is also permissible to coordinate it with the position (mahall) of *lakum* (for you). The Kufans, Yunus and al-Akhfash permitted this, and Abu Hayyan affirmed the coordination with a pronoun in the genitive case even if the governing preposition is not repeated. The meaning under both interpretations is the same: And We have placed for you ma'ayish, and for those whom you do not provide for. Al-Zajjaj said that *man* is in the accusative position governed by a deleted verb, and the sense is: "And We made to live those whom you do not..." etc., i.e. other nations besides you, because the meaning is "We made you to live." It was also said that it is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate deleted because the meaning indicates it, i.e. "and those whom you do not provide for, for them We have placed therein ma'ayish." This is contrary to the apparent sense. Abu Hayyan said: "There is no harm in it, for they permitted 'I struck Zayd, and 'Amr,' with *'Amr* in the nominative as a subject, meaning 'and as for 'Amr, I struck him,' so the predicate is deleted because what precedes it indicates it."

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Mujahid that the intended meaning of "those whom you do not provide for" is the beasts and livestock, and from Mansur that it is the wild animals, and from some of them that it is these and birds. Under these opinions, *man* (used here for those) is used for what does not reason (ma la ya'qilu), by way of extension.

**Page 30**

﴿And there is not a thing﴾ (إنْ) is negating (*in*, "not").

(ومِن) is superfluous, for emphasis. (وشَيْءٍ) is in the position of nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: there is not any thing among the possible things. Thus what was mentioned enters into it at the first level, and restricting it to that alone is deficient. Ibn Jurayj and others claimed that "thing" here refers specifically to rain.

﴿except that with Us are its treasuries﴾. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is the predicate of the subject. (وخزائنه) is raised by it, as its subject because it depends on it, or it is the subject, with the adverbial phrase as its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first subject. *Khaza'in* is the plural of *khizana*, which is not pronounced with a different vowel. It is a noun for the place in which precious wealth is kept and nothing else. By custom, as it is said, it came to refer to the treasuries of kings and sultans that hold people's provisions. His Exalted Majesty's unseen capacities, which are contained under His all-encompassing power, are compared to these treasuries in being hidden from the knowledge of the worlds and protected from the reach of their hands despite their great desire for them, and in being prepared and readily available for His bringing them into existence, such that whenever His will is connected to their existence, they come into being without delay, like the precious wealth stored in royal treasuries. Therefore the mention of "treasuries" is by way of imaginative metaphor (*isti'ara takhyiliyya*), as stated by more than one scholar. It is also permissible that He has likened His exalted power over every thing, and His bringing into existence whatever He wills, to treasuries in which things are deposited, prepared to come out of them whatever He wills. He mentioned this by way of representational metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*). The meaning is: there is not a thing except that We are able to bring it into existence and create it. It has been said that the more fitting view is that it is an illustration of His knowledge of every known thing. Its rationale, as it is said, is that "thing" remains on its generality, as it includes the Necessary and the possible, unlike power. Also, "with" (*'inda*) is more fitting for knowledge, because the thing that is capable of being done is not with Him except after it exists. It has been objected that the existence of capable things in the stores of power is not in terms of external existence but of cognitive existence. Some said: the treasuries are in their literal sense, namely the places in which things are kept, and that wind has a place, rain has a place, and every place has guardians from the angels, peace be upon them. It is not hidden that this cannot be applied together with the generality of "thing."

﴿And We do not send it down﴾, that is, We bring into being whatever We create of those things, connected to some of those things, ﴿except in a known measure﴾, that is, except connected to a specific quantity required by wisdom and called for by the will that follows it, from among the infinite capacities. The specifying of each thing with a particular attribute, a specific measure, and a limited time, rather than otherwise, while all are equal in their forms and the power is validly related to each, necessarily requires a wisdom that makes each thing specific to what it is specific to.

This is to explain the secret of why things do not come into being in multiplicity as they are in the treasuries. It is either a conjunction with an implied element, meaning "We send it down, and We do not send it down except in a measure," through to the end; or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of what preceded, meaning: with Us are the treasuries of every thing, while the circumstance is that We do not send it down except in a measure, through to the end. The first is to explain the vastness of the power, and the second is to explain the utmost wisdom, as our master Shaykh al-Islam said. Al-A'mash read "and We send it down except" through to the end. According to *al-Bahr*, this is a reading of interpretation rather than recitation, because it contradicts the written text of the Mushaf. The better view in interpretation is what we have mentioned.

He expressed the bringing into being and origination of that by "sending down" because it is by way of grace from the upper world to the lower world. It has also been said: because in it is the bringing of a thing from what its essence inclines toward, namely non-existence, to what its essence does not incline toward, namely existence. This is like His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾. It seems that whoever understood "thing" to mean rain was deceived by the apparent sense of "sending down," and so committed something contrary to its apparent sense entirely. And it seems that, because that occurs gradually, it was expressed by "sending down," and the present tense was used to indicate continuity.

Some who hold that the non-existent is a thing (*shay'iyya*) used this verse as evidence for that. The Imam has explained its line of reasoning and the answer to it, and we, along with those who hold the view of thingness, [agree].

[Page 31]

﴿وأرْسَلْنا الرِّياحَ لَواقِحَ﴾ "And We send the winds fertilising" is coordinated with (جَعَلْنا لَكم فِيها مَعايِشَ) "We made for you therein means of livelihood," and what lies between them is a parenthetical (i'tiraḍ) to confirm what preceded and to reinforce what follows. Al-lawāqiḥ is the plural of lāqiḥ (fertilising, pregnant), meaning "bearing." One says "a she-camel is lāqiḥ," i.e., pregnant. Describing the winds by this is a eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh): the wind carrying the rain-bearing cloud is likened to a pregnant she-camel, because it carries that cloud or the water within it. Al-Farrā' said: it is the plural of lāqiḥ by way of relation (nisba), like labin and tāmir, meaning "possessing fertilisation and pregnancy." Al-Rāghib followed this view. Its opposite is called "barren wind" (rīḥ ʿaqīm). Abū ʿUbayda said: ﴿lawāqiḥ﴾ means malāqiḥ, the plural of mulaqqiḥah (causing to conceive), like al-ṭawāʾiḥ in the line of poetry:

"At your service, Yazīd, pressing for a dispute,
and entangled in what the calamities knock down."

That is, al-maṭāwīḥ, the plural of maṭīḥah. It derives from alqaḥa al-faḥl al-nāqah (the stallion impregnated the she-camel) when he deposited his water in her so that she would conceive. The meaning is that the winds impregnate the clouds or the trees, so the term "impregnation" (laqḥ) is used metaphorically for pouring rain into the clouds or the trees. Attributing it to the winds is literal (ḥaqīqa) on the first view and metaphorical (majāz) on the second, since what is deposited in the trees is the cloud, not the wind. The fertilising winds are the south wind, as narrated by Ibn Abī al-Dunyā from Qatāda, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Daylamī narrated something similar from Abū Hurayra with a weak chain of transmission. Ibn Jarīr and others narrated from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr who said: "Allah sends the bearers of good tidings (al-mubashshirāt), which sweep over the earth with a sweep. Then He sends the stirrers (al-muthīrāt), which stir up the clouds and make them fragments. Then He sends the gatherers (al-mu'allifāt), which gather them together and make them heaped up. Then He sends the fertilising ones (al-lawāqiḥ), which impregnate them, and so it rains."

Ḥamza read «وأرْسَلَنا الرِّيحَ» in the singular, as a generic noun (ta'wīl al-jins), so it has the sense of the plural. Therefore ﴿lawāqiḥ﴾ validly becomes a circumstantial (ḥāl) qualifier of it. This is like their saying: "The people destroyed the yellow dinar and the white dirham." This reading does not contradict what has been said in the ḥadīth: "O Allah, make them winds (riyāḥan) and do not make them a wind (rīḥan)," that the plural riyāḥ is used for good and the singular rīḥ for evil. Al-Shihāb said that this is not from the lexical imposition (waḍʿ) but from usage (istiʿmāl), and it is a general rule (amr aghlabī) rather than a universal one. The singular rīḥ has indeed been used for good too, as in His saying: ﴿And they sailed with them on a fair wind﴾. Or the ḥadīth is to be taken in its unrestricted sense, where no indicator accompanies it, such as a qualifier or a circumstantial. As for the claim that the intended "good" is a supplication for long life so that one may see many winds, there is no basis for it.

﴿فَأنْزَلْنا مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ "So We sent down from the sky," after We had produced, by means of those winds, a rain-bearing cloud, water, ﴿فَأسْقَيْناكُمُوهُ﴾ "so We gave you it to drink," i.e., We made it for you a means of watering, by which you water your fields and your livestock. It is, as is said, more eloquent than "saqaynākum" because it indicates that the water was prepared for them to benefit from whenever they wish. Several scholars distinguished between asqā and saqā. Al-Azharī said: The Arabs say, of everything that comes from the bellies of livestock, from the sky, or from a flowing river, "asqaytuhu," meaning "I made a drinking place for him, and I made for him a place of watering from it." When it concerns the lips (i.e., drinking directly), they say saqā and do not say asqā. Abū ʿAlī said: One says "saqaytuhu" until he is satisfied (ruwiya), and "asqaytuhu nahran" meaning "I made it a drinking place for him." Sometimes they use saqā without the hamza, like asqā, as in the verse of Labīd describing a cloud:

"I say, while its sound is far from me,
it sheds the light rain from the summits of the mountains.
It gave drink to my people, the Banū Najd,
and gave drink (asqā) to Numayr and the tribes of Hilāl."

He does not mean by saqā "my people" that it quenches their thirst, but that it gives them rain-watering, so that their lands become fertile. It is unlikely that he would ask for his people to be quenched and for others to be made fertile. What the Imam Azharī said, that asqā is not used for giving someone to drink directly, is not refuted by the verse of Dhū al-Rummah:

"And I water him (asqīhi) until, from what I pour out of it, nearly
his stones and his grounds speak to me."

The Imam said: He meant by "asqīhi," "I pray for him to be watered," and in this sense no one says anything other than asqā, as Abū ʿUbayd said. Here the pronoun has come attached after an attached accusative pronoun that is more definite than it, and Sībawayh's position on such cases is that attachment is obligatory.

﴿وما أنْتُمْ لَهُ بِخازِنِينَ﴾ "And you are not its storers." He, glorified is He, negated for them what He had affirmed for His own majesty in His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾. As if it was said: We are the ones able to create it and store it in the clouds and send it down, and you are not able to do that. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the negation of guarding it, i.e., "you are not guardians of it in its channels, lest it sink away so that you do not benefit from it." It is narrated from Sufyān that the meaning is: "You are not preventers of its descent from the sky."

﴿And indeed, it is We who give life﴾ by bringing life into some bodies that are capable of it, ﴿and cause death﴾ by removing it from them. Life is therefore an existential attribute, and it is, as has been said, an attribute that entails perception and voluntary movement, while death is the cessation of that attribute. Some have said that death is itself an existential attribute that is opposed to life, based on the apparent sense of His words, exalted is He: ﴿He who created death﴾. The verification of this will come, God willing, exalted is He.
