The giving of life and causing of death may also be generalized so as to include animals and plants, as when it is said that what is meant is the granting and withdrawal of the power of growth. The pronoun is placed first for restriction (ḥaṣr). It is either an emphasis (tawkīd) of the first, or a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the sentence following it, and the whole is the predicate of inna (indeed). It has been permitted that it be a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl), but Abū al-Baqā' rejected this on two grounds. The first is that it does not enter upon a verbal predicate. The second is that the lam (emphatic particle) does not enter upon it. This was criticized in al-Durr al-Maṣūn on the ground that the second is an error, for the entry of the lam upon it occurs in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ [إنَّ هَذا لَهو القَصَصُ الحَقُّ]. Its entry upon the present tense is what al-Jurjānī and some grammarians held, and they counted among this His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He is the One who originates and restores﴾ [إنَّهُ هو يُبْدِئُ ويُعِيدُ]. Perhaps that permission comes from one who holds this opinion. It is strange that Abū al-Baqā' rejected it here but permitted it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the plot of those is what will perish﴾ [ومَكْرُ أُولَئِكَ هو يَبُورُ], as he is quoted in al-Mughnī.

﴿And We are the Inheritors﴾, that is, the ones who remain after the passing away of all creation, the owners of dominion when the period of metaphorical dominion has ended, the ones who govern everything, first and last. Or, no one has anything but formal disposition (taṣarruf ṣūrī) and metaphorical ownership. In this there is an indication that the later one is not an heir of the earlier, as may appear from the outward state of affairs. The interpretation of "the Inheritor" as "the one who remains" is related from Sufyān and others, and it was interpreted this way in his words, upon him be blessings and peace: "O Allah, grant us enjoyment of our hearing, our sight, and our strength for as long as You keep us alive, and make it the inheritor from us" (ﷺ).

And this is of the category of metaphor (istiʿārah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 24:

﴿And We certainly know those of you who go before﴾ — i.e., those who have died. ﴿And We certainly know those who come later﴾ — i.e., those who are still alive and have not yet died. Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration from him: "Those who go before" are Adam, peace be upon him, and those of his offspring who have passed on, and "those who come later" are those who are in the loins of men. The same was narrated from Qatadah. From Mujahid: "Those who go before" are the past nations, and "those who come later" are the Ummah of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It has also been said: those who precede in birth and death, and those who come later in that same manner, absolutely; and this has a suitable connection (munasabah). It is narrated from al-Hasan that he said: those who hasten to obedience and those who lag behind in it. It is narrated from Mu'tamir that he said: "We were told that the verse concerns fighting (qital), so I mentioned it to my father, and he said: 'It was revealed before fighting was made obligatory.'" Accordingly, taking jihad as included in the general scope of obedience is of no value. Moreover, interpreting it as "those who go before and those who come later" in the sense of obedience does not have full suitability. The intended meaning of His knowledge, exalted is He, of these people is His knowledge, glory be to Him, of their conditions. The verse serves to explain the completeness of His knowledge, exalted and majestic is He, after the argument for the completeness of His power, may He be exalted, since whatever indicates it is necessarily a proof of it: one who is capable of everything must necessarily know what he does. In the repetition of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We certainly know﴾, there is an evident indication of emphasis.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and a group, narrated through Abu al-Jawza' from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There was a woman who prayed behind the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and she was one of the most beautiful of people. Some of the people would move forward until they were in the first row so as not to see her, and some would hold back until they were in the last row. When he bowed, he would look from beneath his armpits. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse." Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Jawza' that he said regarding the verse "And We certainly know those of you who go before" that it refers to the rows in prayer, and he did not mention anything about the story of the woman. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is more likely to be the sounder."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, urged people to the first row in prayer, so the people crowded toward him. The Banu 'Udhrah had their houses far from the mosque, so they said: 'We will sell our houses and buy houses close to the mosque.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse." You know that the lesson is drawn from the general wording of the text, not from the specific occasion of revelation. For this reason some have said:

The better view is to take it as general, i.e., We know those who are characterized by going before or coming later in birth, death, Islam, rows of prayer, and other matters.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, it is your Lord who will gather them﴾ for the recompense. The placement of the pronoun (hu) is said to be for restriction (qasr), meaning: it is He, glory be to Him, who gathers them and no other. It has been objected to this: in such constructions the verb's occurrence is accepted as established, and there is no dispute over the agent; here, however, that is not the case, so the correct reading is that it serves to convey emphasis (taqwa). This has been challenged on the grounds that this holds only for true restriction (al-qasr al-haqiqi), which is not accepted here. The opening of the sentence with inna (indeed) serves to confirm the promise, and the reminder of what preceded indicates the soundness of the judgment. In the shift (iltifat) and the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) there is an indication of its cause; and in the attribution to his pronoun, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, there is an indication of kindness toward him, upon him be blessings and peace.

Al-A'mash read "yahshiruhum" with a kasra on the shin. ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise﴾, possessing perfect wisdom and being precise in His actions. Wisdom (al-hikmah), according to them, is an expression for knowledge of things as they truly are and the performance of actions as they ought to be done. ﴿All-Knowing﴾, whose knowledge encompasses everything. Perhaps the mention of the attribute of wisdom first is to announce that it necessitates the gathering and the recompense. Some scholars have explicitly stated that the sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) giving the reason (ta'lil).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 15, verse 26:**

﴿And We certainly created man﴾, meaning this species, in that We created its origin and its first individual, with a wondrous creation that comprised the creation of all its other individuals in a summary way.

﴿from clay (salsal)﴾, meaning dry clay that gives a ringing sound (yusalsilu), that is, it makes a sound when struck. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Qatadah, and al-Durr al-Masun (*al-Durr al-Masun*) reports it from Abu Ubaydah. Abu Hayyan reported from it that he said: it is clay mixed with sand, and this is a narration from Ibn Abbas. In another narration from him, it is thin clay from which pottery is made. In another, it is similar to the first. It has also been said that it derives from *salsala*, when it became putrid. The doubling is an intensive form of *salla*: one says *salla al-lahm* and *asalla* when the meat became putrid. This type of doubled noun is a verbal noun (*masdar*) which may be vocalized with an initial fatha or kasra, like *al-zilzal*. Its pattern (*wazn*, morphological form), according to the majority of the Basran grammarians, is *fa'lal*. Al-Farra' and many of the grammarians said it is *fa'fa'*, with the *fa'* and *'ayn* repeated and no *lam*, and this was deemed an error in al-Durr al-Masun, because the minimum number of root letters is three: *fa'*, *'ayn* and *lam*. Some Basran and Kufan grammarians said it is *fa'fal*, and this is also attributed to al-Farra', indeed it is said to be his well-known view. From another Kufan grammarian it is reported that its pattern is *fa''al* with the *'ayn* doubled, and the original form is something like *salall*. When three similar letters came together, the second was replaced with a letter of the same class as the first. Some scholars restricted this disagreement to cases where the meaning is not impaired by dropping the third letter, such as *lamlam* and *kabkab*, for one says *lamma* and *kabba*. But if the meaning is not sound when it is dropped, as in *samsam*, then there is no disagreement about the originality of all of its letters. Al-Yamani said: the statement of those who say the original is *salla'l* does not mean that a *sad* was added to it. Rather, it is quadriliteral, like *zalzal*. Sharing the basic meaning does not require that it be derived from it, since the evidence indicates that the *fa'* is not an added letter; yet the addition of a letter indicates an addition of meaning. It is mentioned in al-Bahr that *salsal* has the meaning of *musalsil* (ringing), like *al-qidad* in the meaning of *al-muqadqid* (crackling). So it is a verbal noun with the meaning of a descriptive adjective, and there are many similar examples.

﴿from black mud (hama')﴾, meaning clay that has changed and blackened from its contact with water. It is said of a single unit: *hamah*. Al-Layth said it is with a vowelled *mim*, but he erred in this. They said: "We do not know *hama'ah* in the language of the Arabs except with a sukun on the *mim*," and this is the view of Abu Ubaydah and most scholars. The prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa al-majrur*) is in the position of a descriptive modifier for *salsal*, as is the common practice with a prepositional phrase following an indefinite noun, meaning: from dry clay existing from black mud. Al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (*badal*) for what precedes it, by repetition of the preposition, so it is as if it were said: We created him from black mud.

﴿shaped (masnun)﴾, meaning formed, from *sanah al-wajh*, which is its form (its outward shape). Ibn Abbas recited for this purpose the verse of his paternal uncle Hamzah, praising the Prophet (ﷺ):

*A radiant one, as if the full moon were the form of his face;*
*his light cleared away the clouds from him, and they dispersed.*

Someone else recited the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*She shows you the form of a face, unblemished,*
*smooth, with no mole or scar upon it.*

Or it means poured, from *sanna al-ma'* (he poured water), and it is also said *shanna* with a *shin*, meaning poured out in the form of a human, just as images are cast from molten substances into moulds. Qatadah and Ma'mar said: *masnun* means foul-smelling. It has been said that it derives from *sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar* (when I rubbed the stone against the stone), so that what flows between them is *sanin*, which can only be foul-smelling. It has also been said that it derives from *sanantu al-hadidah 'ala al-misann* (when I sharpened the iron on the whetstone), when you alter it by sharpening. Its root meaning is continuity in one direction, from the saying "he is on one *sanan* (course)." It is a descriptive adjective of *hama'*. It is permissible that it be a descriptive adjective of *salsal* as well, and there is no objection to placing a non-explicit adjective before an explicit one. Al-Radi said: when an indefinite noun is described by a single word, a prepositional phrase, or a clause, the single word is placed first in most cases, but this is not obligatory, contrary to the view of some scholars. The evidence for this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a blessed Reminder which We have sent down﴾. However, this requires a reason, especially in the speech of Allah, exalted is He, since He does not depart from the original arrangement without a reason. Perhaps the reason here is the correspondence of the first with what precedes it, in that each of them is of the same class of material. It has also been said: the explicit adjective was delayed to indicate that the beginning of its being shaped was not in the state of its being clay, but in the state of its being black mud. It is as if He, glorified is He, poured out the black mud and formed from it the image of a hollow human. It dried until, when struck, it gave a sound. Then He changed it stage after stage until He breathed into it of His spirit. So blessed is Allah, the Best of Creators. It has also been said: *masnun* means *mansub*, that is, his offspring are attributed to him. But this, as you see, is weak.

[Page 34]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 27:**

﴿And the jann﴾ is the father of the jinn, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It is plural as *jinan*, like *ha'it* and *hitan* (wall and walls), and *ra'i* and *ri'yan* (shepherd and shepherds). This was stated by al-Tabarsi. It was also said that he is Iblis, and this is narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah. However, in *al-Durr al-Masun* it is said that he is the father of the jinn. Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of the jinn. The branching of the species, since it arose from a single individual created from a single substance, means that the species was created from that substance.

al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wal-ja'na* (with a hamza). Its accusative case is governed by a verb that is explained by ﴿We created him﴾. Here the accusative is stronger than the nominative, because it is coordinated with the verbal clause. ﴿Before﴾ means before the creation of man. It was said: from this it becomes clear that it is permissible for the *ramad* (the earlier and later generations) to be one of the two weighty ones (*thaqalan*), with the earlier ones being one and the later ones the other. The address in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿among you﴾ [*minkum*], would then be for all of them. This is extremely far-fetched.

﴿From the fire of the samum﴾, that is, the scorching wind that kills. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It blows mostly during the day, though it may also blow at night. It was called *samum* because, through its subtlety, it penetrates the pores of the body. From the same root comes *summ* (poison, which kills). One says: *samma yawmuna yasimmu* when that wind blows on our day. It was also said: the *samum* is a fire without smoke, and from it lightning is produced. Abu Rawq narrated this from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. Thus the genitive construction is an instance of the general being attached to the specific. It was also said: *samum* is the extreme of heat, and the construction is that of a qualified noun attached to its qualifier, the meaning being fire of extreme heat. Some reports indicate that the fire from which the jinn were created is much hotter than the familiar fire.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The dream of a Muslim is one part of seventy parts of prophethood, and this fire is one part of seventy parts of the *samum* from which the jinn were created." Then [the Prophet], upon him be blessings and peace, recited the verse.

The creation from fire has been raised as an objection: how can life be created in fire, which is simple and not composed of parts of differing natures? Life, like temperament (*mizaj*), exists only in composites, and the philosophers stipulated a composite structure for it.

It is answered that this is not granted, because if life is created in immaterial beings, as in the angels according to one view, and in the intellects that the philosophers affirmed, then *a fortiori* it may be created in simple beings. Indeed, there is no barrier even to its being created in single indivisible parts. This goes against the Mu'tazilah, who stipulated a composite structure made of atoms (*jawahir*). They have no argument except objections weaker than a spider's web. Moreover, the objection does not arise at all, because the meaning of the jinn being created from fire is that fire is the largest and predominant part of them, just as earth is in man. Thus they are not simple.

Some said that the jinn are airy or fiery bodies, in the sense that these elements predominate in them, and that they are composed of the four elements, as the angels are according to one view.

Then, the apparent report from most of the philosophers is a denial of the jinn. This is not the view of all of them. A great many of their early thinkers went to the affirmation of their existence, and this is the view of the majority of the adherents of the religions and of the practitioners of spiritual sciences (*ruhaniyyat*). They call them the lower spirits (*al-arwah al-sufliyyah*), and claimed that they respond more quickly than the celestial spirits (*al-arwah al-falakiyyah*), though the latter are stronger.

Yes, those who affirm them differed. Some claimed that they are neither bodies nor inhering in bodies, but are self-subsistent substances, though they are of different kinds in their quiddity, just as the quiddities of accidents differ although they are equal in needing a substrate. Some of them are noble, free, and fond of goodness, and some are base, vile, and fond of evil. No one knows the number of their kinds except God, Exalted is He. It is not far-fetched that among their kinds there are those capable of difficult acts beyond human power. Likewise, it is not far-fetched that each kind has a connection with a particular kind of bodies of this world.

Among people there are those who claimed that these human spirits and rational souls, when they separate from their bodies and increase in power and perfection through what they encounter in that spiritual world, namely the unveiling of spiritual secrets, then, when there occurs the birth of a body resembling the body they left, a certain connection to this body arises for that separated soul because of that resemblance. It becomes an helper to the soul of that body in its actions and in its management of that body. If this state occurs in good souls, that helper is called an angel (*malak*) and that aid is called inspiration (*ilham*). If it occurs in evil souls, that helper is called a devil (*shaytan*) and that aid is called whispering (*waswasah*).

Some said that they are bodies, but they differed. Some said that they are of differing quiddities even though they share one attribute. Others said that they are equal in their complete quiddity.

The Imam [al-Razi] extended his discussion of this matter in his commentary on the surah of the jinn. It is mentioned in the commentary on this verse that they differed concerning the jinn. Some said:

They are a kind distinct from the devils. The more correct view is that the devils are a category of the jinn. Whoever among them is a believer is not called a devil, and whoever among them is a disbeliever is called by this name. The proof of the soundness of this is that the word *jinn* is derived from concealment (*istitar*), and so whoever is concealed is one of the jinn. This is the end of his statement. What he mentioned as the more correct view is what the majority held. However, the proof he mentioned is weak.

Wahb said: among the jinn there are those who have offspring, eat, and drink like the sons of Adam, and among them are those who are like the wind, who do not reproduce, eat, or drink, and these are the devils.

Ibn 'Arabi mentioned that the procreation of the jinn is by the deposit of air in the womb of the female, just as human procreation is by the deposit of water in the womb. He said they are confined to twelve principal tribes, which then branch into clans. Wars occur among them, and some whirlwinds occur during their battles, since a whirlwind (*zawba'ah*) confronts two winds, each preventing the other from penetrating it, which leads to spinning. Not every whirlwind is a war.

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma'* and Abu Nu'aym and al-Daylami and others narrated, with a sound chain (as al-'Iraqi said), from Abu Tha'labah, traced to the Prophet: "The jinn are of three kinds: one kind has wings and flies in the air; one kind is snakes and dogs; and one kind alights and travels." In this division there is a difficulty for me that becomes apparent upon reflection. Perhaps its gist is that one kind is predominantly characterized by flying in the air, one kind is predominantly characterized by settling and migrating, and one kind is predominantly characterized by staying and residing in certain dwelling places. They are described as snakes and dogs because of their frequent assuming of those forms, unlike the other two kinds. Although they may take on various forms because they are jinn, and it has been said that they are capable of this, this has been disputed on the grounds that it would imply that no trust could remain in anything. It was answered that God, Exalted is He, has guaranteed this community protection from anything occurring among it that would cause doubt in religion or the removal of trust in a scholar or in anyone else. Thus the aforementioned implication is impossible according to the Law. Nevertheless, their assuming of such forms is not frequent. Perhaps it is said that the capacity to assume forms belongs only to the category of those who reside, and that ascribing it to the jinn in general is sufficiently justified by its validity with respect to some of the categories. But this is very far-fetched, so let it be carefully considered.

al-Haythami said: the men of this hadith have been deemed reliable, though some of them are weak. If the hadith is weak for this reason, then there is no basis for saying or reporting it. God, Exalted is He, knows the reality of the matter best.

God willing, the full treatment of this discussion will come later, with the help of God, the King, the All-Knowing.

Then, the course of the noble verse, as has been said, is for the demonstration of God's complete power, Exalted is His majesty, and for explaining the beginning of the creation of the two weighty ones (*thaqalan*). It is therefore an alert to a premise upon which the possibility of resurrection (*hashr*) depends, namely the receptivity of matter to gathering and to revival. So consider this carefully.

(ﷺ) ﴿And when your Lord said﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb: "Remember" (udhkur). The mention of the time, as has been noted many times, is because it is included in the reminder of what took place within it. Also, the reference to the attribute of Lordship (rubbūbiyyah) together with its attachment to his pronoun (ﷺ), upon him be the peace, indicates the reason for the ruling and honours him (ﷺ). The meaning is: "Remember the time when He said to the angels..."

﴿to the angels﴾. The apparent meaning is that they are the angels of heaven and earth. Some Sufis claimed that they are the angels of the earth alone, but he has no evidence for this.

﴿Indeed, I am going to create﴾, in what is to come. This form, unlike the present-tense form, carries the indication that God, exalted is He, is definitively the doer of that without any diverting or deflecting factor.

﴿a human being﴾, that is, a person. He used this word to refer to him by considering the visibility of his skin (bashrah), which is the outer surface of the hide, as opposed to adamah (the inner, darker skin). Abu Zayd reversed this, but Abu al-'Abbas and others from the Sufis and the wool-and-fur scholars, and similar, corrected him on this point. Some of the great Sufis have another explanation for the naming, which we will mention, God willing, in the chapter on allusion (ishārah). The word is used equally for the singular and the plural.

Al-Rāghib mentioned that the plural of bashrah is bashar and abshār. It has also been said that what is intended is a dense body that touches and comes into contact, or a body with its skin exposed, and that a human being was not intended, although in reality it is one. Some of those who said that it is what is intended said: "This is not the wording of the very event at the time of the address; rather, the apparent meaning is that it was said to them: 'I am going to create a creature with such and such attributes,' but when it was narrated, only the designation was retained."

﴿from clay﴾ is connected to "creator," or to a hidden word functioning as a qualifier.

﴿a human being from black mud, moulded﴾. Its explanation and grammatical analysis have already been given, so reflect on this, for there is nothing old in the covenant.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 29 (part 1 of 4):

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾ I have done to him what makes him balanced and well-proportioned, ready (mustaʿiddan) for the outpouring of the spirit (ruh). It was also said: I have formed him in human forms and a human creation. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾. In common usage, nafkh (blowing) is the sending of wind from the mouth or elsewhere into the cavity of a body fit to hold it and be filled by it. The meaning here is an analogy for the bestowing, actually, of that by which life exists upon a matter receptive to it, and there is no literal blowing there.

Hujjat al-Islam said: It is expressed by blowing, which is a cause for kindling the wick of the receptive clay that has passed through its stages until it became balanced and proportioned and fully prepared by the light of the spirit, just as blowing is a cause for kindling receptive firewood by fire, speaking of its result and its cause, which is that kindling. Sometimes the cause is used as a metonymy (kinayah) for the derived act that results from it, by way of figurative speech, even if the derived act is not in the form of the act from which it is derived. Then, this spirit, according to him and likewise according to a group of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun), is not a body that inheres in the body as water inheres in a vessel, for example, nor is it an accident (ʿaraḍ) that inheres in the heart or the brain as blackness inheres in the black or knowledge in the knower; rather, it is a simple immaterial substance (jawhar mujarrad), neither inside the body nor outside it, neither connected to it nor separated from it. They have several proofs for this.

The First Proof: Man is able to perceive universal matters, and that happens through the imprinting of the forms of the perceived objects in the perceiver. So if the locus of those forms is a body, then it either inheres undivided or divided. The first is impossible, because the part of a body that is not divided is a point-like extremity, and a point cannot be a locus for intelligible forms, since it is not something to which a temperament (mizaj) can be attributed, so that its state of readiness would vary in receptivity and non-receptivity. Rather, if it were receptive of the said forms, that reception would necessarily be present always. If that were so, the received would be present always, because the active, separate principles (al-mabadi' al-fa''alah al-mufariqah) are universal in their outpouring, and so it is not particularized except by differences in the states of the receptacles. Thus if the receiver were fully prepared, the received would be necessarily present, and then all bodies having points would be intelligent. It would also be necessary for the body after death to remain intelligent, because the locus of the forms remains in its readiness; but that is not the case. The second is also impossible, because what inheres in the divisible is divisible, so that form would necessarily be divisible forever, and that is impossible for reasons established among them.

The Second Proof: This is what the Shaykh relied upon, and he claimed that it is the most excellent of what he had in this matter. It is that we are able to conceive of our own essences (dhawat), and whoever conceives of an essence has the quiddity (mahiyyah) of that essence. Therefore we have the quiddity of our own essence. Then it is either that our conception of our essence is due to another form equal to it that occurs in it, or it is not, but rather because its own self is present to it. The first is impossible, because it leads to the combination of two like things (al-jamʿ bayn al-mithlayn). So the second is determined. And whatever its essence is present to its own essence is subsistent by its own essence. Therefore the rational faculty, which is the spirit and the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqah), subsists by itself, and every body or corporeal thing does not subsist by itself. His students raised many objections, and he answered them.

The Third Proof: This is what Aflatun (Plato) relied upon, namely that we imagine forms that have no existence in the external world, and we distinguish between them and other things. These forms are existent matters, and their locus cannot be corporeal. For the whole of our body, in relation to the things we imagine, is a little of much; how then can great forms fit into small quantities? It cannot be said that some of those forms are impressed in our bodies and some in the air surrounding us, since the air is not part of our bodies, nor is it an instrument for our souls in their acts, and this is evident. Therefore the locus of these forms is something non-corporeal, and that is the rational soul.

The Fourth Proof: If the locus of perceptions were a corporeal thing, it would be possible for knowledge to subsist in one part of that body and ignorance in another part, so that one and the same thing would be knowing and ignorant of one and the same thing at one and the same time.

The Fifth Proof: If the spirit were impressed in a body such as the heart or the brain, it would either always perceive that body, or not perceive it in that way, or perceive it at some times and not others. The divisions are all invalid, so the claim that it is impressed is invalid. The explanation: the spirit's perception of that body is either because the instrument is present to it, or because another form from that instrument occurs in it. If it is the first, then the spirit, if it is able to perceive that instrument and perceive the fact of its being conjoined to it, then as long as the instrument is conjoined, the spirit must perceive it, so it would always be perceiving that instrument; and if the spirit is unable to perceive the instrument, then it must never perceive it. It is evident that if the spirit's perception of that instrument were due to conjunction, it would necessarily perceive it always or never perceive it in that way, and both divisions are invalid. As for if its perception of it is due to the occurrence of another form from it, then the spirit, if it is in that instrument and the second form is present in it, the second form of the instrument would be inhering in the instrument too, because what inheres in what inheres in a thing inheres in that thing, and so the combination of two like things would follow. If the spirit is not in that state but rather is immaterial, then that is what is sought. Other arguments have also been adduced.

The Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned in al-Mabahith twelve proofs, of which the one above is one; he went on at length about them in criticism and approval. In establishing this claim he relied on something other than that, saying: What we rely upon is to say that every rational person finds within himself that he is the one who existed before. His selfhood (huwiyyah) is either a body, or subsists in a body, or is neither of the two. The first is invalid. As for the first point, because a human may know his selfhood while being oblivious to all his outward and inward limbs. As for the second point, because the corporeal parts are constantly dissolving and changing, since the causes of dissolution, from external and internal heat and from psychic and bodily motions, do not single out one part over another; and the body is composed of compound organs, which are composed of simple organs like flesh and bone. So every part of the flesh is like another in readiness for dissolution, and when all the parts are equal in that, the relation of the dissolving agents to each part is the same as to another part, so the onset of dissolution is not more applicable to one part than to another. Thus it is established that the human selfhood is neither a body nor subsisting in a body, because what subsists in a body must change when the body changes, since accidents cannot transfer, so that a human would not find within himself that he is the one who existed before. Since this knowledge is one of the self-evident sciences, we know that the human selfhood is not a body nor dependent on one; it is a simple immaterial substance, and that is what was sought. It is not necessary that the other animals have this substance, because although we know that they know their own selfhoods, we do not know that they know from themselves that they are the ones who existed before. One may also argue for this claim by saying: We have shown that what perceives all kinds of perceptions of all perceived objects is one thing in the human. So we say: that perceiver is either a body or subsists in a body, or neither. The first is evidently invalid, because a body, as a body, cannot be a perceiver. The second is also invalid, because that attribute either subsists in all the parts of the body or in some parts and not others. The first is invalid, otherwise every part of the body would be seeing, hearing, imagining, reflecting, and intelligent, and that is not the case. It is also invalid to say that some organ holds the faculty that perceives all these perceptions, because it would follow that there would be in the body one organ that hears, sees, imagines, reflects, and understands, and we do not find that in ourselves. By this it also becomes evident that the saying is invalid: perhaps the faculty that perceives all perceptions subsists in a subtle body confined to some organ. This is because we do not find in our bodies any place containing this subtle body that hears, sees, imagines, reflects, and understands. Nor can anyone say: Grant that you do not know this place, but that does not prove its non-existence. For we say: We have already shown that we are the ones who hear, see, imagine, and understand. So if some body, whether a part of the body or confined to a part of it, were characterized by the faculty related to all these perceptions, our reality and selfhood would be nothing but that body. If we did not know it, we would not know the reality of ourselves, and that is invalid. Thus it is established that what is characterized by the faculty that perceives all perceptions is not a body at all, nor subsisting in one.

[Page 39]

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 29 (part 2 of 4)]

It is therefore a simple substance (jawhar mujarrad), and this is what was sought. Those who hold that the soul is immaterial (al-dhahibun ila al-tajarrud) have said that it is attached to the body in the way that a lover is attached to the beloved through a natural, innate passion (ishq jabali ilhami), such that this attachment does not end as long as the body remains fit to be attached to it. Indeed, the soul's attachment is far stronger than this attachment, and it is the attachment of governing and directing (tadbir wa-tasrif). Its ascription to His pronoun, exalted is He, in the verse is because He, glorified and exalted, created it without an intermediary, in a manner that resembles the origin and the material, or for the sake of honour (li-l-tashrif).

Hujjat al-Islam (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali) was asked about this, and he said: "If the sun were to speak and say, 'I have poured out upon the earth from my light,' that would be truthful, and the meaning of the attribution would be that the light that reaches the earth is of the same kind as the light of the sun in some respect, although it is extremely weak in comparison to it." You have known that the soul is exempt from direction and place, and that its power includes knowledge of all things. That is a likeness and a correspondence, and for this reason it was singled out for ascription. This likeness does not apply to corporeal things at all.

No one may say: "In declaring the soul exempt from place there is an ascription to it of an attribute of God, exalted is His majesty and sanctified are His attributes, rather it is an ascription of His most specific attributes, glorified is He. And this entails the absence of distinction (tamayyuz)." For they have said: just as it is impossible for two bodies to be in one place, it is impossible for two things to coexist in no place, because the reason two bodies cannot be in one place is that if they were combined, neither would be distinguished from the other. Likewise, if two things existed, each of which is in no place, there would be no distinction or difference between them. For this reason they said: two blacks cannot be in one substrate, to the point that it was said: "two similar things are like two opposites."

We say: distinction is not restricted to place. Rather, it can occur through place, as two bodies in two places; or through time, as two blacknesses in one substance at two times; or through definition and reality (al-haqiqa), as differing accidents in one substrate, such as taste, colour, coldness and moisture in one body. The distinction of each of these from the others is through its own essence, not through place or time. Likewise knowledge, will and power: the distinction of each is also through its essence, even though all of them belong to one thing. If differing accidents of distinct realities can be conceived in one substrate, then it is all the more conceivable that things of differing realities, by their own essences, exist in no place.

As for existence not being in a place, it is one of His most specific attributes, glorified is He, and it is not confined to a limit of prevention. Rather, the most specific of His attributes is that He, exalted is His majesty, is al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting), that is, subsisting by His own essence, while everything else subsists through Him. And He, blessed and exalted, exists by His own essence, while everything other than Him exists not by its own essence. Rather, things have from their own essences nothing but non-existence, and they have existence only from another, by way of loan (ala sabil al-ariya). Existence belonging to Him, glorified is He, is essential and not borrowed. Therefore self-subsistence belongs to none but God, mighty and majestic. End of quotation.

What they have said about the immateriality of the soul contradicts the position of the majority of the People of the Sunna. Shaykh Abd al-Ra'uf al-Manawi said: "All the sects have plunged into the深 depths of speech about the soul, yet they have gained nothing of value and returned with no benefit. There are more than a thousand opinions about it, and none of them, according to what Ibn Jama'a said, is a sound statement. Rather, they are all speculative analogies and rational manifestations." The majority of the People of the Sunna hold that it is a subtle body (jism latif) that differs from bodies in its quiddity (mahiyya) and attributes, acts within the body, and inheres in it as oil inheres in the olive and fire in charcoal. It is referred to by "I" and "you."

Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) adopted this view. Al-Laqqani said: "The majority of the theologians (mutakallimun) hold that it is a body that differs in quiddity from the body from which the organs are generated, luminous, heavenly, light, living in itself, penetrating the substance of the organs, flowing through them as the flow of rosewater in the rose and fire in charcoal. It is not subject to change or dissolution. Its remaining in the organs is life, and its separation from them to the world of spirits is death."

Some have claimed that the human being is this perceptible frame (al-haykal al-mahsus), and that the soul is an accident subsisting in it. Some later scholars of the contemporary period attributed this view to the majority of the theologians, and made it, together with the impossibility of the union of the receiver and the agent, an argument for refuting the claim that the servant is the creator of his acts. Imam (al-Razi) in his tafsir refuted that claim and approved what we have transmitted from the majority, saying: "They said: it is not permissible that the human being be an expression for this perceptible frame, because its parts are always in decay, growth, increase and decrease, completion and dissolution. Without doubt, the human being, insofar as he is himself, is something that remains from the beginning of his life to its end, and what remains is not what is not remaining. Therefore, that which everyone points to by saying 'I' must be other than this frame."

[p. 40]

Then they differed about what it is that is pointed to by "I." The opinions on this are numerous, but the most solid of them in terms of accuracy and summary is that it consists of corporeal parts that flow through this frame as water flows through the rose and oil through sesame. Then the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) among them said: the bodies that remain from the beginning of life to its end differ in quiddity from what the frame is composed of. They are living in themselves, perceiving in themselves, luminous in themselves. When they mix with that and become pervasive in it, it becomes illuminated by their light and moves by their motion. Then it is constantly in dissolution, dispersal and change, while those parts, because they differ from it in quiddity, remain in their state. When it decays, they separate from it to the world of holiness if they are blessed, or to the world of calamities if they are wretched. End of quotation.

From this, the invalidity of the argument for the immateriality of the soul by refuting that the human being is an expression for the perceptible frame becomes known, as the words of the author of al-Hayakil (Ghiyath al-Din al-Dawwani, or his commentator) suggest, as the words of his commentator al-Jalal indicate. He said regarding the second frame: "You never neglect your essence, and no part of your body is forgotten by you at times. The whole is perceived only through its parts. If you were this whole, your consciousness of your essence would not continue with its forgetting. So you are beyond this body." Al-Jalal said: "Therefore the soul is not a body at all, because the most that this establishes is the existence of the soul beyond this body, not that it is, in addition to that, immaterial, since it may be a subtle body, as you know."

The Qadi claimed that the view of most theologians is that the soul is an accident and that it is life itself. Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq (al-Isfara'ini) adopted this, and was not concerned with the consequence that an accident subsists in an accident. This claimant objected to the view that it is a body, saying: "If it were a body, motion and rest would be possible for it as for all bodies, and so all of them would be spirits, and the soul would have to have another soul ad infinitum." In reply: this follows only if the body were a soul because it is a body. It is not so; rather, it is a soul by a meaning that God, exalted is He, specified for it. You know that the one who holds that it is a body says that it is living in itself, so no infinite regress follows. Between it and the body, according to him, there is a connection through a subtle vapour called the animal spirit (al-ruh al-hayawani). In al-Hayakil it is defined as: "a subtle vaporous body generated from the subtle humours, emanating from the left ventricle of the heart and spreading through the body after acquiring the luminous power from the rational soul. Were it not for its subtlety it would not flow, and it is the vehicle of the soul's activities. When it is cut off, its activity is cut off."

Some have said: it is the balanced temperament (i'tidal mizaj) of the blood of the heart. The matter in this is easy. Some verifiers held that the term "spirit" is applied to the spirit that was described as a subtle body flowing through the body as the flow of rosewater in the rose, and it is other than the animal spirit, and to a noble divine matter that shines upon that subtle body. Perhaps this is the cause of the spirit's life in the first sense, its perception and its luminosity. It is called the spirit of command (al-ruh al-amri), and it is the meaning intended by the spirit in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the spirit﴾ [17:85]. They frequently apply "spirit" in the first sense to the human soul, and in the second sense to the rational soul. The one of which it is said that it is "a simple substance, neither body nor corporeal, neither connected nor separate, neither inside the world nor outside it, and that it is a light from the lights of God, exalted is He, subsisting not in a where, from God, mighty and majestic, its east, and to Him, glorified is He, its west," is the spirit in this sense.

They differed as to whether its origination is before the bodies or after them. Hujjat al-Islam said: "The truth is that spirits came into being when the body became prepared to receive them, just as the image comes into being in the mirror with the occurrence of polish, even though the one whose image it is precedes the polished surface in existence." This was held by Aristotle (Aristu) among the philosophers and his followers. They argued for it: if spirits existed before bodies, they would be either one or many. If one, then either it would become multiple upon attachment to the body or not. If it did not become multiple, then the one spirit would be the spirit of every body, and if that were so, what one person knows all would know, and what one person is ignorant of all would be ignorant of, and that is impossible. If it became multiple, then something without quantity would be divided, which is also impossible. If many, then each one must be distinguished from its companions either by its quiddity, its necessary properties, or its accidents. The first two are impossible, because spirits are united in species, and the members of one species are equal in their essential and necessary properties. As for accidents, their origination is only through the cause of matter, which here is the body, and before it there is no matter, so it is not possible that there be differing accidents there.

After Hujjat al-Islam presented this argument in this manner, he was asked: "What do you say about the report: 'God, exalted is He, created the spirits two thousand years before the bodies'? And about the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: 'I am the first of the prophets in creation and the last of them in being sent, and I was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay'?"

He, may God have mercy on him, said: "Yes, this indicates by its apparent meaning the priority of the existence of the spirit over the body. But the matter of apparent meanings is easy, because the scope of interpretation (ta'wil) is broad. They have said that a decisive proof is not to be opposed by an apparent meaning; rather, the apparent meaning is to be interpreted in its light, as in the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunna concerning God, exalted is He, which contradict what the decisive proof establishes." At that point it may be said: perhaps what is meant by the spirits in the first report are the angels, peace be upon them, and by bodies the bodies of the world, such as the Throne, the Chair, the heavens and the like. If you reflect on the greatness of these bodies, you will hardly think of the bodies of human beings, and you will not understand them from the absolute term "bodies." The relation of human spirits to the spirits of the angels, peace be upon them, is like the relation of their bodies to the bodies of the world. If the door of knowledge of the spirits of the angels were opened to you, you would see human spirits as a lamp kindled from a great fire that encompasses the world, and that fire is the last of the spirits of the angels."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 29 (part 3 of 4):

As for his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "I am the first of the prophets in creation" (*ana awwalu al-anbiya' khalqan*), the word *khalq* (creation) here means measuring and decreeing (*taqdir*), not bringing into existence (*ijad*). He, may God bless him and grant him peace, did not exist as a created, actual being before he was born. But the ends are prior in decree and subsequent in existence. This is the meaning of the saying of the wise: "The first of thought is the last of action." Thus the complete house is first among things for the engineer in terms of decree, and last in terms of existence. What precedes its existence, such as the laying of bricks and the like, is a means to it and is intended for its sake. Since the purpose of the creation of human beings is their attainment of the happiness of nearness to the Divine Presence, and they could not attain this except through the instruction of the prophets, peace be upon them, prophethood was intended. What is intended is its perfection and its end, not its beginning. The preparation of its beginning is a means to that, and its perfection is through him (ﷺ). Therefore he was first in decree and last in existence. And his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "I was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay" (*kuntu nabiyyan wa-Adamu bayn al-ma' wa-al-tin*), is also an indication of this, and that God, glorified is He, did not will the creation of Adam except to extract the pure from his offspring. He continued to purify gradually until he reached the perfection of purity. This is not understood except by knowing that the house, for example, has two existences: an existence in the mind of the engineer, so that it is as if he sees its form, and an existence outside the mind, caused by the first existence. Thus the first existence is necessarily prior to it.

At this point it is said: God, exalted is He, first decrees, then brings into existence in accordance with the decree, second. The decree is inscribed on the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*), just as the engineer's design is first inscribed on a tablet or a sheet. The complete house thus becomes existent with the perfection of its form, a kind of existence that is the cause of real existence. Just as this form is inscribed on the engineer's tablet by means of the pen, and the pen moves in accordance with knowledge, or rather knowledge moves it in this way, so the establishment of the forms of Divine affairs is inscribed first on the Preserved Tablet by means of the Divine Pen (*al-qalam al-ilahi*), and the pen moves in accordance with the eternal prior knowledge. The tablet is an expression for an existent that is receptive to the imprinting of forms, and the pen is an expression for an existent from which forms flow onto the tablet. It is not a condition of either that they be bodies. It is not improbable that the Pen of God and His Tablet are fitting for His finger and hand, all of which is as befits His Divine Essence, and He is exalted above the reality of corporeality. It may also be said that they are two spiritual substances (*jawhararni ruhaniyyan*): one of them is a learner, which is the tablet, and the other a teacher, which is the pen. This has been indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He taught by the pen﴾. When you understand the two meanings of existence, our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was before, in the first of the two meanings and not in the second. End of quotation.

Objections have been raised to this inference from several aspects. Some of them apply to the view of the philosophers who also argue this way, and some do not depend on their view at all. The first: why is it not permissible to say that the souls were one before the bodies, and then multiplied? And one cannot say: if the whole were one and receptive to division, its unity would have to be continuous, and so it would be a body. For we say: it is granted that whatever has a continuous unity is one and receptive to division, but we do not grant that each one that is receptive to division has a continuous unity, because a universal affirmative proposition does not convert like itself.

The second: Suppose we grant that they were multiple. Why do you say that each must be distinguished by a particular attribute? For if distinction were by some thing that is specifically attributed to them, that thing would also be distinguished from others. Its distinction would then be either by that same thing it distinguishes, which entails circularity, or by a third thing, which entails an infinite regress. Also, distinction does not belong to any particular thing except after its distinction, so if the distinction of a thing from others were by its being attributed to something, that would entail circularity.

The third: Suppose we grant that there must be a distinguisher. Why is it not permissible that it be intrinsic (*dhati*)? Its explanation is what they mentioned about the difference of souls in species.

The fourth: Suppose we grant that they are not distinguished by any intrinsic thing. Why is it not permissible that they be distinguished by accidents? Your statement that their origination is caused by matter, which here is the body, and there is no body. We say: why is it not permissible that there be a body to which it is attached, and before it another, and so on? There is no escape from this except by nullifying metempsychosis (*tanasukh*), so the proof of the origination of souls depends on that nullification. Yet the philosophers built this on origination, saying after completing their proof: If the origination of the soul is established, then there must be a cause for its origination, and that is the origination of the body. So when the body originates and a soul becomes attached to it by way of metempsychosis, and it is established that the origination of a soul is the cause of another soul's origination from the separate principles, then two souls would have to be combined in one body, and so the circularity arises.

The fifth: Suppose we grant that it was not attached to a body before. Why is it not permissible that it be characterized by an accident in virtue of which it was distinguished, and that each accident has another accident as its cause, without a first?

The sixth: the counter-argument. The souls, according to both groups, remain after separation, and their distinction is not by essence and its concomitants but by accidents. But the hylic souls (*al-arwah al-hayulaniyya*), which did not acquire any of the accidents, when they separate, have no accident in them except that they were attached to bodies. If this amount suffices for the occurrence of distinction, then let it suffice also that they are such that after that there comes to them an attachment to distinct bodies. Their statement: why is it not permissible that they were previously one and then were broken up? We say: it is not permissible, because whatever is divided must have its part differ from its whole, since a thing together with another is not the same as it without another. If that difference is by essence or its concomitants, then each of the parts must differ from the others by essence, and those parts would have been distinct forever, and would have existed before attachment.

Now, these things currently attached to bodies were distinct before attachment to them. Even if the difference is not by essence or its concomitants, the part must be smaller in magnitude than the whole. Otherwise neither would be more entitled than the other to be the part of the other, the reverse being the case. Thus it is established that each one is receptive to division, so each must have magnitude. Suppose we grant that the abstract (*al-mujarrad*) cannot be divided after its unity, but the individuations of those parts occur only after the division that takes place after attachment to the body. So the individuation of each of those parts occurs after attachment to the body, and the individuation of each of those souls, insofar as it is a soul, is originated, which is what is required.

As for their statement: why do you say that distinction exists only with the attribution of a quality? We reply: it is answered in the manner of what they mentioned concerning the individuation of individuation. And as for their statement: why do you say that souls cannot be distinguished by the constitutive attributes? We reply: suppose the matter is as you have said, except that we do not know by intuition that each of its kinds is predicated of several individuals by necessity. For we know that it is not necessary that each human be different from all people in essence. When in each of its kinds there exists an individual, the argument is complete.

And their statement: this argument is based on the nullification of metempsychosis. We say: this is not so, because when we find two individuals of one species, we know that this individuality is not caused by that essence, for whatever is like that has its species within its individual. Since it is not like that, we know that its individuality is not among the concomitants of its quiddity. It is therefore due to an external cause. You have known that the cause is matter, and the matter of the soul is the body. So its individuation must be for attachment to a specific body, and it will necessarily be unindividuated before that body, and thus nonexistent before it.

By this it becomes clear that whatever has a species predicated of many in actuality is originated. It is thus evident that whenever it is granted that souls are united in species, their origination follows, and one does not need to nullify metempsychosis for the preceding circularity to arise. Their statement: why is it not permissible that they be characterized by an accident, etc.? We say: it is not permissible that their distinction be by that, because the individual soul, distinct from others, is a specific judgment that necessarily requires a specific cause. That cause cannot be inherent in it, because that depends on its being distinct from others. If that distinction depended on the inherence of that accident, circularity would follow. Therefore that cause is something returning to the receptacle, and before the body there is no receptacle, so there is no distinction.

The mutakallimun refute what has been mentioned by the entailment of an infinite regress, which is refuted by the proof of application (*burhan al-tatbiq*).

As for the counter-argument, the answer to it is that the hylic souls are distinguished from one another first by their attachment to a specific receptacle. Then, from the distinction of each of them, there follows its awareness of its own particular essence. It has been shown that the awareness of a thing of its own essence is a state additional to its essence. Then that awareness continues, so distinction necessarily remains.

The conclusion is that distinction must first arise through another cause, so that each of the souls has awareness of its own particular essence. In hylic souls that cause is their attachment to bodies. As for those that exist before bodies, if they were distinguished, the distinguisher would have to be other than the awareness, so that the awareness would be consequent upon it. It has been shown that there is no such distinguisher. Therefore it is impossible for distinction to occur, and the difference becomes evident. God is the One who grants success.

The author of al-Mu'tabar (*Sahib al-Mu'tabar*) argued for their origination by saying: if they existed before the bodies, they would either be attached to other bodies first, or not. The first is false, because it is a doctrine of metempsychosis, and metempsychosis is false, because if our souls had previously been in another body, we would now know some of the past states and remember that body, and we do not. The second is likewise false, because then they would be idle (*mu'attala*), and there is nothing idle in nature. This proof, with all its premises, is very weak, so do not rely on it. Some of the ancient philosophers claimed that the souls are eternal, and they presented several matters for this.

The first: whatever comes into being must have a matter that serves as a cause for it to become more apt for existence after it had been more apt for non-existence. So if souls were originated, they would be material, and they are not, so they are not. The second: if they were originated, their origination would be due to the origination of bodies. But the bodies of the past are infinite, so the souls now are infinite. But that is impossible, since they are receptive to increase and decrease, and what is receptive to these is finite. So they are now finite. Therefore the origination of bodies is not the cause of their origination, and their emanation from their causes does not depend on the occurrence of any event, so they are eternal.

The first argument: if the souls were not pre-eternal, they would not be everlasting, since it has been established that every contingent being is perishable. But the souls are everlasting by consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement), so they are pre-eternal.

This is answered as follows. If by their being material (maddiyyah) they mean that their coming into being depends on the coming into being of the body, then that is so. If they mean that they are impressed (munta'bi'ah) in the body, then why do you say that if their coming into being depended on the coming into being of the body, they would have to be impressed in it? Moreover, the opponent may deny the corruption entailed by the claim that souls are now infinite in number. The premise that everything capable of increase and decrease is finite is clearly not among the self-evident premises (awwaliyyat, first principles). Therefore it is not valid except with a proof, and a proof is not established except for what admits of being applied (al-intibaq), as explained in its proper place. Their statement, "If they were not pre-eternal, they would not be everlasting," is a proposition for which they have no proof to establish it, so it is not accepted.

Furthermore, that souls are of one species (mutahhidah bi'l-nau') has been expressly stated by a group of theologians, such as al-Ghazali and others. The Shaykh among the philosophers also held this view, but he did not offer for it any objection, let alone a proof. Others have argued for it with the following points.

The first: souls share in being human souls. If some of them were distinguished from others by an essential constituent (muqawwim dhati) despite this shared feature, composition would follow, and they would then be corporeal.

The second: we see people sharing in the capacity for knowing intelligibles and in the capacity for acquiring morals. Souls are therefore equal in their capacity to be characterised by perceptive and motive acts. This necessitates that they be equal absolutely, for we conceive of no attributes of theirs except being perceiving and being moved by will, and they are equal in both. So they are equal in all their conceivable attributes. If they then differed, the difference would be in unconceived attributes. And if we opened this door, it would become impossible to judge that two things are alike, since they might differ in something we do not conceive. That would lead to undermining the sameness of things that are the same.

The third: it has been shown in its proper place that every quiddity (mahiyyah) that is immaterial (mujarradah) must be cognisant of the reality of its own essence. But the soul of Zayd, for example, is immaterial, so it is cognisant of this. Furthermore, it knows only a quiddity capable of perception and motion. So the quiddity of Zayd is this amount, which is shared between him and all other souls, by the arguments that they have given to show that existence is shared. Then the whole of his quiddity is predicated of all other souls. It is impossible that this shared element should be a differentia constituting something else, since it is not in need, in Zayd, of a differentia distinguishing it from others. So it does not need one in the others either, for one nature cannot be both in need and independent at once. Thus agreement in species is established. These are weak proofs.

As for the first: one may say, why is it not possible that these souls, although differing in species, do not share in genus? Then the difference does not entail their being composite. Sharing in being human souls and the like may be sharing in attributes that are necessary to their substance but not constitutive of it. Thus they differ in their complete quiddities while sharing in external accidents, like the sharing of the differentiae that constitute species of one genus in that genus. So composition does not follow. And even if we grant that these attributes are essential, why is it not possible that souls are composite in their quiddities without being corporeal? For example, black and white are both included under one genus, colour, so each of them is composite, though not with corporeal composition. The same may be said here. How not, when they have said: substance is predicated of soul and of body.

As for the second: its basis is induction (istiqra'), and this is weakened for two reasons. First, we cannot judge of every human being that he is capable of all perceptible things. Second, we cannot judge of the soul, of which we know its receptivity to one attribute, that it is receptive to all attributes. How could we, when the enumeration of attributes is impossible?

As for the third: it entails that all immaterial beings be one species, which has no way of being established. A group has held that they differ in species, and this is the view that is considered by the author of al-Mu'tabar, who prolonged the discussion on this. The best thing he relied on in arguing for it is the difference among people in knowledge and ignorance, strength and weakness, anger and forbearance, and other things. He said: this is not due to difference in temperament (mizaj), since we find two people equal in temperament who differ in character, and vice versa. Also, the soul of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, reaches a strength by which it is able to act upon the matter (hayula) of this world, and it is known that this is not due to the strength of his temperament. So that difference is due only to a difference in substances. You know that this is not in truth among the demonstrative proofs, but rather among weak persuasions. So reflect upon all that we have mentioned. Later, God willing, there will be a completion of the discussion on this point, and by the life of God, it is long-tailed. In sum, comprehending the reality of the spirit (ruh) is a difficult matter, and the path to it is rugged. God the Glorified has made this among His greatest signs, which indicate the majesty of His essence and the perfection of His attributes. Glory be to Him, what a God He is in His exaltation, and what a Lord He is in His perfection.

﴿So fall down before him in prostration﴾: an order to the angels, peace be upon them, to prostrate before Adam, peace be upon him, in the manner of greeting and honour. Or it is an order to prostrate to God, the Exalted, and he, peace be upon him, was in the position of a qiblah, since in him appeared the marvels of the traces of His power, Mighty and Majestic is He, as in the saying of Hassan:

Is he not the first to have prayed towards your qiblah,
and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the Sunnahs?

In their being ordered to "fall" (al-wuqu'), that is, to drop down, there is evidence that the command was not merely to bow, as has been said, but to prostrate in the sense that is immediately understood.

[p. 45]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 30:

﴿Then the angels prostrated﴾, i.e., He created him, shaped him, and breathed into him of His spirit, and so the angels prostrated to him ﴿all of them﴾, such that none of them was exceptional, ﴿together﴾, such that none of them lagged behind any other in that act; rather, they performed the act together at one time. This is according to what al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad held regarding the implication of ajma'in (ajma'un) as indicating togetherness at the time of the act. But the Basrans said that it is like kull (all), to convey generality absolutely.

From here it was prohibited to conjoin the two (kull and ajma'), so one does not say "the people came, all of them and together" (kulluhum wa-ajma'un). They responded to this by the words of the Exalted, quoting Iblis: ﴿Surely I shall mislead them, all of them﴾, since it is evident that there is no togetherness there. Al-Kashshaf replied that the derivation from jam' (collection) requires it, because it is taken to refer to the most complete state; so when you understand the encompassing from another word, namely kull, it is necessary that it be at one time, otherwise it would be superfluous. The rebuttal by the verse arises from failing to grasp the way of the implication. From this the flaw of the view is known: that if the matter were so, it would be a circumstantial (hal) and not an emphasis. So the truth in the question lies with al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad, and that is what conforms to the eloquence of the revelation. The Basrans claimed that it is emphasized with two emphases only for intensifying the generalization and preventing specification.

Some claimed that it is not emphasized with ajma' without kull, by way of preference; but the preferred view, in agreement with Abu Hayyan, is its permissibility, because of its frequent occurrence in eloquent speech, so there are several verses in the Qur'an of this kind, and in the Sahih (the hadith): "Whoever has killed a man, for him is his spoil, all of it (ajma')," and "pray sitting, all of you (ajma'una)."

Perhaps the origin of the claim is the obligation to place kull first when the two are combined; and this is refuted by the fact that the self (nafs) must be placed before the eye ('ayn) when they are combined, while the emphasis with 'ayn alone is permissible. What they mentioned about the obligation of placing kull first is only based on what you have learned of the truth, for the sake of preserving simplicity and compound structure. This is it. Furthermore, the discussion has already passed concerning verifying whether their prostration occurred as a consequence of the conditional command that was related, as this noble verse implies, or upon the immediate command, as some verses require; so reflect on this.

﴿Except Iblis﴾ is a continuous exception (*istithna' muttasil*), and this may be understood in three ways. First, he was a single jinn among thousands of angels, so he is counted among them by way of *taghlib* (counting the minority with the majority). Second, there is a kind of angels called *jinn* who reproduce, and he is one of them. Third, he was an angel and not a jinn. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿he was of the jinn﴾, is to be interpreted (*mu'awwal*), as you will learn, God willing. His statement, glorified is He, ﴿refused to be among those who prostrate﴾, is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) explaining how the non-prostration implied by the exception came about. This is based on the principle that a negative exception from an affirmative statement implies an affirmative, and an affirmative exception from a negative implies a negative. This is what the soul inclines towards, since mere non-prostration may occur with hesitation, whereas it is known from this verse that his non-prostration was accompanied by refusal (*iba'*) and arrogance (*istikbar*).

It is also permitted that the exception be disjunctive (*munqati'*), so that the clause ﴿refused﴾ and what follows is connected to what precedes it. The reasoning for this is that *illa* is taken to mean *lakin* (but), and "Iblis" is its noun, while the clause is its predicate. This is what has been said. In *al-Hama'* (*Hama' al-Hawami'*) it is stated that the Basrans estimate a disjunctive exception as *lakinna* (with the doubled nun), and they say: it is estimated thus only because it is in the status of a separate sentence from the first. Thus your saying *ma fi al-dar ahad illa himaran* (there is no one in the house except a donkey) is in the sense of *lakinna fiha himaran* (but in it there is a donkey), as a *istidrak* (corrective statement) which contrasts what follows *lakinna* with what precedes it. However, they have extended the usage, making *illa* operate like *lakinna*. Because *lakinna* may not be followed except by a single noun, whereas *lakinna* may only be followed by a complete sentence, they named it "exception" (*istithna'*), in imitation of it when it is a true exception, and to distinguish it from *lakinna*. The Kufans estimate it with *siwa* (except). Some people, among them Ibn Ya'sun, said: with *illa* followed by a noun in a disjunctive exception, the statement is a resumed statement. He said, regarding the line, *wa ma bil-rab'i min ahad illa al-awari* (and in the abode there is no one except the *awari*), that *illa* here has the sense of *lakinna*; *al-awari* ("the *awari*", i.e. the stable things) is its noun, governed by it, and the predicate is omitted, as if he had said: "but the *awari* are in the abode." The predicate of *illa* is omitted just as the predicate of *lakinna* is omitted in the line, *wa lakinna zinjiyyan 'azima al-mashafir* (but a black man with large lips).

From this it is apparent that although the Basrans estimate it with *lakinna*, they do not parse it in this way; it is an estimation of meaning, not an estimation of grammatical parsing. Perhaps the preceding explanation is based on the view of Ibn Ya'sun, except that he did not explicitly state that the predicate is expressed. Indeed some have explicitly stated this, and God willing, a complement to this discussion will come in this surah, so understand. The basis for the disjunction is obvious, because it is well known that he was not of the species of the angels, peace be upon them. Disjunction, as many have said, is established by his not being included in the excepted group (*mustathna minhu*) or in its ruling. As for what has been said, that he would then not be commanded to prostrate, so that there would be no problem, and the excuse for this is that the jinn were also commanded, and mention of the angels, peace be upon them, sufficed in place of them, and that this is the meaning of disjunction, and the blame directed at it comes from narrowness of disposition, (this is not accepted).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 32:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), answering the question of one who asks: "Then what did the Lord, exalted is He, say when he refused?" So it is said: He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ That is, what reason do you have, as the answer implies. His saying, exalted is He: (mā manaʿaka allā takūna) means: what prevented you from not being [among] ﴿those who prostrate﴾, for what I created, although they and their rank in nobility are of the same rank. The form of the imperfect (al-istiqbāl) seems to hint at the greater ugliness of his state. Perhaps the rebuke is not merely for his staying apart from those noble ones, but for several matters related separately, indicating that ( each ) of them suffices for the rebuke, for the manifestation of the falsehood of what he committed, and for its enormity. I have entirely omitted the narration of the rebuke in other surahs, being content with its narration in another place. And the apparent meaning is that
Page 47
the saying of Allah, exalted is He, to him was not through an intermediary, and that is a lofty station, when it is in the manner of magnification and honour rather than humiliation and abasement, as is not hidden.

He said: this is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question) following the pattern of what came before. ﴿I would never prostrate﴾ The *lam* is for emphasizing the negation, meaning: it contradicts my condition, and it is not fitting for me to prostrate ﴿to a mortal﴾, a corporeal, dense being, ﴿whom You created from clay, from black mud molded﴾. This is a general indication of his claim to superiority and the nobility of his substance. It is related from him, may Allah curse him, that he stated this explicitly in another verse. The accursed one intended by this description to show the greater baseness of the origin of the one to whom he did not prostrate, far be it from him. In more than one place, he contented himself with relating only part of what he claimed to be a cause of baseness. His deflecting his answer away from the question was an attempt to escape the debate, and how could he manage that? It is as if it were said: "I did not refuse to join the ranks of those who prostrate, but rather I refused what is not befitting my station, namely prostrating to one who is inferior." The accursed one erred in thinking that all superiority is by reason of substance, and he did not realize that it is also by reason of the agent (*al-fa'il*, efficient cause), by reason of form (*al-surah*, formal cause), and by reason of the end (*al-ghayah*, final cause). Rather, the criterion of virtue and perfection is being free of blameworthy qualities and adorned with divine knowledge:

*So the left is a right hand while the cup is in it, and the right is a left hand when no cup is in it.*

And by Allah, how well said is the one who said:

*Be the son of whomever you wish, and acquire good manners;
its content will suffice you, away from lineage.*

*Indeed the youth is the one who says, "Here I am,"
the youth is not the one who says, "My father was..."*

Moreover, in what he claimed of the superiority of fire over dust there is clear prohibition, and the discussion of that has already been presented.

﴿Qāla﴾ [He said] is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*), as mentioned earlier as well.

﴿Fa-khruj minhā﴾ [So get out of it]. It is said: the apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the heaven, although it has not been mentioned. This is supported by the apparent meaning of His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Fa-ihbiṭ minhā﴾ [So descend from it]. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the host of angels, peace be upon them. Leaving it would then mean departing from the heaven, since his being withdrawn from them to one side is not considered "leaving" in the usual sense, and this is sufficient as an indicator.
