It is also said that the pronoun refers to the Garden, based on His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾, and because the whispering occurred there. This is refuted by the fact that the whispering took place after the command to leave.

﴿Fa-innaka rajīm﴾ [For you are accursed]: expelled from every good and honour. Whoever is driven away is stoned with stones, so the statement is a metonymy (*kināya*). It is also said: what Satan is stoned with shooting stars? This is a threat of being stoned with them. This statement has also included the answer to his doubt, since it implied his wretched state. It is as if it were said: what prevents you from prostrating is your wretchedness, the evil of your end, and your distance from good, not the nobility of your origin that you claim. It is also said that this statement implies the answer, because it is known from it that nobility comes from the ennoblement and honouring of God, the Exalted. Thus what he claimed of his own superiority is nullified, since God, the Exalted, distanced him, humiliated him, and brought Adam, peace be upon him, near and honoured him. It is also said that it implies an answer through silence, as it is said: the answer to what one does not accept is silence.

In interpreting *al-rajīm* as "the one stoned with shooting stars" there is a subtle indication that the accursed one, when he boasted of fire, was punished with it in this world. He is thus like a worshipper of fire who longs for it while it burns him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 35:

﴿And indeed upon you is the curse﴾ — the removal (al-ib'ad) from mercy, in the manner of wrath. And this, from Allah the Exalted, is a punishment in the Hereafter, and in this world it is a cutting off from receiving His overflowing bounty (faydh) and His divine success (tawfiq), glory be to Him. And from the human being it is a supplication for that. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is the curse of Allah the Exalted, due to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And indeed upon you is My curse﴾ ﴿until the Day of Judgment﴾ — until the Day of Recompense. In this there is an indication that its recompense is delayed until then. And the curse, despite its utmost severity, is not the recompense for his deed; rather, that is realized on that Day. In this there is what there is of awe-inspiring terror. And that being made the final limit of the duration of the curse — it was said: this is not because it ends there, but because at that time he will be tormented with such varieties of torment that the curse will be forgotten by him, so it becomes like something that has passed away. And it was said: he was limited by that only because it is the farthest limit that people set in their speech. It is therefore like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, according to one view.

Some of them said: the intended meaning of the curse is the cursing of the creatures against him; the curse of Allah the Exalted upon him is other than that, and that (the creatures' curse) ends when the Trumpet is blown and the Day of Judgment comes, unlike Allah the Exalted's cursing of him and His removing him (from mercy), for that is continuous until eternity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 36:

﴿He said: My Lord, then give me respite﴾ — i.e., grant me a delay, postpone me, and do not cause me to die. The fa' (the particle "then") is connected to an implied element understood from the speech, meaning: since You have made me one who is stoned (accursed), then grant me respite ﴿until the day they are raised﴾ — i.e., Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring, for the requital. He intended by this to find an opening for misleading them and to take his vengeance upon them. It has been said: and so that he might escape death, since there is no death after the resurrection. This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. It seems that he, upon him be the curse, sought the postponement of his death for this reason, and did not content himself with what Allah, glorified is He, indicated in the phrase "until the appointed time" (of postponement), because it is possible that the postponement of punishment is like that of all those whose punishments are deferred to the Hereafter among the disbelievers.

﴿قال﴾ The Lord, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾. That is, you are among them, included in their category and joined to their group. Some of the eminent scholars said: In the answer's coming as a nominal sentence, together with the reference to the inclusion of what the other [questioners] asked, in a way that indicates the questioner follows them in that matter, there is evidence that it is an announcement of the respite that has been decreed for them, not the creation of a special respite for him that came in answer to his supplication. That is, you are among those whose terms were deferred from eternity, as the wisdom of creation requires. Thus the *fa'* (ف) links the announcement of respite to the request for respite, as in his saying:

*So if You show mercy, You are worthy of that, and if You drive away, who else will show mercy besides You?*

It does not link the respite itself to him. His request for respite was for the postponement of death, since by it his being among them is realized, not for the postponement of punishment, as has been said. Placing him in the group of those whose punishment was deferred until the Hereafter, in the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, from among those who came before among the jinn and those who came after among the two species (humans and jinn), does not suit the position of seeking respite while alive. Also, that deferment is known from the attribution of the Day to the Religion together with its attribution in the question to the Resurrection. End of quotation. It has also been said: the *fa'* is connected, like the first *fa'*, to an omitted element, and the statement is an answer to him in general, meaning: since you called upon Me, indeed you are among those given respite.

﴿Until the Day of the time made known﴾. This is the time of the first Blast (of the Trumpet), as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur).

Describing it as "the known" (al-ma'lum) may mean either that Allah the Exalted has kept its knowledge to Himself, or that its condition is known: that whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon at it, except whom Allah the Exalted wills. Others said: he, upon him be the curse, was granted his request in full, and it was only a respite until the time of the first Blast, which is the last of the days of accountability (al-taklif). The "time" that is adjacent to a thing and connected to it is bounded by it, so the first day of Judgment and the first day of Resurrection are, as it were, part of that time. They supported this by the argument that the accursed one is aware, so he would not ask for what he knows will not be granted to him. And by the argument that the absence of a mention of an end-point in al-A'raf indicates that the request was granted. The first argument was objected to on the grounds that it is neither clear nor explicit, and that its being merely the stronger assumption (ghalib al-zann) does not suffice in such a matter. The second was objected to on the grounds that the omission of the end-point in Surat al-A'raf may be like the omission of the particle fa' in the requests for respite and granting of respite, relying on what is mentioned here and in Surat Sad, since the presentation of one statement in several different styles is not rare in the Noble Book.

Among those who hold the difference (between the two accounts) is one who said: the intended "known day" is the day on which Allah the Exalted knew that his term would end, which is the day of the emergence of the beast (al-dabbah), for it is the one that kills him. We have already cited this view from some of the early scholars (al-salaf), and it is very strange. Stranger than it is what has been said: that he perished in one of the battles of the Prophet (ﷺ). We have mentioned earlier that this is something that can hardly be accepted in its apparent sense at all. The well-known view, relied upon by the majority, is what we have mentioned: that
[Page 49]
he dies at the first Blast, and between it and the second Blast, at which the creation will stand before the Lord of the worlds, there are forty years. It is related from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "I came to Madinah wishing to meet the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, and there I found a great circle in which Ka'b al-Ahbar was narrating, and he was saying: 'When the death of Adam, peace be upon him, approached, he said: O Lord, my enemy Iblis will gloat over me when he sees me dead, and he is awaiting the Day of Resurrection.' So it was answered: 'O Adam, you will return to Paradise, and the accursed one will be deferred until the respite, so that he may taste the pain of death in the number of the first and the last.' Then he said to the Angel of Death: 'Describe to me how you will make him taste death.' When he described it, Adam said: 'O Lord, that is enough for me.' The people cried out and said: 'O Abu Ishaq, how is that?' He refused, but they insisted, so he said: 'Allah the Glorified says to the Angel of Death immediately after the first Blast: Power has been placed in you equal to the power of the people of the seven heavens and the seven earths. Today I have clothed you in all the garments of wrath and anger. Go forth with My anger and My might against My accursed one, Iblis, and make him taste death. Bear upon him in it the bitterness of the first and the last of the two weights (al-thaqalayn, humans and jinn), multiplied many times over. Let there be with you seventy thousand of the Zabaniyah, who are filled with rage and fury, and let each of them have a chain from the chains of Hell and a shackle from its shackles. Tear out his foul soul with seventy thousand of its hooks. Call Malik to open the gates of the Fires.' Then the Angel descends in a form such that, if the people of the heavens and the earths looked upon it, they would die suddenly from its terror. He reaches Iblis and says: 'Stand before me, O wicked one, that I may make you taste death. How many lifetimes have you reached and how many generations have you led astray? This is the known time.'" He said: "The accursed one flees to the east, and there he finds the Angel of Death between his eyes. He flees to the west, and there he finds him between his eyes. He plunges into the seas, stirring up their vapour, but it does not receive him. He keeps fleeing through the earth with no escape and no refuge. Then he stands in the middle of the world at the grave of Adam, peace be upon him, and rolls in the dust from east to west and from west to east, until he reaches the place where Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down, and the Zabaniyah have set up their hooks for him, and the earth has become like a burning ember. The Zabaniyah surround him and stab him with the hooks, and he remains in agony and torment for as long as Allah the Exalted wills." It is said: "Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both, will look out today upon your enemy tasting death, and they will look and see what he is in of the intensity of torment, and they will say: 'Our Lord, You have perfected Your favour upon us.'"

It has come in some reports that when he finds no escape, he comes to the grave of Adam, peace be upon him, scatters dust upon his head, and cries out: "O Adam, you are the origin of my affliction!" It is said to him: "O Iblis, prostrate now to Adam, peace be upon him, and what you see will be lifted from you." He says: "No! I did not prostrate to him while he was alive, so how would I prostrate to him now that he is dead?" And this, if it is authentic, indicates that the accursed one has reached a degree of obstinacy to which minds cannot attain.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 39:

﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray"﴾, meaning: because of Your misguiding me. ﴿I will surely adorn [evil] for them﴾, meaning: he swore, "I will surely adorn [evil] for them", ﴿for them﴾, meaning: for his offspring. This is understood from the context even though it was not mentioned explicitly, and it is stated explicitly elsewhere in the words of the Accursed, quoted by God: ﴿I will surely seize his offspring﴾. The object of ﴿I will adorn﴾ is omitted, meaning: the sins. ﴿On the earth﴾, meaning: this spread-out mass (al-jirm al-mad'uww). It seems the Accursed indicated by this that "I am able to deceive Adam and make the eating from the tree appealing to him while in heaven; so I am even more able to make [sins] appealing to his offspring on the earth." It is also possible that he meant by "the earth" the lower world (al-dunya), because it is the place of its enjoyments and its abode. Some scholars mentioned that this meaning is customary (ʿurfi) for "the earth", and that it was mentioned with this word to belittle it. Perhaps the restriction, as has been said, is to indicate that adornment has a place where its acceptance is strong; that is, "I will surely make sins appealing to them in the lower world, which is the abode of delusion." It has also been permitted that the meaning intended is this, and that the verb is treated as intransitive and then construed with ﴿fi﴾ (in). This indicates that [the earth] is the place where adornment is established, and that it is the firm settling of the contained within its container. Similar to it is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

Yet if she excuses herself with the dryness of her udders to the guest, my blade cuts at her hamstrings.

The meaning is: "I will beautify the lower world and adorn it for them, until they are occupied with it away from the Hereafter." It has also been permitted to make the "ba'" (with) a particle of oath, and "ma" a verbal-source particle, meaning: "I swear by Your misguiding me that I will surely adorn [evil]." His swearing by the might of God, explained as His power and dominion, does not contradict his swearing by this, since it is a branch of it and an effect of its effects. So perhaps he swore by both together, and on one occasion he reported his oath by this, and on another by that. Some have claimed that the causal reading is preferable, because it occurred in another place: ﴿By Your might﴾, while the story is one and the same, and interpreting it as two separate exchanges has no justification. Also, swearing by misguidance is not customary. This ends his words. But there is clear scrutiny of this, for His saying ﴿By Your might﴾ may also admit of being an oath. Al-Tibi has explicitly stated that the Shafi'i school holds that swearing by God's might and majesty is a binding oath in law. So the verse, according to the one who claims this, is against him, not for him. Yes, his claim that swearing by misguidance is not customary is accepted, and in my view it is enough to prefer the causal reading. And since it is not customary, and does not imply glorification, swearing by it does not count as a binding oath in law, for those who hold that an oath by an attribute of God takes effect require that it imply glorification and that such swearing be customary. In attributing misguidance to Him, exalted is He, without any denial from Him, there is a statement that evil, like good, comes from God, mighty and majestic. The Mu'tazilah interpreted this and said: the intended meaning is ascribing it to error, as in "I declared him a sinner (fassaqtuhu)", meaning I attributed sinfulness to him, not that I made him so. Or the intended meaning is that He did a good deed to him, which led him, due to his corruption, to error, when He commanded him to prostrate and he refused and became arrogant. Or [they said] He led him astray from the way to Paradise and abandoned guiding him and showing him grace (lutf). They also excused God, exalted is He, for granting him respite, although that leads to the ugly misguidance, by saying: God knew about him and about those who followed him that they would die in disbelief and go to the Fire, whether he was given respite or not; and that in granting him respite there is an indirect encouragement for whoever opposes him, because they deserve greater reward. 

You know that in granting Iblis, may the curse be upon him, respite, and in empowering him to misguide and in giving him authority over most of the children of Adam, there is something that rejects the claim, famous among the Mu'tazilah, that it is obligatory to uphold what is best (al-aslah) [for the servant]. Also, whoever claims that a wise person or someone else confines a people in a house and sends into it a great fire and many deadly serpents, without intending harm to any of those people through burning or stinging, has departed from human nature.

So then what human nature judges is that God, exalted is He, intended by the respite to lead some people astray. Glorified is He, a God who does what He wills and decrees what He desires. As for some Mu'tazilah clinging to the interpretation of what preceded by His saying ﴿and I will surely mislead them﴾, since it indicates that misguidance is His act, and so it should not be attributed to God, exalted is He, it is answered that what is meant here is driving toward error, not creating it; and interpreting what follows by what precedes is better than the reverse. In sum, the weakness of this argument is clear, so it cannot serve as a basis for them.

﴿all of them﴾, meaning: all of them. So it is here for mere inclusiveness.

[p. 50]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 40:

﴿Except Your sincere servants among them.﴾ [The lam is vowelized with a fatha (al-mukhlaṣīn... read as al-mukhlaṣīna, the sincere ones chosen by You)], which is the reading of the Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj. That is, those whom You have made sincere (akhlaṣtahum) for Your obedience and purified from everything that contradicts that. The apparent expression would have been "and among them are those whom I will not mislead," for example, but he departed from it to what he mentioned, because sincerity (ikhlas) and being purely devoted to God Most High entail that. So this is mention of the cause while meaning its effect and its necessary consequence, by way of kinaya (metonymy). In it is also the establishment of a matter by its evidence, so it is among the explicit statements of it. The rest of the Seven and the majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning: those who made their deeds sincerely for You, and did not associate anyone with You in them.

[p. 51]

Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿This is a path incumbent upon Me﴾, meaning a truth that I must observe, ﴿straight﴾, with no deviation in it, so that it does not turn away from Him to anything else. The reference is to what the exception contains, namely the salvation of the sincere (al-mukhlisin) from His seduction. The word ʿalayya (عَلَيَّ) is used for obligation. The Mu'tazila (a theological school that holds that God is bound by what is best, al-aslah) take it in its literal sense, since they maintain that God is obligated to bring about what is good. The Ahl al-Sunna (the adherents of the Sunna, the orthodox majority) said: although this is a favour from Him, glorified is He, it is likened to a binding right, because its establishment is certain and its occurrence is assured by the requirement of His promise, exalted is He. So ʿalayya was used for this reason. Alternatively, the reference is to what al-mukhlisin contains, with the kasra (al-mukhlisīn, "the sincere," with the vowel i), from sincerity (al-ikhlas), in the sense that it is a path that leads to reaching Me without crookedness or error. It is like your saying "your path is ʿalayya" when the passing along it has ended. The choice of the particle of elevation (ḥarf al-istiʿlāʾ, ʿalā) over the particle of termination (ḥarf al-intihāʾ, ilā) is to emphasize uprightness and to testify to the elevation of the one who remains upon it. So it is more indicative of the firm ability to arrive. This is an analogy (tamthīl), so there is no elevation of anything over Him, glorified is He, exalted is God above that by a great exaltation. ʿAlayya in it does not mean ilayya (إلَيَّ, "to Me"). Indeed, Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) transmitted from al-Hasan (al-Basri) that he interpreted it with ilayya. He also transmitted from Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam and Abdullah ibn Kathir that they recited «This is a straight path» (هَذا صِراطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ) and said: "ʿalayya is ilayya and is equivalent to it," and the matter in this is easy. It is connected to a verb of passing (yamurru) understood as implied, and ṣirāṭ (path) contains that meaning, so it is connected to it.

Some of them said: the reference is to their division into two groups, meaning that this division into one who goes astray and others is a matter whose outcome is to Me, and this is not for you. The Arabs say: "your path in this matter is ʿalā so-and-so," in the sense that the consideration of your affair comes to him. From Mujahid and Qatada it is related that this is a threat directed at the one addressed, as you say to someone else, "do what you wish, for your path is ʿalayya," meaning "you will not escape me." Similar to it, according to what al-Tabarsi (al-Tabrisi) said, is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. The thing indicated by this interpretation is what was sworn to, together with the emphasis upon it. The most evident of these views, it is said, is the first. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) chose that it refers to sincerity. It has also been said: the most evident is that the reference is to what occurred in the words of Iblis, may the curse be upon him, when he said: ﴿Surely I will sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, ﴿then I will surely come at them from before them and from behind them﴾, and so on. I do not know what the basis is for its being more evident.

And al-Dahhak, Ibrahim (al-Nakhaʿi), Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatada, Humayd, Abu Sharaf (mawla of Kinda), Yaʿqub, and a great many others recited «ʿaliyyun mustaqīmun» (عَلَيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ) with ʿaliyyun raised and tanwin on it, meaning: exalted, because of the loftiness of his station.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 42:

﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾, that is, no dominion or power to act through misguidance. The intended "servants" are those referred to as "the sincere ones" (al-mukhlisin), so the idafah (possessive construction) is for a known reference (al-'ahd). On this view, the exception in His words, ﴿except those of the deviators who follow you﴾, is disjunctive (munqati', i.e., not included in the preceding category). Many have chosen this view, and it is cited as evidence by the dropping of the exception in Surah al-Isra'. It is also permitted that the intended "servants" are all servants in general, and the exception is then connective (muttasil), with the statement serving as a confirmation of His words: ﴿except Your servants among them, the sincere ones﴾. For this reason it was not joined by a conjunction to what precedes it. The change of wording (from "My servants" to "Your servants") serves to exalt the sincere ones by making them those who remain after the exception.

In the verse there is evidence for those who permit the exception of the majority (istithna' al-akthar). This was the view of Abu 'Ubayd, al-Sirafi, and most of the Kufans, and it was chosen by Ibn Kharuf, al-Shulubin, and Ibn Malik. These also permitted the exception of half. Some of the Basrans held that the excepted part may not be half or more of what it is excepted from, and that it must necessarily be less than half. This was chosen by Ibn 'Usfur and al-Amidi, and Abu Bakr al-Baqillani among the usulis (jurists of legal theory) held this view. Another group of scholars from both regions held that the excluded part may be half or less, but not more; this is the view of the Hanbalis. The grammarians agreed, as Abu Hayyan said, and likewise the usulis according to al-Imam al-Amidi, contrary to what al-Qarafi's transmission from al-Madkhal of Ibn Talhah implies, that the excepted part may not wholly encompass what it is excepted from. Strangely, Ibn Malik transmitted from al-Farra' the permissibility of saying "a thousand except two thousand." It was also said: if the thing excepted from is an explicit number, the exception of half or more is forbidden; if it is not an explicit number, neither is forbidden. The investigation of this question belongs to the books of usul. What is mentioned in some books of Arabic grammar from Abu Hayyan is that he said: what is established from Arab speech is only the exception of the lesser part, and all that is cited as evidence to the contrary is open to interpretation. You know that this verse, together with what has preceded, refutes the view of those who stipulate the lesser part, because of the corruption that follows from it: the exception of the deviators here would entail that they are fewer than the sincere ones, who are those remaining after the exception from the kind of servants; and the exception of the sincere ones there would entail that they are fewer than the deviators, who are those remaining after the exception from that. Thus each of the sincere and the deviators would be fewer than itself, and this is, as you see, absurd.

Some have answered that the excepted category here is the kind "servants," which includes both the responsible (mukallafun) and others, including those who died before reaching responsibility. There is no doubt that the deviators are fewer than those remaining after the exception, namely the sincere ones and those who died without being responsible. In the other verse, the excepted category is the responsible, since they are the ones whose being led into error and misguidance can be understood, for one who is not responsible has no act described as such. The sincere ones are also fewer than those remaining after the exception, and there is no objection to this. Some have also mentioned that the figurative (ido'iyya) majority and minority are sufficient for the validity of the condition. Al-Sakkaki mentioned at the end of the section on argumentation that you may not say "I owe so-and-so a thousand except nine hundred and ninety-nine" unless you place that one in the position of a thousand by some rhetorical aspect; yet he is among those who require that the excepted part be less than the remainder. The apparent sense of the usulis' statements contradicts this.

It is also permitted that the exception is disjunctive even if the intended category is the kind. The statement would then be a refutation of the accursed one (al-mal'un) in what might suggest that he has authority over those among His servants who are not sincere, for the limit of his power is that he may deceive them, but he cannot compel them to follow him, as he himself said: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾.

So the summary of the meaning is that over those who follow you, you have no authority or compulsion; rather they obeyed you in misguidance and followed you by their own bad choice. The inclusion of the deviators within the servants does not harm the disjunction, according to what they have said, that what matters in connection and disconnection is the ruling. The words of some suggest that the verse may be a confirmation of him, may God curse him, in the explicit exception, and a refutation in making sincerity the cause of deliverance, as his statement indicates, for children and the insane were delivered from his misguidance despite the absence of this cause.

(Min) in all the aforementioned respects is for explaining the kind, i.e., those who are the deviators. Al-Jubba'i used the negation of his having authority over the servants to refute the claim of those who say that Satan can cause people to fall and remove their intellects. The discussion of the Mu'tazilah's denial of Satan's derangement (takhabbut al-shaytan) and the refutation against them has already been presented.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 43:

﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all.﴾ The pronoun (al-damir) refers either to those who followed (man ittaba'a) or to the misguided (al-ghawin). The second view is preferred because it is closer in position and because its agreement with the pronoun is more evident. The first view is supported by the consideration that [the followers] are included in the warning against following [the misguided], although the second [reference] was brought in order to clarify the first.

(Ajma'in) is a corroborative emphasis (tawkid) for the pronoun. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from it, and in that case al-maw'id (the promise/appointed place) is taken as a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi), so that the condition for a hal coming from a genitive-attached noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is fulfilled. That condition is that the noun governed by the construct (al-mudaf) functions as a verb-like governor (ya'malu 'amal al-fi'l); this is what they stipulated. Alternatively, the condition is that the mudaf be a part of the mudaf ilayhi, or like a part of it, as mentioned by Ibn Malik and others, so that the agent of the hal and its referent coincide in reality or in effect. However, in that case a mudaf must be assumed before it, because Hell is not the very promise but its place; so the place of their promise or their location is assumed. This is not by way of interpreting it as an active participle (ism al-maf'ul), as has been wrongly supposed.

It is also permitted that al-maw'id be a noun of place (ism makan). In that case there is no need to assume a mudaf, except that there is a discussion about the permissibility of the hal here, because a noun of place does not govern as its verb does, as has been established in grammar. And the governing factor being the meaning of the construct (ma'na al-idafa), namely specification (al-ikhtisas), according to the view that it is the preposition governing the mudaf ilayhi, is not accepted by the scholars of verification (al-muhaqqiqin), because that is among the meanings that do not make the hal accusative.

And there is no concealing what there is in making Hell a promise for them of mockery (tahakkum) and metaphor (isti'ara), as if they were on an appointment. In it there is also an indication that what has been prepared for them therein is of a horror that cannot be described.

[Page 53]

"Seven gates" (lahā sab'atu abwāb): meaning seven levels (ṭabaqāt) which they descend into according to their ranks in misguidance and in following (others). This is related from ʿIkrima and Qatada. Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd* and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Baʿth*, and others, related through several chains from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his countenance, that he said: "The gates of Hell are seven, some above others. The first is filled, then the second, then the third, until all of them are filled."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are: Jahannam, al-Saʿir, Laẓā, al-Ḥuṭama, Saqar, al-Jaḥīm, and al-Hawiya, which is the lowest of them. Other arrangements have come down from al-Aʿmash, Ibn Jurayj and others. Al-Suhayli, in *Kitab al-Aʿlam*, mentioned that the names of these gates have appeared in books of *raqāʾiq* (devotional and softening literature), but they are not found in any authentic report. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the Hadith indicates that some of them are descriptions of the Fire, such as al-Saʿir, al-Jaḥīm, al-Ḥuṭama and al-Hawiya, and some are proper names for the whole Fire, such as Jahannam, Saqar and Laẓā. For this reason we have set aside mention of them. End of quotation. The report I find closest to authenticity, as far as I know, is that which is related from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his countenance, because of the large number of its narrators. All the reports require the stipulation that Jahannam is applied to a particular level, just as it is applied to the whole Fire. It has also been said: the "gates" are in their literal sense, and what is meant is that it has seven gates which they enter, because of their great number and in order to hasten their punishment.

The clause, as Abu al-Baqa' said, may be a second predicate, and it may be a new (independent) sentence. It cannot be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from Jahannam, because "inna" does not govern the ḥāl.

"For each gate of them" (li-kulli bābin minhum): from among the followers and the misguided. "A portion divided" (juzʾun maqsūm): a specific group, separated from others, according to what its preparedness (istiʿdād) requires. So there is a gate for the sinful monotheists, a gate for the Jews, a gate for the Christians, a gate for the Sabians, a gate for the Magians, a gate for the polytheists, and a gate for the hypocrites. This arrangement has been related in some reports. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that Jahannam is for those who claim lordship, Laẓā is for worshippers of fire, al-Ḥuṭama for worshippers of idols, Saqar for the Jews, al-Saʿir for the Christians, al-Jaḥīm for the Sabians, and al-Hawiya for the sinful monotheists. Other things have been related as well. In short, both the arrangement of the gates and the identification of their people differ among the reports.

Perhaps the wisdom in specifying this number is that the sum of the causes of destruction is confined to the sensible things perceived by the five senses, and to the requirements of the appetitive (shahwāniyya) and irascible (ghaḍabiyya) powers; or that the origins of the sects that enter it are seven.

Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ read *juzzin* with a doubled zayn without hamza. Its basis is that he dropped the hamza, transferred its vowel to the zayn, then paused with the doubling, and then treated the connected reading as if it were a pause. Ibn Wathhab read *juzuʾin* with a ḍamma on the zayn and a hamza. "And of them" (wa-minhum) is a ḥāl from "juzʾun"; a ḥāl from an indefinite noun is permitted because it is preceded by it and described. Alternatively it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase which occurs as the predicate. It has been preferred that this avoids the problem of a ḥāl coming from the subject (mubtadaʾ). Some scholars therefore required that the nominative noun be the agent of the adverbial phrase. It cannot be a ḥāl from the pronoun in "maqsūm", because that is an attribute of "juzʾ", and an attribute cannot govern what precedes the modified noun. Likewise it cannot be an attribute of "bāb", because that would require saying "minhā" (from them, feminine). Treating "al-abwāb" as if it were rational beings has no basis here, as is not hidden. And God knows best.

* * *

From the esoteric (ishāra) allusions: "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will come to know." In this is an allusion to the blame of one whose concern is his belly and the fulfilment of his desires. Abu ʿUthman said: "The worst of people in condition is one whose concern is that, for he is deprived of arriving at the sanctuary of nearness."

"And they said: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely mad." They accused him—and he is far above that, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace—of madness, indicating that its cause was his claim that the Reminder had been sent down to him, which their minds could not contain. The allusion in this is that it is not fitting for one whose intellect cannot contain what Allah, glorified is He, has bestowed upon His friends (awliyāʾ) of secrets, to hasten to deny them and to accuse them of what is not fitting, as is the habit of many deniers today toward the perfected friends of God. They have ascribed to madness what they say of divine secrets and gnostic knowledge of the Lord, and they claim that what they say of such things is mere nonsense and falsehood that imagination produced for them through spiritual exercises. By "perfected friends" I mean none but those whose agreement with the Sharia in what they do and abandon has been established among the fair-minded, not those who claim to be part of their company while they are friends of Satan and his party, and his party is his party, like some of the Sufis of this age. For the heretics, in comparison with them, are pious monotheists, as is not hidden to one who has examined their conditions.

"Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians." Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: that is, We sent down this Reminder as a healing, mercy and clarification of guidance, so that whoever is marked with happiness and illuminated by the sanctification of the innermost secret (sirr) from the defilement of opposition benefits from it. "And indeed We are its guardians" in the hearts of Our friends, for they are the treasuries of Our secrets.

"And We have placed in the sky constellations and adorned it for the beholders." God, glorified is He, indicated the sky of the Essence (dhāt) and the constellations of the Attributes and Majesty. Thus there travel in that the heart, the innermost secret, the intellect and the spirit. The spirit attains tawḥīd (unity), tajrīd (abstraction) and tafrīd (singularity); the intellect attains gnostic knowledges and unveilings; the heart attains passionate love, affection, fear, hope, contraction (qabḍ) and expansion (basṭ), knowledge, awe, intimacy and expansiveness; and the innermost secret attains annihilation (fanāʾ) and subsistence (baqāʾ), intoxication (sukr) and sobriety (ṣaḥw).

"And We guarded them from every accursed devil." This is an allusion to the prevention of the unveiling of the beauty of His Attributes, glorified is He, and the majesty of His Essence, exalted is He, from the eyes of triflers, claimants, falsifiers, and those who deviate from the truth. "Except one who steals a hearing" (illā man istaraqa al-samʿ): snatches something from the inhabitants of those holy presences from among the perfected ones. "Then a clear flame pursues him" (fa-atbaʿahu shihābun mubīn): the fire of bewilderment, so that he perishes in the wastelands of confusion, or becomes a ghoul who misleads the travellers who seek what benefits them.

It has also been said that the allusion here is: We placed in the heaven of the intellect the constellations of stations and the degrees of the intellects, from the potential (hylic) intellect (al-ʿaql al-hayūlānī), the intellect in habit (al-ʿaql bi-l-malaka), the actual intellect (al-ʿaql bi-l-fiʿl), and the acquired intellect (al-ʿaql al-mustafād), and We adorned them with sciences and knowledges for the reflective beholders; and We guarded them from the devils of false imaginings, except one who snatches an intellectual judgment by stealing a hearing, because he is close to the horizon of the intellect; then the clear flame of demonstrative proof pursues him, drives him off, and nullifies his judgment. End of quotation. And there is no hiding what there is in adorning each of the aforementioned ranks of intellects with sciences and knowledges for reflective people, from the (speculative) view upon the one who reflects.

It has also been said: the allusion is that He, exalted is He, placed in the heaven of hearts the constellations of gnostic knowledges through which the planets of aspirations (himam) travel, and made them an adornment for those who look upon them and witness them, from among the angels and spiritual beings, and guarded them from the devils. So if Iblis or his hosts drew near to the heart of a gnostic, it would be burned by the light of his knowledge and turned back, disgraced.

"And the earth—We have spread it out and cast into it firm mountains, and We have caused to grow in it of every well-balanced thing." An allusion: God, exalted is He, spread out with the lights of the manifestation of His beauty and majesty, glorified is He, the earth of the hearts of His friends, so that the Throne and what it encompasses, compared to it, is like a ring in a desert, nay, far less than that. In a report: "My earth and My heaven have not contained Me, but the heart of My believing servant has contained Me."

Then, when He manifested Himself upon it, it trembled from His awe, so He cast upon it the firm mountains of tranquillity, and it settled. He caused to grow in it, with the waters of seas of the pure light of His unseen, all the plants of knowledges, unveilings, ecstasies, states, stations and courtesies, and each of these is weighed by the balance of His knowledge and wisdom. Some have said: the souls of worshippers are the earth of worship, the hearts of gnostics are the earth of gnosis, and the spirits of the longing are the earth of love. The firm mountains are hope, fear, desire and awe. The blossoming is the lights that shine forth in them from the light of certainty, the light of recognition, the light of presence, the light of witnessing, the light of unity, and so on. It has also been said: by "the earth" is indicated the earth of the self (nafs), meaning: We spread the earth of the self with the light of the heart, and cast into it the firm mountains of virtues, and caused to grow in it everything of innate perfections, voluntary actions, virtuous dispositions and sensory perceptions, determined and measured by the balance of wisdom and justice.

"And We have made for you therein means of livelihood" (maʿāyish) through particular arrangements; "and [We have made] for those for whom you are not providers" (wa-man lastum lahu bi-rāziqīn): those who are attributed to you and connected to you. Some have said: the cause of livelihood differs. The livelihood of the seekers is by the blessing of His approach, glorified is He; the livelihood of the gnostics is by the gentleness of His beauty, glorified is He; and the livelihood of the monotheists is by the unveiling of His majesty, exalted is He.

"And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures" (wa-in min shayʾin illā ʿindanā khazāʾinuh): that is, there is not a thing but that it has a treasury with Us in the world of decree (ʿālam al-qaḍāʾ). "And We do not send it down" (wa-mā nunazziluh): into the world of witnessing (ʿālam al-shahāda), "except in a known measure" (illā bi-qadarin maʿlūm): of form, measure, arrangement, time and place, according to what its preparedness requires. It has been said: the allusion in this is to calling the servants to the realities of trust in God (tawakkul), severing of means, and turning away from other than God. From here Ḥamdūn said: "God, glorified is He, has cut off the hopes of His servants, glorified and exalted is He, by this verse; so whoever after this raises a need to other than God, may He be glorified, is ignorant and blameworthy." Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, when he recited this verse, used to say: "Then where are you going?" It is said: His treasuries, exalted is He, are in the earth; they are the hearts of the gnostics, and in them are the jewels of secrets. And among them is one who said:

The souls are treasuries of success (tawfiq), the hearts are treasuries of realization (tahqiq), and the tongues are treasuries of remembrance (dhikr), and so on. ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ upon the hearts, meaning the divine breaths (nafahat), ﴿fertilizing﴾ with wisdom and gnosis. Ibn 'Ata' said: The winds of care (ʿinaya) fertilize steadfastness in acts of obedience, the winds of generosity fertilize in the hearts knowledge of the Benefactor, and the winds of reliance (tawakkul) fertilize in the souls trust in God Most High and dependence upon Him. Each of these winds produces an increase in the bodies and an increase in the hearts, and wretched is the one who is deprived of them. ﴿Then We sent down water from the sky﴾, that is, from the sky of the spirit (ruh), water of true sciences (ʿulum haqiqiyya). ﴿And We gave you it to drink﴾ and gave you life through it. ﴿And you were not its keepers﴾, that is, of that water, ﴿for you were empty of knowledge before We taught you﴾. ﴿And indeed We, it is We who give life﴾ to the hearts with the water of knowledge and witnessing, ﴿and cause to die﴾ the souls through earnestness and struggle. It has been said: We give life through knowledge and cause death through annihilation (fana') in unity (wahda). It has been said: We give life to the hearts of the obedient from the death of separation by Our witnessing, and We cause the souls of the seekers to die through fear of Us and the subjugation of Our greatness, from the life of desires. Al-Wasiti said: We give life to whomever We will through Us, and cause to die whomever We will from Us. Al-Warraq said: We give life to the hearts with the light of faith, and cause the souls to die by following Satan. It has been said, and it has been said: ﴿And We are the inheritors﴾ of existence, and the ones who remain after annihilation. ﴿And We have certainly known those of you who go before﴾, and they are the longing seekers striving to advance. ﴿And We have certainly known those who lag behind﴾, and they are those drawn toward the world of the senses through the dominance of the attributes of the self, seeking to hang back from the world of holiness (quds) and the gardens of intimacy. From here Ibn 'Ata' said: Among the hearts are hearts whose aspiration is elevated above impurities and looking at created things, and among them are those tied to them, joined to their filth, never separated from them for the blink of an eye. It has been said: those who go before are the seekers of the unveiling of the lights of beauty (jamal) and majesty (jalal), and those who lag behind are the people of outward forms (rusum), seeking portions and worldly accidents. It has been said: the first are the people of sobriety (sahw) who hasten when called to obedience, and the others are the intoxicated of unity (tawhid), gnosis and love. It has been said: the first are those who hold to the firm resolutions, and the others are those who take the concessions. It has been said: other than that.

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels: Indeed I am creating a human from clay, from black mud molded into shape﴾. In this is an indication of the great rank of Adam, peace be upon him, in that He, glorified be He, announced his creation before creating him. He named him "human" (bashar) because He, exalted be His majesty, touched his creation with His own hands, and He did not attribute "hands" (yad) to anyone except to him. He is the divine copy (nuskha) comprising the attributes of beauty and majesty. ﴿So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration﴾. He, glorified be He, attributed the spirit to Himself, honoring it and magnifying its worth, because it is a hidden secret of His secrets, exalted be He. For this reason it has been said: Whoever knows his self knows his Lord. He, blessed be His majesty, linked the command to prostrate with the fashioning and the breathing, because the lights of the Names and Attributes and the brilliance of the veils of the Essence (dhat) appear only at that moment. For this reason, when the matter was completed and the copy was bound, the lights of Truth appeared and the lines of secrets were read, and they regarded themselves as insignificant. ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾. ﴿Except Iblis﴾, because God Most High blinded his eye from witnessing what they witnessed. ﴿He refused to be among those who prostrate﴾. Had he witnessed that, he would have prostrated as they did. ﴿He said: I would never prostrate to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud molded into shape﴾. The accursed one erred in his claim that he was better than Adam, peace be upon him, and it did not occur to him that the sincere lover obeys the command of his beloved however it comes. From here it was said:
"Were he to say in arrogance: Stand upon embers of ghada wood, I would stand, obeying, and not hesitate."
Some people of unity said: The accursed one thought he was firmly established in his tawhid, since he did not prostrate to other than God, the Exalted, but he erred also, because there is no "other" there, for in the reality of the gathering of gatherings (jam' al-jam') otherness (ghayriyya) is lifted and duality (ithnaniyya) vanishes. You know that this is far removed from what his words indicate, and that if otherness is lifted in this station it is lifted absolutely, so no otherness remains between Adam and Iblis, nor between them and any person among external or mental persons. From here one of them said:
"Adam is not in existence, nor is Iblis, nor the kingdom of Solomon, nor Bilqis.
All is an expression, and You are the meaning, O He who is to hearts a magnet."
Al-Husayn ibn Mansur said:
"My denial of You is sanctification, and my intellect in You is bewildered.
So who is Adam but You, and who is Iblis in between?"
Such speech has spread today in the markets and in the gatherings of the ignorant and the sinners, and the rent has widened beyond mending, the matter has grown severe, and there is none to repel it besides God Most High. ﴿He said: Get out of it, for you are accursed﴾, expelled from the courtyard of nearness, for nearness requires obedience, and the more the servant draws near to his Lord, the more he becomes humble and submissive. ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgment﴾. He, glorified be He, did not mean that after that nearness would be attained for him, contrary to some people of unity; rather He, exalted be He, meant some of what we have already mentioned.

﴿He said: My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will certainly make [evil] attractive to them on earth, and I will certainly mislead them all﴾, that is, I will certainly make desires attractive to them in the lower direction. ﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾, those whom You have made sincere for Yourself and chosen for Your love, or those who are sincere in their obedience to You and turn to none other than You. In this is much praise of sincerity, and in a report: "The world is ruined except the knowledgeable; the knowledgeable are ruined except those who act; those who act are ruined except the sincere; and the sincere are in danger." That is, a great honor, as the Sayyid al-Sanad mentioned in some of his glosses.

﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those of the deviators who follow you﴾, that is, those who resemble you in deviation and distance. ﴿And indeed Hell is the promised place for them all﴾. ﴿It has seven gates﴾, the number of the five senses and the two forces, the appetitive and the irascible. These two forces are two great gates to the misguidance that leads to the Fire.

Ibn Jarir reported from Yazid ibn Qusayt, who said: "The prophets, peace be upon them, had places of worship outside their villages, so when one of them wished to seek information from his Lord about something, he went out to his place of worship, prayed what God had prescribed, and then asked what was on his mind. Once a prophet was in his place of worship when Iblis came and sat between him and the qibla. The Prophet said: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan, three times. Iblis said: Tell me, by what do you escape me? The Prophet said: Rather, tell me by what you overcome the son of Adam. Each of them pressed upon the other. The Prophet said: God Most High says: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those of the deviators who follow you﴾. Iblis said: I heard this before you were born. The Prophet said: And God Most High says: ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan reaches you, seek refuge in God﴾. By God, I have never sensed you without seeking refuge in God from you. Iblis said: You have spoken truly; by this you escape me. The Prophet said: Tell me by what you overcome the son of Adam. He said: I seize him at the time of anger and at the time of desire." ﴿For it has seven gates; each gate has a portion allotted to it﴾.

So each gate has a group overpowered by the strength of that gate. We ask God Most High to protect us from them, by the sanctity of the master of people of intellect, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace.

Page 57

Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs, [and it means] they will abide in them, remaining there forever. By "the God-fearing," according to al-Kashshaf (the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhshari) citing Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is meant those who guarded against disbelief and immoral acts, and who have sins that are expiated by the prayers and other acts of worship. In this is the implication that the God-fearing in the absolute sense is one who guards against what must be guarded against of what has been forbidden. The Imam reported from the majority of the Companions and the Successors, and mentioned that it is the view transmitted from al-Khayr (Ibn 'Abbas), that what is meant by them is those who guarded against shirk (associating partners with God). Then he said: "This is the correct truth. What indicates it is that the God-fearing is the one who performs taqwa (God-consciousness) once, just as the one who strikes is the one who performs a strike once. Thus, it is not a condition for the truthfulness of the description (of being God-fearing) that one should perform all kinds of taqwa. What establishes this is that one who performs a single instance of the kinds of taqwa is performing taqwa, for the instance necessarily includes the reality (of the category). And everyone who performs taqwa must be God-fearing, so the one who performs a single instance must be God-fearing. For this reason, they said: the apparent meaning of a command does not imply repetition. Thus the apparent meaning of the verse requires that the gardens and springs be granted to everyone who guards against a single sin. However, the community (ummah) agrees that guarding against disbelief is a condition for obtaining this ruling." Also, this verse came after the words of Iblis: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, and after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, over My servants you will have no authority﴾. Therefore, faith was taken into account in this ruling, and so it is necessary that no other condition be added to it, because specifying the general term (by a restriction) is contrary to the apparent meaning; so whenever the specification is less, it is more in accord with the principle and the apparent meaning. Thus it is established that the stated ruling encompasses all who say, "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" (ﷺ), even if they are among the people of disobedience. This is a clear demonstration and an evident statement." End of quotation. It may be said: there is no doubt that the context indicates that the God-fearing are the sincere ones previously mentioned, and that the unrestricted is to be understood in terms of the complete, and the complete is what al-Zamakhshari pointed to; there is no harm in understanding it that way, and it has been said that it is the more appropriate.

The bringing out of the sinners from the Fire is established by other texts; likewise the admission of those who repent into Paradise, and indeed others as well. Therefore whoever holds this view is not obliged to adopt what the Mu'tazilah (a theological school) hold regarding the eternal damnation of the people of major sins, as is not hidden. The definite article in (al-jannat wa-'uyun) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), and it is either collective, so that each one of the God-fearing has a garden and a spring, or distributive, so that each one has gardens and springs. The "springs" may, as has been said, refer to the rivers mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing are promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾ and the rest of the verse. It may also be that they are springs (sources) distinct from those rivers, and this is the apparent meaning. As for whether each of the God-fearing has his own springs exclusively, or whether they are not exclusive but flow from one to another, there are two possibilities: it is possible that each one has a spring and benefits from it along with those in his company; and it is possible that the spring flows from one of them to another, because they are purified of resentment and envy. The vowel of the 'ayn in (\*'uyun*) is the original form, and this is how Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs and Hisham recited it; the rest recited it with the opposite vowel, which is for harmony with the yā'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 46:

﴿Enter it﴾ is a command to them to enter, from Him, exalted is He. It is by way of implying the verb "to say," as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "and it has been said to them, 'Enter it.'" Thus it cannot be objected that, after the judgment that they are in Paradise, how can it be said to them, "Enter it?" It is also permissible to take it as implying that it is said to them, and the association (muqāraná) is conventional because the two are connected. It was also said: it is implied "it is said to them," so it is a new (independent) sentence. The reason for mentioning this command after the preceding judgment is that, since they possessed many gardens, whenever they went out from one garden to another, it was said to them, "Enter it," and so on to its end. This applies only on the assumption that each one has gardens, and what is other than that is included in "entered" (dakhala) [i.e., the verb's meaning covers it]. Al-Ḥasan recited "Udkhilūhā" (adkhilūhā) as a past passive verb of the form of ifʿāl, with the hamza being for cutting (qaṭʿ) [a hamzat al-qaṭʿ]. The standard analysis is that the tanwīn before it should not be vowel-kasred, but al-Ḥasan kasred it according to the principle of meeting two unvocalized letters (iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn), treating the hamzat al-qaṭʿ like the hamzat al-waṣl in being dropped. Yaʿqūb, in the transmission of Ruways, recited it likewise, except that he put a ḍamma on the tanwīn by transferring the vowel of the hamzat al-qaṭʿ onto it. And from him (Yaʿqūb) also "Adkhilūhā" with a fatḥa on the hamza and a kasra on the khā', as a command to the angels to cause them to enter it; in this reading the tanwīn is given a fatḥa by transferring the fatḥa of the hamza onto it. In the reading with the past form, there is no need to imply the verb "to say," and the agent in "it" is God, exalted is He, meaning: God, glorified is He, caused them to enter it.

﴿In peace﴾ meaning: while associated with it, i.e., "safe" (sālimīn), or "with a greeting (musallaman) upon you." According to the first, what is meant is their safety from calamity and the cessation (of harm) at present; and what is meant by safety in His words, exalted is He, ﴿secure﴾ is security from such befalling them in the future. Therefore there is no need to restrict "safety" to what is bodily, while "security" is for other than that.

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment (ghill) is in their breasts﴾, that is, rancor. Its root, as it is said, is from al-ghilalah, which is what is worn between the two garments, the shi'ar (undergarment) and the dithar (outer garment). The word is also borrowed for the coat of mail, just as the coat of mail is borrowed for it. It is also said that rancor was called ghill because it is taken from insagha fi kadha and taghallala, meaning to enter into something. From this comes the term ghalal for water flowing between trees. The word ghill is sometimes used for what is concealed in the heart and is blameworthy, such as envy, hatred, and other things.

It is said that this removal takes place in this world. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Kathir al-Nawa, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far, "So-and-so narrated to me from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all, ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾." He said: "By Allah, it is indeed concerning them. It was revealed about them, and about whom else would it be revealed if not about them?" I said, "And what kind of resentment is it?" He said: "It is the resentment of the Jahiliyyah. Between the Banu Taym, the Banu 'Adi, and the Banu Hashim there was enmity in the Jahiliyyah. When these people embraced Islam, they loved one another. Then Abu Bakr was afflicted with a pain in his side, and 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, began heating his hand and cauterizing Abu Bakr's side with it, may Allah be pleased with him. Then this verse was revealed."

This is suggested, as it is said, by what Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, and others reported through several chains from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, that he said to Ibn Talhah: "I hope that I and your father are among those about whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will remove...﴾, the verse." A man from Hamadhan said: "Indeed Allah, Glorified is He, is more just than that." 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, shouted at him with a shout by which the palace shook, and said: "Then who, if we are not those?"

It is also said that this is in the Hereafter, after entering Paradise.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported through the route of al-Qasim from Abu Umamah, who said: "The people of Paradise enter Paradise with what was in their breasts in this world of mutual enmity and rancor. When they draw near one another and face each other on the thrones, Allah the Exalted removes from their breasts whatever rancor was in them in this world."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from 'Abd al-Karim ibn Rushayd, who said: "The people of Paradise reach the gate of Paradise, looking at one another with the glances of ... (qiran). When they enter it, Allah the Exalted removes from their breasts the rancor."

It is also said that this takes place before entering. Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from al-Hasan, who said: "It reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The people of Paradise will be held back after they have crossed the Sirat, until the wrongs they committed against one another in this world are settled, and they enter Paradise with no rancor in their hearts against one another.'"

This and similar reports support what the Imam said concerning the God-fearing. It is also said that the meaning of the verse is that Allah the Exalted purifies their hearts from envying one another over ranks in Paradise, removes from them every rancor, and places within them mutual affection and love. The verse clearly indicates the existence of rancor in their breasts before the removal, so reflect on this.

﴿Brothers﴾ (ikhwanan) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in ﴿in gardens﴾ (fi jannat). It is a ḥāl that is muradifah (synonymous) if ﴿Enter it﴾ (udkhulu-ha) is also made a ḥāl from that, or a ḥāl from the subject of ﴿Enter it﴾, which is muqaddarah (anticipated) if the removal is in Paradise, or from the pronoun in ﴿secure﴾ (aminin), or from the attached pronoun in ﴿their breasts﴾ (sudurihim). This is permitted because the attached noun is a part of that. This is also a muqaddarah ḥāl. The same can be said about the Exalted's statement: ﴿on thrones facing one another﴾. It is also permissible that both are ṣifatan (descriptive adjectives) for ﴿brothers﴾, or two ḥālāt from the implied pronoun in it, because it has the meaning of the participle, meaning "sincerely associating with one another." It is also permissible that ﴿facing one another﴾ (mutaqabilin) be a ḥāl from the implied pronoun in ﴿on thrones﴾, whether it is a ḥāl or a ṣifah.

Abu Hayyan does not consider it permissible for a ḥāl to come from the attached pronoun if it is a part of it or like its part, and he restricts this to cases where the attached noun is something that governs the attached pronoun in the nominative or accusative. He claimed that permissibility in the two previous cases is something Ibn Malik alone held. He did not realize that he had transmitted it in his Fatawa from al-Akhfash and a group who agreed with him on it.

He chose that ﴿brothers﴾ is accusative by way of praise (madh). ﴿Thrones﴾ (al-Surur) with two dammas is the plural of sarir, which is well known. It is derived from surur (joy), since that belongs to those who possess blessings. Its application to the bier of the deceased is by way of resemblance in form and as an optimistic omen of the joy that reaches the deceased upon returning to the presence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and his release from his prison, which is indicated by what has come in some reports: "This world is the prison of the believer."

The Kalb and some of the Banu Tamim pronounce the ra' with a fatha, as does every doubled faʿil form. It is also pluralized as asirrah. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that these are made of gold, adorned with rubies, chrysolite, and pearls, and the breadth of each is like the distance between San'a' and al-Jabiyah. Being on thrones indicates that they are in complete elevation and honor.

It is reported from Mujahid that the thrones turn with them wherever they turn, so they are always facing one another in all their states, and no one looks at the back of another. Thus, al-Taqabul (facing) is confrontation, which is the opposite of al-Tadabur (turning one's back). Describing them thus indicates that they are in the most noble states of companionship. It is also said that it indicates that they gather and converse with one another. It is also said that the meaning of ﴿facing one another﴾ is equal in intimacy and mutual visiting.

In some reports it is said that when a believer in Paradise wishes to meet his believing brother, each of them goes to his companion, and they meet and converse.

﴿Fatigue shall not touch them therein﴾, i.e., in those gardens: ﴿nasab﴾ (fatigue), some kind of weariness. This may mean that they have no need to exert effort to obtain what they require, since everything they desire is available to them without any work at all. Or it may mean that such weariness does not afflict them, even when they engage in vigorous movements, because of the completeness of their strength. Some reports state that the strength of one of them equals the strength of forty men of this world. The clause ﴿they shall not touch them﴾ is a grammatically resumptive clause (isti'naf nahwi, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes it) or an explanatory clause (bayani), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the pronoun in (في جَنّاتٍ, in gardens), or from the pronoun in (إخْوانًا, as brothers), or from the pronoun in (مُتَقابِلِينَ, facing one another), or from the pronoun in (عَلى سُرُرٍ وما هم مِنها بِمُخْرَجِينَ, on couches, and they will not be removed from it). That is, they will abide therein forever. The intended meaning is the continuation of the negation, because the completion of the blessing lies in eternal abiding. This would repeat (آمِنِينَ, secure) if it is taken to mean security from their removal from the Garden and their transfer out of it, and this repetition is accepted for emphasis and emphatic care. But if it is taken to mean security from the loss of the bliss, joy and health they enjoy, there is no repetition. Some scholars discussed whether repetition necessarily follows, arguing that security from a thing does not entail its non-occurrence, such as the security of the disbelievers from the plotting of God, the Exalted, for example, and that the intended meaning may be the cessation of their selves through death, not their removal from the Garden. This was countered by saying that the second view is far-fetched, for one does not say of the dead that he is "in it" even if he is buried therein, unlike the first. Moreover, when God gives them the good news of security from it, how could it be imagined that it might not occur?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants﴾. It has been said: absolutely (without restriction). And it has been said: those whom He described as "the God-conscious" (al-muttaqun), i.e., inform them. ﴿That I am the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾. This is a summary of what preceded of promise and threat, and an emphasis of it. (﴿Anā﴾) is either a subject (mubtada'), or an emphasis, or a separator (fasl), and [the pronoun] "huwa" is either a subject or a separator. And "an" and what follows it — Abu Hayyan said: it fills the place of the two objects of ﴿nabbi'﴾ if we say it takes three objects, and one place if we say it takes two. In the mention of forgiveness there is an indication, as has been said, that the intended meaning of "the God-conscious" is not those who guard against all sins, for if that were intended, mentioning it would have no purpose. And it has been said: its mention in that case is to remove the misconception that those other than those God-conscious ones will not be in Paradise, by stating that He will enter it even if he does not repent, since He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. This has a basis. And in describing His Essence, exalted is He, with forgiveness and mercy rather than punishment, where He, glorified is He, did not say: "And I am the Punisher, the Painful," there is a preference for the side of promise over threat. Although "al-alim" (painful), as many have said, is in reality an attribute of the punishment, the construct phrase does not harm this, because it does not require the attachment of the annexed noun to the annexing noun in actuality; as when one says "my striking is severe," it is valid to mean by it that it is severe when it occurs, and mere slight connection suffices for the construct. The use of the two attributes in the intensive forms (ṣīghatay al-mubālagha) strengthens the matter of preference. Likewise what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the chain of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from a man of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked upon us from the door through which the Banu Shayba enter, and said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, and when he reached al-Hijr he came back to us backwards and said: 'When I went out, Jibril (peace be upon him) came and said: O Muhammad, Allah the Exalted says: Why do you make My servants despair? ﴿Inform My servants that I am the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ — the verse.'"

And the precedence of the promise also supports this, and in it is an indication of the precedence of mercy, as the well-known report states.

Yet, with all of this, there is in the verse that which makes hearts humble. Abd ibn Humayd and a group narrated from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: "It reached us that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: 'If the servant knew the extent of Allah's pardon, he would not refrain from the unlawful; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy himself.'"

And al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Abu Hurayra that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah, glorified is He, created mercy on the day He created it as one hundred mercies. He retained with Himself ninety-nine mercies and sent down into His creation, all of them, one mercy. If the disbeliever knew all that He has of mercy, he would not despair of His mercy; and if the believer knew all that Allah the Exalted has of punishment, he would not feel safe from the Fire.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants﴾. It has been said: absolutely (without restriction). And it has been said: those whom He described as "the God-conscious" (al-muttaqun), i.e., inform them. ﴿That I am the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾. This is a summary of what preceded of promise and threat, and an emphasis of it. (﴿Anā﴾) is either a subject (mubtada'), or an emphasis, or a separator (fasl), and [the pronoun] "huwa" is either a subject or a separator. And "an" and what follows it — Abu Hayyan said: it fills the place of the two objects of ﴿nabbi'﴾ if we say it takes three objects, and one place if we say it takes two. In the mention of forgiveness there is an indication, as has been said, that the intended meaning of "the God-conscious" is not those who guard against all sins, for if that were intended, mentioning it would have no purpose. And it has been said: its mention in that case is to remove the misconception that those other than those God-conscious ones will not be in Paradise, by stating that He will enter it even if he does not repent, since He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. This has a basis. And in describing His Essence, exalted is He, with forgiveness and mercy rather than punishment, where He, glorified is He, did not say: "And I am the Punisher, the Painful," there is a preference for the side of promise over threat. Although "al-alim" (painful), as many have said, is in reality an attribute of the punishment, the construct phrase does not harm this, because it does not require the attachment of the annexed noun to the annexing noun in actuality; as when one says "my striking is severe," it is valid to mean by it that it is severe when it occurs, and mere slight connection suffices for the construct. The use of the two attributes in the intensive forms (ṣīghatay al-mubālagha) strengthens the matter of preference. Likewise what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the chain of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from a man of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked upon us from the door through which the Banu Shayba enter, and said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, and when he reached al-Hijr he came back to us backwards and said: 'When I went out, Jibril (peace be upon him) came and said: O Muhammad, Allah the Exalted says: Why do you make My servants despair? ﴿Inform My servants that I am the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ — the verse.'"

And the precedence of the promise also supports this, and in it is an indication of the precedence of mercy, as the well-known report states.

Yet, with all of this, there is in the verse that which makes hearts humble. Abd ibn Humayd and a group narrated from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: "It reached us that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: 'If the servant knew the extent of Allah's pardon, he would not refrain from the unlawful; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy himself.'"

And al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Abu Hurayra that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah, glorified is He, created mercy on the day He created it as one hundred mercies. He retained with Himself ninety-nine mercies and sent down into His creation, all of them, one mercy. If the disbeliever knew all that He has of mercy, he would not despair of His mercy; and if the believer knew all that Allah the Exalted has of punishment, he would not feel safe from the Fire.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 51:

Then, when Exalted is He had mentioned the promise and the threat, He mentioned what would confirm that, in line with what they contained of glad tidings and destruction, by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And inform them about the guests of Ibrahim﴾, and so on. It has also been said that this is an elaboration of what the preceding verse contained of both of them, not of the threat alone as has been said. By "the guests of Ibrahim" is meant the angels, peace be upon them, who gave him the good news of a son and of the destruction of the people of Lut, peace be upon him. They were called "guests" because they appeared in the form of the kind of guests who used to visit him, peace be upon him, and no one would visit him without his hosting them. Because his palace had four doors, one on each side, so that no one would escape him, he was called the father of guests (Abu al-Daifan). The number of them has been disputed, as has already been mentioned. The word (ḍayf) is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the more eloquent usage is that it is not made dual, plural, or feminine for the dual, plural, or feminine forms, so there is no need to strain with an implied noun, i.e., "companions of a guest," as al-Nahhas and others have said. Exalted is He did not refer to their title of messengership because they were not sent to him, peace be upon him, but to the people of Lut, peace be upon him, as will come, God willing, mentioned.

And Abu Haywa read ﴿wa-nabbi'hum﴾ with the hamza replaced by a yā'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 52:

﴿When they entered upon him﴾ is in the accusative case, as an object of a deleted verb coordinated with ﴿tell﴾ (nabbi'), meaning: "and remember the time of their entering upon him." Or it is an adverb (zarf) modifying "guest" (ḍayf), on the basis that it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an adverb modifying it on the basis that it is now a verbal noun annexed to its object, the implied meaning being "the companions of a guest," as I heard from al-Nahhas and others. It may also be an adverb modifying a predicate (khabar) annexed to "guest," i.e., "the news of Abraham's guest at the time of their entering upon him." ﴿Then they said﴾ at that time: ﴿"Peace!"﴾ is a portion excerpted from a quoted sentence governed by "said," and it is not governed by it; that is, "I greet you with a peace from safety," or "we greet you with a greeting of peace." It has also been said that it is an attributive adjective of a deleted verbal noun, its estimated form being "they said a saying, 'Peace!'" ﴿He said: "Indeed we are fearful of you."﴾ That is, afraid, for wajil is the agitation of the soul in anticipation of something disliked. His saying, peace be upon him, this was, according to more than one scholar, after he had brought forward to them the roasted calf, but they did not eat from it, and it was the custom that when a guest does not eat from what is presented to him, they assume that he has not come with good intent. It has also been said that it was at the beginning of their entering, when they entered upon him, peace be upon him, without permission and at a time when one does not call upon someone in such circumstances. This was objected to on the grounds that if it were so, they would have answered then with what they answered, and he, peace be upon him, would not have brought food near them. Also, the words of the Exalted: ﴿When he saw that their hands did not reach toward it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them﴾ are evident regarding what preceded, and perhaps this declaration was after the sensing of fear.

It has been said: it is possible that "said" here is metaphorical, in that signs of fear had appeared upon him, peace be upon him, until he became like one who speaks it explicitly. The bringing near of food was not mentioned here, being sufficient with its mention in another place, just as his, peace be upon him, not returning the greeting to them is not mentioned for that reason. What benefits you here has already been detailed in Hud, so recall it.
