**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 15, verse 53:**

﴿They said: "Do not be afraid."﴾ Do not fear. Al-Hasan read «لا تُوجَلْ» (lā tūjal), with a dammah on the tā' and in the passive voice, from al-ijjāl (causing fear). It was also read «لا تُواجِلْ» (lā tuwājil), from wājalahu, meaning awjalahu (made him afraid). And it was read «لا تَأْجَلْ» (lā ta'jal), with the wāw changed to an alif, as in the Arabic saying tābah for tawbah.

﴿Indeed, We give you good news﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) that carries the sense of a reason for the prohibition against fear. The one who receives good news is hardly approached by fear or sorrow in his courtyard. How could he be, when this is good news of his survival and the survival of his household in health and safety for a long time?

﴿of a boy﴾ This is Ishaq (peace be upon him), because he is named explicitly in another passage. God, glorified is He, gave the good news here to Ibrahim, and in another verse to his wife, and each has its own aspect. Perhaps the reason it is given here is that it better suits informing the Arabs of what happened to their most distant forefather (peace be upon him). Perhaps God did not mention the good news of Ya'qub because He was content with what is mentioned in Surah Hud. The tanwīn (indefinite ending) here is for magnification, meaning a boy of great rank. ﴿Knowing﴾ means possessing much knowledge. It has been said that the purpose of this is to indicate that he will be a prophet. This is in line with God's saying, ﴿And We gave him the good news of Ishaq, a prophet﴾.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 54:**

﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings of this"﴾ [even] ﴿though old age has touched me﴾, and it has affected me. The interrogative is for expressing wonder. (*ʿalā*) has the meaning of *maʿa* (with), as in His Exalted words: ﴿and gave wealth, in spite of love for it﴾, according to one of the two opinions regarding the pronoun. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). Thus he, peace be upon him, was expressing wonder at their giving him good tidings while he was in this condition, which is incompatible with that. It is also possible that the interrogative is for denial (*inkār*), with (*ʿalā*) according to what you have heard, meaning that the good tidings should not occur together with the mentioned condition. Some of those who claim affiliation to the people of knowledge hold that it is better to take (*ʿalā*) in the sense of (*fī*, in), as in His Exalted words: ﴿and he entered the city at a time of heedlessness﴾ and His Glorified words: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾, for two reasons: the avoidance of having to supply an implied element, and that accompaniment, given that it is true at the first touch, does not contradict the good tidings. By my life, this is a kind of nonsense, as is not hidden from any person. Then he, peace be upon him, went further in this, saying: ﴿Then with what do you give me good tidings﴾, that is, then with what marvel do you give me good tidings, or with what thing do you give me good tidings? For good tidings of something that does not normally occur is a good tiding without anything. It is also permitted that the (*bāʾ*) be for accompaniment (*mulābasa*), and the interrogative be a question about the manner and way, meaning: you give good tidings while being in association with what manner? And there is no way to that in the usual course.

Al-A'raj read *"bashshartumūnī"* without the interrogative hamza. Ibn Muhaysin read *"al-kubr"* with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf* and a *sukūn* on the *bāʾ*. Ibn Kathir read with a *kasra* on the *nūn*, doubled, without a *yāʾ*, on the basis of the assimilation of the plural *nūn* into the protective *nūn* (*nūn al-wiqāya*), and sufficing with the *kasra* instead of the *yāʾ*. Nafi' read with a *kasra* on the *nūn*, lightened (single). Abu Hatim objected to this, saying that a form like this occurs only in poetry, and this is something not to be paid attention to. It is explained as the deletion of the *nūn* of nominative (*nūn al-rafʿ*), as is the school of Sibawayh, to avoid the accumulation of two like letters, and by retaining the protective *nūn* to indicate the *yāʾ*. It has been said: the protective *nūn* was deleted, the *nūn* of nominative was given a *kasra*, and the *yāʾ* was deleted, making do with the *kasra*. Deletion in this manner is common and eloquent, and it has been read in this way in many places. The first (explanation) is preferred for its lesser burden, and for the possibility that no *nūn* was deleted in this reading, by its being that he sufficed with the *kasra* of the *nūn* of nominative from the beginning. This is contrary to what is transmitted in the books of grammar and morphology, even if some of them hold it.

Page 62
Al-Hasan read like Ibn Kathir, except that he retained the *yāʾ*. The rest of the Seven read with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn*, and this is the *nūn* of nominative.

﴿They said: "We give you good news of the truth"﴾: that is, of a matter that is certainly established, or of certainty that admits no doubt, or of a manner that is true. This is the command of the One who has the command, who is able to create a child without two parents, so how much more able is He to bring it about from an old man and an old woman. ﴿So do not be one of those who despair﴾: that is, those who despair of the breaking of habit (khariq al-'adah) on your behalf. For the manifestation of extraordinary events (khawariq) at the hands of the Prophets, peace be upon them, is so frequent that, in relation to them, it is not considered a violation of habit. It seems that his intention, peace be upon him, was to magnify the blessing of God Most High upon him, within the framework of ordinary wonder that is based on the way of God Most High as followed among His servants, exalted and high is He, and not to regard that as improbable in relation to His power, exalted is His majesty. For he, peace be upon him, and the Prophet in general, is far greater in rank than that. This is indicated by the words of the angels, peace be upon them: ﴿So do not be one of those who despair﴾, with the emphasis it contains, rather than their saying: "one of those who doubt" or the like.

"He said, 'And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those who are astray?'" The interrogative here is one of denial, meaning: no one despairs of the mercy of his Lord ﴿except the ones who are astray﴾, i.e., the disbelievers who err from the path of knowing God, so they do not recognize the vastness of His mercy and the perfection of His knowledge and power, glorified and exalted is He. This is like the saying of his son Ya'qub (Jacob): ﴿Indeed, no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾. What he (peace be upon him) intends is to negate despair from himself in the most emphatic manner, meaning: there is no despair in me regarding the mercy of the Exalted; rather, what I say is to show that my condition is incompatible with the outpouring of that magnificent blessing upon me. And in the mention of the title of Lordship and mercy there is what is not hidden of eloquence.

Ibn Wththab, Talhah, al-A'mash and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿al-qanntiyn﴾ (al-qaṇṭiyn), and the two Nahwiyyan (al-Kisa'i and Hamzah... as transmitted) and al-A'mash read ﴿yaqnit﴾ with a kasra on the nun, while the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and al-Ashhab read it with a damma, which is irregular (shadhdh); its past tense follows the same pattern in its three vowelings.

The verse has been used to explain "al-Dallin" in the sense mentioned, since you have heard what you have heard of the verse, that despair (qunut), which is, as al-Raghib said, despair of good, is disbelief (kufr). The matter is disputed. The Shafi'is hold that this and likewise feeling secure from the plotting of Allah (al-amn min al-makr) are among the major sins (al-kaba'ir), on account of the hadith traced to Ibn Mas'ud, or raised to the Prophet ﷺ: "Among the major sins are associating partners with Allah the Exalted, despairing of the mercy of Allah the Exalted, and feeling secure from the plotting of Allah the Exalted."

Al-Kamal ibn Abi Sharif said: The conjunction linking these to shirk, taking "disbelief" in its general sense, requires a distinction. If by despair is meant denying the vastness of God's mercy in forgiving sins, and by security is meant believing that there is no plotting at all, then each of them is disbelief by consensus, since it is a rejection of the Glorious Qur'an. But if what is meant is considering sins grave and deeming forgiveness of them unlikely to a degree that enters the definition of despair, and the overcoming of hope which places one within the definition of security, then it is a major sin by consensus. End of quote. The discussion of this has already preceded, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 57:

﴿He said, "What then is your business, O messengers?"﴾ That is, what is your affair, your momentous matter for which you were sent, apart from the good tidings? Perhaps he (peace be upon him) knew that the complete purpose was not the good tidings, from a statement of theirs omitted here in the course of the dialogue. The insertion of "he said" (qāla) between his two speeches (peace be upon him) indicates that something was left unmentioned. Their address to him (peace be upon them) with the title of messengers, after his earlier address had been without that, together with its being introduced by the fā' (the "then" of consequence), clearly shows that their omitted statement contained what he understood from it. So there is no need to resort to the view that his knowledge that the good tidings were not the whole purpose was due to their being a group, since good tidings do not require a group. That is why one was sufficient in the cases of Zakariyya and Maryam (peace be upon them both). Nor is there need to say that they gave him the good tidings in passing, to remove his fear, for if the good tidings had been the whole purpose they would have begun with them. Yet there is an objection to this: it has been said that punishment, like good tidings, also does not require a group. Do you not see that Gabriel (peace be upon him) overturned their cities with one of his wings? Furthermore, his statement "and that is why he was satisfied with one, etc." is refuted by the fact that Zakariyya (peace be upon him) did not suffice with one in his good tidings, as indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: God gives you good news of Yahya﴾. As for Maryam (peace be upon her), only one came to her for the breathing of the Spirit and the gift, as indicated by His words: ﴿to bestow upon you a pure boy﴾, and His words: ﴿So We breathed into it of Our Spirit﴾. The good tidings were a necessary part of that gift and contained within it, and were not the intended purpose in themselves. Furthermore, his statement "if the good tidings had been the whole purpose, they would have begun with them" is undermined by what occurred in the story of Maryam (peace be upon her), when she said: ﴿Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing.﴾ ﴿He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord, to bestow upon you a pure boy."﴾

It may therefore be that their words ﴿Do not fear﴾ were a preparation for the good tidings. This has been answered by saying that the objection does not apply, because Maryam (peace be upon her), owing to the purity of her station, as soon as she first saw him in human form, hastened to seek refuge, so she did not let him begin with the good tidings. This differs from our present case. As for what preceded, the meaning is that the customary practice among people is that one is sent for good tidings, while a group is sent for other things such as war, seizure and the like. God Most High arranges the affairs of people according to what they are accustomed to, so the story of Gabriel (peace be upon him) does not refute this. And if it is said that by "the angels" in that verse is meant Gabriel (peace be upon him), as in the saying "so-and-so rides horses and wears garments," meaning the genus that is truly applied to one of them, this was said by some of the verifiers. The earlier point, that the knowledge came from a statement made during the dialogue and omitted, has been criticized as far-fetched, and the insertion of "he said," the fā', and the address with the title of messengers do not favour it. As for the first, it is possible that it is there because a transition to another topic has occurred, and such things are common in speech. As for the second, it is possible that the fā' is explanatory, meaning: "If this is established, then tell me, what is your business for which you came, apart from good tidings?" As for the third, it may be said that he (peace be upon him) did not know that they were angels sent from God Most High until after the good tidings, and he did not know how to address them with that title when denying or marvelling at their good tidings. Likewise, he would not have known how to respond in that way, as will not be hidden from people of sound taste. Indeed, it may even be said that he would not have known how to address them thus at the words ﴿Indeed, we are apprehensive of you﴾, even on the supposition that he knew this before the good tidings, since the situation there is too constrained to prolong the speech with such an address. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verses 58–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said: "Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people"﴾. They are the people of Lut, peace be upon him. They are referred to indefinitely and described as guilty to belittle them and to censure them. ﴿Except the family of Lut﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible for this to be an exception from "a people" with regard to the description, so the exception is disjunct (munqati', exception where the excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes), because they are not a guilty people. The possibility of a predominance (taghlib) with this consideration, so that the exception becomes connected (muttasil, exception where the excluded item belongs to the category of what precedes), is not what the context requires. Even if it is granted, it does no harm to what was mentioned, because it is based on the literal meaning, and it does not preclude the validity of connection under another reading. It is also permissible for it to be an exception from the pronoun concealed in "guilty" (mujrimin), so the exception is connected, since the pronoun refers only to the people. On the first reading, the family are excluded from the ruling of sending, where the sending meant is a particular sending, namely one for destruction, not the general sending, because the sense requires this. His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them, all of them﴾ is the predicate of "the family", as you heard earlier. It is reported from al-Radi that the disjunct exception is put in the accusative, according to Sibawayh, by what precedes illa in the sentence, just as the connected exception is put in the accusative by it. Even though illa here has the meaning of lakin ("but"), the later Basran grammarians, when they saw it with the meaning of lakin, said that it itself governs the accusative, like the accusative of lakinna with nouns, and its predicate is usually omitted, as in: "The people came to me except a donkey," meaning: "but a donkey did not come." They said: Its predicate may occur explicitly, as in His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the torment﴾. The Kufans said: illa in this context means siwa ("other than"), and the accusative after it in the disjunct case is like the accusative in the connected case. The Basran interpretation is preferable, because the disjunct exception necessarily differs from what precedes it in affirmation and negation, as in lakin, whereas with siwa this is not necessary, because you say: "I have two dinars owed to me by you, other than the such-and-such dinar," and that is when it is a description. Also, the meaning of lakin is correction (istidrak), and what is intended by it here is to prevent the addressee from supposing that what follows falls under the ruling of what precedes, even though it does not. This is exactly the meaning of the disjunct exception. The end of his words.

Some have claimed that there is a difficulty, from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, in illa being an exception particle that functions like lakin, and he said: It is in meaning a predicate, but not a true predicate, as the grammarians have explicitly stated. From what we have quoted, the problem with this is known. Indeed, al-Zamakhshari stated that the sentence, on the assumption of disjunction, runs in the manner of the predicate of lakin, which clearly indicates that it is not a predicate in reality. He mentioned that he only said this because the predicate is omitted, meaning: "but the family of Lut, We did not send to them," and what is mentioned is its evidence, because the two entail each other. For this reason he did not make it the predicate itself, but rather said it runs in its manner. In this there is an oversight concerning its being based on what was reported from Sibawayh. Some claimed that he said this because a sentence introduced by an (an) cannot be the predicate of lakin, so let it be checked. It was also said: He said this because what is mentioned is illa, not lakin, and this is as you see. On the assumption of connection, the family are excluded from the ruling of the item excluded from (the category), which is guilt, and included in the ruling of sending in the general sense, so the angels were sent to them all, to destroy these and to save those. On this reading, the sentence ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾ is an independent sentence, an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them when they said: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people﴾ ﴿except the family of Lut﴾: "Then what is the state of the family of Lut?" They said: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾, and so on. His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿except his wife﴾ is, on both assumptions, according to the Divine Mercy of God, an exception from the pronoun in the genitive in "We will surely save them". He did not permit that it be an exception from an exception in any respect. He said: That is only possible where the ruling is one and the same, as in the statement of the one who divorces: "You are divorced three times except two, except one," and the one who acknowledges that he owes someone ten dirhams except three, except one dirham. Here, the two rulings differ, because "the family of Lut" is connected to "We sent" or to "guilty," while "except his wife" is connected to "We will surely save them." So how can it be an exception from an exception? The end of his words.

It may be supposed that if sending means destruction, there is no difference, since the meaning would be: "except the family of Lut, We did not destroy them," which is the same as "We will save them," so it would be an exception from an exception on one of the two readings. Ibn al-Humam's commentator, the author of al-Taqrib, answered this by saying that the condition of the aforementioned exception is that no word intervene between the two exceptions which has multiple items that could be excluded. Here, "We will surely save them" has intervened. If it were said: "except the family of Lut, except his wife," that would be permissible. This was objected to on the grounds that it does not remove the difficulty, because the cause of its impermissibility then would be the presence of an intervening element, not the difference between the two rulings, so there is no point in expressing it in that way. In al-Kashf it is said: What is meant by the unity of the ruling is its unity in both person and number. So it is not objected that if sending means destruction, His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾ and His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿except the family of Lut﴾ have the same meaning, so the exception is from the first in meaning. The unity was only stipulated because a connected item, like its name, does not permit a sentence to intervene between the staff and its bark, and likewise in the disjunct case. By this, the situation of what preceded becomes most clear. In the same work also: If you ask, why does the exception not refer to both of them? I say: Because the exception is attached to an independent sentence, and the disagreement concerns its reference to two or more sentences, not to one sentence or part of a previous sentence. This is the position, though the meaning differs in that matter, and the point of disagreement is conjoined sentences, not those where one part is separated from another. The end of his words. The matter is as he said in identifying the point of disagreement. The question has been addressed by few grammarians, and there are various positions on it.

The first, which is the most correct and which Ibn Malik adopted, is that the exception returns to all of them unless there is evidence that only some are intended, as in His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿And those who accuse their wives…﴾ (Q 24:4), the verse, where "except those who" refers to their wickedness and the non-acceptance of their testimony, while the lashing is excluded by evidence. The difference of the governing element does no harm, because that is based on the view that illa itself is the governing element. The second is that it returns to all if the whole is directed toward one purpose, as in: "I have made my house a waqf for my paternal uncles, and I have dedicated my orchard to my maternal uncles, and I have made my water-supply a charity for my neighbours, except if they travel," and otherwise it is for the last only, as in: "Honour the scholars, and keep your house as a waqf for your relatives, and free your slaves, except the wicked among them." The third: if the coordination is by waw, it returns to all; or by fa' or thumma, it returns to the last. This is the view of Ibn al-Hajib. The fourth: it is specific to the last, and Abu Hayyan chose this. The fifth: if the governing element is one, it applies to all; if it differs, it applies to the last, because differing items cannot be carried into one exception. This is the view of al-Bahabadhi, and it is based on the view that the governing element of the exception is the preceding verbs and not illa. Now, the words of some imply that if one made the exception from "the family of Lut," it would follow that his wife was either not destroyed or not guilty, and this is a gross error, because the exception from "the family of Lut," if we say it is one, is by consideration of the ruling against them of salvation and non-destruction, or by non-guilt and righteousness. Then "except his wife" would be a woman who is ruled to be destroyed or guilty. What guides you to this is what al-Radi mentioned concerning cases where the exception is multiplied and each subsequent item can be excepted from what it follows, as in: "The Meccans came to me, except Quraysh, except the Banu Hashim, except the Banu 'Aqil." He said: In a positive sentence in this case, for each odd item, only the accusative as an exception is permitted, because it is from a positive sentence. The analogy would be that for each even item the substitution (badal) and the accusative as exception are permitted, because it is not positive and the item excepted from is mentioned. In the case of odd and even items that are not positive, the situation is the reverse of this. This is based on the view of the majority that an exception from a negative is an affirmation, and from an affirmation is a negation, in contrast to al-Kisa'i, who said: The excluded item is silent concerning the negation or the affirmation of the ruling for it, and there is no indication in the sentence of either. The affirmation in the statement of monotheism is derived from the custom of the Law. Just as this question was disputed among the grammarians, it was disputed among the leading mujtahid scholars, and the verification of this belongs in its proper place.

Ibn al-Munir chose that "except the family of Lut" is an exception from "a guilty people," on the basis that it is disjunct. He said: This is preferable and more plausible, because in excepting them from the pronoun referring to a people who are denying, there is a remoteness, since the function of the exception is to remove what, were it not for the exception, would have entered into the ruling of the first. Here, entry is impossible with indefiniteness, and for this reason you rarely find an indefinite noun excepted from except in a negative context, because then it generalizes, so entry is realized were it not for the exception. For this reason, "I saw a people except Zayd" is not good, but "I did not see anyone except Zayd" is good. The end of his words. It has been answered that this is not like "I saw a people except Zayd," but rather like "I saw a people who did wrong, except Zayd," for the description identifies them and makes them as if they were limited. Al-Suyuti, in Hama' al-Hawami, said:

"An indefinite noun may not be excepted in an affirmative sentence unless it conveys a benefit. So one does not say: 'A people came except a man,' or 'Men stood except Zayd,' because there is no benefit. But if it conveys a benefit, it is permitted, as in: 'He remained among them a thousand years, except fifty years' (Q 29:14), and: 'Men who were in your house stood, except a man.'"

The people here mean the inhabitants of the town, as is explicitly stated in another verse, so they are in meaning limited. The scrupulous scholar relates from al-Sakkaki that he stated at the end of the section on inference in his book that excepting from a non-limited group is permitted by metaphor. Yet some of the usuli scholars also permitted excepting from an indefinite noun in an affirmative sentence and stated the matter without qualification. Indeed, what is explicitly stated in many grammar books is like what is in al-Hama'.

Some claimed that the exception should be from the explicit noun and that the pronoun is disjunct. This was justified on the ground that the pronoun in the description is the very item described, qualified by the description. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that some learned persons raised this, together with several questions, in prose and verse, to al-Kamal Ibn al-Humam, and did not mention that he answered them. The answer to what is claimed here has already been alluded to. As for the answer to the rest of what he found difficult and was asked about by al-Kamal, examining the question suffices, since it is something to be marvelled at. For this reason al-Shihab said: I think that Ibn al-Humam only kept silent about answering that because its refutation is obvious, and it should not come from one adorned with the ornament of excellence. Yes, every calculation that suggests itself to the mind is remote, namely that the exception is from the explicit noun. But al-Radi (stated) that if two or more items come together, each of which could be excepted from both, then there is a distinction. Either they differ in meaning or they do not. If they differ and it is possible for them to share in

That exception is not far-fetched: both (nouns) share it, as in *ma barra abun wa-ibnun illa Zaydan*, meaning "Zayd is a righteous father and a righteous son." If sharing is not possible, as in *fadala ibnun aban illa Zaydan* (a son surpassed a father except Zayd), or if the exception is distant, as in *ma daraba ahadun ahadan illa Zaydan*, then the usual rule is that the doer differs from the one acted upon. We then examine. If it is clearly determined that the excepted noun belongs to one of the two and not the other, it is an exception from that one, and it follows it directly, as in *ma fada wasiyyun nabiyyan illa Aliyyan* (the executor did not surpass the Prophet except Ali), may God ennoble his face. If it may belong to each of the two, then if the excepted noun comes after both, it is an exception from the last one, as in *ma fadala ibnun aban illa Zaydan* and likewise *ma fadala aban ibnun illa Zaydun*, because restricting it to the nearer one is preferable, since its reference to both is impossible. If it comes before both together, then if one of the two is in the nominative, either in form or in meaning, the exception is from that one, because its position is after the verb; it is as if the exception directly follows it, as in *ma fadala illa Zaydan aban ibnun* or *min ibnin*. If neither is in the nominative, the first is more appropriate for it because it is nearer, as in *ma faddaltu illa Zaydan wahidan ala ahadin*, and a governing element is assumed for the latter. If it comes between the two, the one before it has the stronger claim, because the basic position of the excepted noun is after the noun it excepts from, as in *ma fadala aban illa Zaydun ibnun*, and a governing element is likewise assumed for the latter. If the two do not differ in meaning, they share it. If the governing elements differ, as in *ma daraba ahadun wa-ma qatala illa Khalidan*, [it is an exception from the second] because the doer of *qatala* is a pronoun referring to *ahad*. End of quotation.

Ibn Malik ruled, regarding a case where two items, each of which is suitable as the thing excepted from, precede the exception, that the exception is from the last one, and he stated this without qualification. Consider this together with what we are discussing. Al-Qadi al-Baydawi said: "On the reading of disconnection (*infisal*), (*illa imra'atahu*) may be treated as an exception from (*ali Lut*) or from the pronoun in ﴿*lamunajjuhum*﴾ [We will surely save them]. On the reading of connection (*ittisal*), the second option is required, because the two rulings differ, unless you treat the clause ﴿*Inna lamunajjuhum*﴾ as a parenthetical insertion." End of quotation. His position contradicts what is reported from al-Zamakhshari, clearly so: al-Baydawi allowed an exception from the excepted item in disconnected exception, whereas al-Zamakhshari prohibited it absolutely. Al-Baydawi also made the difference of rulings a feature of connected exception, whereas al-Zamakhshari asserted it absolutely as well, and al-Baydawi explained the difference of rulings in a manner like what al-Zamakhshari stated. Our master Sirri al-Din did not accept this and said: "The rulings meant are: the ruling conveyed through the exception of the second from the first, which, on the assumption of connection, is the act of destruction (*ijram*) applied to the exception 'except his wife'; and the ruling intended to be conveyed, namely the judgment that she is destroyed. As for the unity of this intended ruling with the ruling conveyed by the exception on the assumption of disconnection, it is that on that assumption *illa* carries the sense of *lakin* (but), and (*wa-inna lamunajjuhum*) is its predicate, established like the exclusion from it. So the ruling resulting from the exception from it is the very ruling intended to be conveyed." It is also said, on the assumption of connection and parenthetical insertion, that although the two rulings differ outwardly, since the parenthetical clause is like an explanation of what the first exception requires, it is in meaning as if it were that clause, and exclusion from it becomes like exclusion from it. This differs from the case where it is a new independent sentence (*istinaf*), for then it is disconnected, serves as an answer to an implied question, the answer is not complete without the exception, and it is not free of objection. Some scholars, in justifying the exception on this view, said: there are two rulings, the act of destruction and the act of deliverance, so the second draws the exception to itself, so that the separation is avoided, unless it is made a parenthetical insertion, for it has latitude enough to come between an adjective and what it describes, so it may be an exception from (*ali Lut*). For this reason al-Radi allowed the statement: "*Akram al-qawmi wa-l-nuhati basriyyuna illa Zaydan*" [the most honorable of the people and the grammarians are the Basrans except Zayd]. It is objected that the ruling conveyed by the exception is not the ruling intended to be conveyed, which remains as it is; and the matter does not require what you have heard, and it is as you have heard. What naturally comes to mind is what al-Zamakhshari stated. In the Shihabi glosses it is said that this is the correct view both in understanding (*dirayah*) and in transmission (*riwayah*). As for the first: the ruling intended by the exclusion from it is the ruling excluded from the first noun, and the second is an incidental ruling derived from the interpretation of *illa* as *lakin*, which is a hypothetical matter. As for the second: because of what is mentioned in *al-Tashil* that when exceptions are multiplied, the ruling excluded from is the ruling of the first. Among the evidence for this is that if the exception were "emptied" (*mufarragh*) in this case, as when you say: "*Lam yabqa fi al-dari illa al-ya'afiru abqaha al-zamanu illa Ya'fura saydin minha*" [nothing remained in the house except the wild oxen which time has preserved, except a wild ox of the hunt among them], its case-ending would necessarily be determined by the first governing element, as in your saying: "*ma indi illa ashratun illa thalathatun*" [I have only ten except three]. Furthermore, his statement is based on a matter and a preventing factor that is semantic, not on the impermissibility of an intervening disconnected clause between the exception and what it excepts from, as is claimed; though that also prevents, as al-Radi explicitly stated. So reflect on it. Understand this, and may God, glory be to Him, guide you. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read *lamunjuhum* with the lighter form (without doubling).

﴿*Qaddarna innaha lamina al-ghabirin*﴾ [We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind]: that is, among those who remain in the punishment of God, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada; or among those who remain with the disbelievers, to be destroyed along with them. Its root is from *al-ghabarah*, which is the remainder of milk in the udder. Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, read *qadarna* with the lighter form. The hamza of *inna* is pronounced with a kasra, because the verb is suspended (*ta'liq*) by the presence of the initial *lam* (of emphasis), which holds the front position of the sentence. Suspension with *inna* is, according to the well-known view, one of the special features of verbs of the heart. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is because the verb of decree includes the meaning of knowledge; for this reason the scholars explained God's decree of the actions of servants as knowledge. By "including that meaning" some have meant the technical sense, and others have said it is a figurative extension from its meaning, which is, as it were, contained within it, since one decrees only what one knows. This is al-Zamakhshari's position, clarified in detail. Then he said: this is not a case of one verb being given the meaning of another, so as to be objected that it would not benefit al-Zamakhshari, since the meanings of the two verbs remain distinct. Rather, it is, according to their principle, a metonymy (*kinayah*) that is known and established, not a hidden intended meaning. Al-Qadi said: it may be said that it is treated as if it were a verb of speech, since decree in the sense of judgment is a kind of speech. As for me, I do not object to Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) that suspension is due to the inclusion of the meaning of knowledge; I object only to his denial that it is something determined and intended. End of quotation. I object to it because it is a Mu'tazili position that the apparent meanings of scripture reject. For this reason Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, as reported from him by Ibn Abi Hatim, said: "Between me and the Qadariyya (the determinists-denying predestination) stands this verse," and he recited it.

The apparent view is that this is part of the speech of the angels, peace be upon them, and they attributed this act to themselves, though it is the act of God, glory be to Him, because of their nearness and special status. This is like the statement of a royal court official: "We commanded and decreed such-and-such," while the real commander is the sovereign. It is also said that it is far-fetched; it is the speech of God Almighty, so it does not need interpretation. It was also said that it does not need that interpretation either if the meaning of "decreed" is knowledge in a figurative sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verses 58–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said: "Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people"﴾. They are the people of Lut, peace be upon him. They are referred to indefinitely and described as guilty to belittle them and to censure them. ﴿Except the family of Lut﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible for this to be an exception from "a people" with regard to the description, so the exception is disjunct (munqati', exception where the excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes), because they are not a guilty people. The possibility of a predominance (taghlib) with this consideration, so that the exception becomes connected (muttasil, exception where the excluded item belongs to the category of what precedes), is not what the context requires. Even if it is granted, it does no harm to what was mentioned, because it is based on the literal meaning, and it does not preclude the validity of connection under another reading. It is also permissible for it to be an exception from the pronoun concealed in "guilty" (mujrimin), so the exception is connected, since the pronoun refers only to the people. On the first reading, the family are excluded from the ruling of sending, where the sending meant is a particular sending, namely one for destruction, not the general sending, because the sense requires this. His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them, all of them﴾ is the predicate of "the family", as you heard earlier. It is reported from al-Radi that the disjunct exception is put in the accusative, according to Sibawayh, by what precedes illa in the sentence, just as the connected exception is put in the accusative by it. Even though illa here has the meaning of lakin ("but"), the later Basran grammarians, when they saw it with the meaning of lakin, said that it itself governs the accusative, like the accusative of lakinna with nouns, and its predicate is usually omitted, as in: "The people came to me except a donkey," meaning: "but a donkey did not come." They said: Its predicate may occur explicitly, as in His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the torment﴾. The Kufans said: illa in this context means siwa ("other than"), and the accusative after it in the disjunct case is like the accusative in the connected case. The Basran interpretation is preferable, because the disjunct exception necessarily differs from what precedes it in affirmation and negation, as in lakin, whereas with siwa this is not necessary, because you say: "I have two dinars owed to me by you, other than the such-and-such dinar," and that is when it is a description. Also, the meaning of lakin is correction (istidrak), and what is intended by it here is to prevent the addressee from supposing that what follows falls under the ruling of what precedes, even though it does not. This is exactly the meaning of the disjunct exception. The end of his words.

Some have claimed that there is a difficulty, from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, in illa being an exception particle that functions like lakin, and he said: It is in meaning a predicate, but not a true predicate, as the grammarians have explicitly stated. From what we have quoted, the problem with this is known. Indeed, al-Zamakhshari stated that the sentence, on the assumption of disjunction, runs in the manner of the predicate of lakin, which clearly indicates that it is not a predicate in reality. He mentioned that he only said this because the predicate is omitted, meaning: "but the family of Lut, We did not send to them," and what is mentioned is its evidence, because the two entail each other. For this reason he did not make it the predicate itself, but rather said it runs in its manner. In this there is an oversight concerning its being based on what was reported from Sibawayh. Some claimed that he said this because a sentence introduced by an (an) cannot be the predicate of lakin, so let it be checked. It was also said: He said this because what is mentioned is illa, not lakin, and this is as you see. On the assumption of connection, the family are excluded from the ruling of the item excluded from (the category), which is guilt, and included in the ruling of sending in the general sense, so the angels were sent to them all, to destroy these and to save those. On this reading, the sentence ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾ is an independent sentence, an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them when they said: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people﴾ ﴿except the family of Lut﴾: "Then what is the state of the family of Lut?" They said: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾, and so on. His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿except his wife﴾ is, on both assumptions, according to the Divine Mercy of God, an exception from the pronoun in the genitive in "We will surely save them". He did not permit that it be an exception from an exception in any respect. He said: That is only possible where the ruling is one and the same, as in the statement of the one who divorces: "You are divorced three times except two, except one," and the one who acknowledges that he owes someone ten dirhams except three, except one dirham. Here, the two rulings differ, because "the family of Lut" is connected to "We sent" or to "guilty," while "except his wife" is connected to "We will surely save them." So how can it be an exception from an exception? The end of his words.

It may be supposed that if sending means destruction, there is no difference, since the meaning would be: "except the family of Lut, We did not destroy them," which is the same as "We will save them," so it would be an exception from an exception on one of the two readings. This was objected to on the grounds that it does not remove the difficulty, because the cause of its impermissibility then would be the presence of an intervening element, not the difference between the two rulings, so there is no point in expressing it in that way. In al-Kashf it is said: What is meant by the unity of the ruling is its unity in both person and number. So it is not objected that if sending means destruction, His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾ and His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿except the family of Lut﴾ have the same meaning, so the exception is from the first in meaning. Ibn Malik ruled, regarding a case where two items, each of which is suitable as the thing excepted from, precede the exception, that the exception is from the last one, and he stated this without qualification. Consider this together with what we are discussing. Al-Qadi al-Baydawi said: "On the reading of disconnection (*infisal*), (*illa imra'atahu*) may be treated as an exception from (*ali Lut*) or from the pronoun in ﴿*lamunajjuhum*﴾ [We will surely save them]. On the reading of connection (*ittisal*), the second option is required, because the two rulings differ, unless you treat the clause ﴿*Inna lamunajjuhum*﴾ as a parenthetical insertion." End of quotation. His position contradicts what is reported from al-Zamakhshari, clearly so: al-Baydawi allowed an exception from the excepted item in disconnected exception, whereas al-Zamakhshari prohibited it absolutely. Al-Baydawi also made the difference of rulings a feature of connected exception, whereas al-Zamakhshari asserted it absolutely as well, and al-Baydawi explained the difference of rulings in a manner like what al-Zamakhshari stated. Our master Sirri al-Din did not accept this and said: "The rulings meant are: the ruling conveyed through the exception of the second from the first, which, on the assumption of connection, is the act of destruction (*ijram*) applied to the exception 'except his wife'; and the ruling intended to be conveyed, namely the judgment that she is destroyed. As for the unity of this intended ruling with the ruling conveyed by the exception on the assumption of disconnection, it is that on that assumption *illa* carries the sense of *lakin* (but), and (*wa-inna lamunajjuhum*) is its predicate, established like the exclusion from it. So the ruling resulting from the exception from it is the very ruling intended to be conveyed." It is also said, on the assumption of connection and parenthetical insertion, that although the two rulings differ outwardly, since the parenthetical clause is like an explanation of what the first exception requires, it is in meaning as if it were that clause, and exclusion from it becomes like exclusion from it. This differs from the case where it is a new independent sentence (*istinaf*), for then it is disconnected, serves as an answer to an implied question, the answer is not complete without the exception, and it is not free of objection. Some scholars, in justifying the exception on this view, said: there are two rulings, the act of destruction and the act of deliverance, so the second draws the exception to itself, so that the separation is avoided, unless it is made a parenthetical insertion, for it has latitude enough to come between an adjective and what it describes, so it may be an exception from (*ali Lut*). For this reason al-Radi allowed the statement: "*Akram al-qawmi wa-l-nuhati basriyyuna illa Zaydan*" [the most honorable of the people and the grammarians are the Basrans except Zayd]. It is objected that the ruling conveyed by the exception is not the ruling intended to be conveyed, which remains as it is; and the matter does not require what you have heard, and it is as you have heard. What naturally comes to mind is what al-Zamakhshari stated. In the Shihabi glosses it is said that this is the correct view both in understanding (*dirayah*) and in transmission (*riwayah*). As for the first: the ruling intended by the exclusion from it is the ruling excluded from the first noun, and the second is an incidental ruling derived from the interpretation of *illa* as *lakin*, which is a hypothetical matter. As for the second: because of what is mentioned in *al-Tashil* that when exceptions are multiplied, the ruling excluded from is the ruling of the first. Among the evidence for this is that if the exception were "emptied" (*mufarragh*) in this case, as when you say: "*Lam yabqa fi al-dari illa al-ya'afiru abqaha al-zamanu illa Ya'fura saydin minha*" [nothing remained in the house except the wild oxen which time has preserved, except a wild ox of the hunt among them], its case-ending would necessarily be determined by the first governing element, as in your saying: "*ma indi illa ashratun illa thalathatun*" [I have only ten except three]. Furthermore, his statement is based on a matter and a preventing factor that is semantic, not on the impermissibility of an intervening disconnected clause between the exception and what it excepts from, as is claimed; though that also prevents, as al-Radi explicitly stated. So reflect on it. Understand this, and may God, glory be to Him, guide you. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read *lamunjuhum* with the lighter form (without doubling).

﴿*Qaddarna innaha lamina al-ghabirin*﴾ [We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind]: that is, among those who remain in the punishment of God, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada; or among those who remain with the disbelievers, to be destroyed along with them. Its root is from *al-ghabarah*, which is the remainder of milk in the udder. Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, read *qadarna* with the lighter form. The hamza of *inna* is pronounced with a kasra, because the verb is suspended (*ta'liq*) by the presence of the initial *lam* (of emphasis), which holds the front position of the sentence. Suspension with *inna* is, according to the well-known view, one of the special features of verbs of the heart. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is because the verb of decree includes the meaning of knowledge; for this reason the scholars explained God's decree of the actions of servants as knowledge. By "including that meaning" some have meant the technical sense, and others have said it is a figurative extension from its meaning, which is, as it were, contained within it, since one decrees only what one knows. This is al-Zamakhshari's position, clarified in detail. Then he said: this is not a case of one verb being given the meaning of another, so as to be objected that it would not benefit al-Zamakhshari, since the meanings of the two verbs remain distinct. Rather, it is, according to their principle, a metonymy (*kinayah*) that is known and established, not a hidden intended meaning. Al-Qadi said: it may be said that it is treated as if it were a verb of speech, since decree in the sense of judgment is a kind of speech. As for me, I do not object to Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) that suspension is due to the inclusion of the meaning of knowledge; I object only to his denial that it is something determined and intended. End of quotation. I object to it because it is a Mu'tazili position that the apparent meanings of scripture reject. For this reason Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, as reported from him by Ibn Abi Hatim, said: "Between me and the Qadariyya (the determinists-denying predestination) stands this verse," and he recited it.

The apparent view is that this is part of the speech of the angels, peace be upon them, and they attributed this act to themselves, though it is the act of God, glory be to Him, because of their nearness and special status. This is like the statement of a royal court official: "We commanded and decreed such-and-such," while the real commander is the sovereign. It is also said that it is far-fetched; it is the speech of God Almighty, so it does not need interpretation. It was also said that it does not need that interpretation either if the meaning of "decreed" is knowledge in a figurative sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verses 58–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said: "Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people"﴾. They are the people of Lut, peace be upon him. They are referred to indefinitely and described as guilty to belittle them and to censure them. ﴿Except the family of Lut﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible for this to be an exception from "a people" with regard to the description, so the exception is disjunct (munqati', exception where the excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes), because they are not a guilty people. The possibility of a predominance (taghlib) with this consideration, so that the exception becomes connected (muttasil, exception where the excluded item belongs to the category of what precedes), is not what the context requires. Even if it is granted, it does no harm to what was mentioned, because it is based on the literal meaning, and it does not preclude the validity of connection under another reading. It is also permissible for it to be an exception from the pronoun concealed in "guilty" (mujrimin), so the exception is connected, since the pronoun refers only to the people. On the first reading, the family are excluded from the ruling of sending, where the sending meant is a particular sending, namely one for destruction, not the general sending, because the sense requires this. His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them, all of them﴾ is the predicate of "the family", as you heard earlier. It is reported from al-Radi that the disjunct exception is put in the accusative, according to Sibawayh, by what precedes illa in the sentence, just as the connected exception is put in the accusative by it. Even though illa here has the meaning of lakin ("but"), the later Basran grammarians, when they saw it with the meaning of lakin, said that it itself governs the accusative, like the accusative of lakinna with nouns, and its predicate is usually omitted, as in: "The people came to me except a donkey," meaning: "but a donkey did not come." They said: Its predicate may occur explicitly, as in His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the torment﴾. The Kufans said: illa in this context means siwa ("other than"), and the accusative after it in the disjunct case is like the accusative in the connected case. The Basran interpretation is preferable, because the disjunct exception necessarily differs from what precedes it in affirmation and negation, as in lakin, whereas with siwa this is not necessary, because you say: "I have two dinars owed to me by you, other than the such-and-such dinar," and that is when it is a description. Also, the meaning of lakin is correction (istidrak), and what is intended by it here is to prevent the addressee from supposing that what follows falls under the ruling of what precedes, even though it does not. This is exactly the meaning of the disjunct exception. The end of his words.

Some have claimed that there is a difficulty, from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, in illa being an exception particle that functions like lakin, and he said: It is in meaning a predicate, but not a true predicate, as the grammarians have explicitly stated. From what we have quoted, the problem with this is known. Indeed, al-Zamakhshari stated that the sentence, on the assumption of disjunction, runs in the manner of the predicate of lakin, which clearly indicates that it is not a predicate in reality. He mentioned that he only said this because the predicate is omitted, meaning: "but the family of Lut, We did not send to them," and what is mentioned is its evidence, because the two entail each other. For this reason he did not make it the predicate itself, but rather said it runs in its manner. In this there is an oversight concerning its being based on what was reported from Sibawayh. Some claimed that he said this because a sentence introduced by an (an) cannot be the predicate of lakin, so let it be checked. It was also said: He said this because what is mentioned is illa, not lakin, and this is as you see. On the assumption of connection, the family are excluded from the ruling of the item excluded from (the category), which is guilt, and included in the ruling of sending in the general sense, so the angels were sent to them all, to destroy these and to save those. On this reading, the sentence ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾ is an independent sentence, an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them when they said: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people﴾ ﴿except the family of Lut﴾: "Then what is the state of the family of Lut?" They said: ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾, and so on. His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿except his wife﴾ is, on both assumptions, according to the Divine Mercy of God, an exception from the pronoun in the genitive in "We will surely save them". He did not permit that it be an exception from an exception in any respect. He said: That is only possible where the ruling is one and the same, as in the statement of the one who divorces: "You are divorced three times except two, except one," and the one who acknowledges that he owes someone ten dirhams except three, except one dirham. Here, the two rulings differ, because "the family of Lut" is connected to "We sent" or to "guilty," while "except his wife" is connected to "We will surely save them." So how can it be an exception from an exception? The end of his words.

It may be supposed that if sending means destruction, there is no difference, since the meaning would be: "except the family of Lut, We did not destroy them," which is the same as "We will save them," so it would be an exception from an exception on one of the two readings. Ibn al-Humam's commentator, the author of al-Taqrib, answered this by saying that the condition of the aforementioned exception is that no word intervene between the two exceptions which has multiple items that could be excluded. Here, "We will surely save them" has intervened. If it were said: "except the family of Lut, except his wife," that would be permissible. This was objected to on the grounds that it does not remove the difficulty, because the cause of its impermissibility then would be the presence of an intervening element, not the difference between the two rulings, so there is no point in expressing it in that way. In al-Kashf it is said: What is meant by the unity of the ruling is its unity in both person and number. So it is not objected that if sending means destruction, His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them﴾ and His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿except the family of Lut﴾ have the same meaning, so the exception is from the first in meaning. The unity was only stipulated because a connected item, like its name, does not permit a sentence to intervene between the staff and its bark, and likewise in the disjunct case. By this, the situation of what preceded becomes most clear. In the same work also: If you ask, why does the exception not refer to both of them? I say: Because the exception is attached to an independent sentence, and the disagreement concerns its reference to two or more sentences, not to one sentence or part of a previous sentence. This is the position, though the meaning differs in that matter, and the point of disagreement is conjoined sentences, not those where one part is separated from another. The end of his words. The matter is as he said in identifying the point of disagreement. The question has been addressed by few grammarians, and there are various positions on it.

The first, which is the most correct and which Ibn Malik adopted, is that the exception returns to all of them unless there is evidence that only some are intended, as in His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿And those who accuse their wives…﴾ (Q 24:4), the verse, where "except those who" refers to their wickedness and the non-acceptance of their testimony, while the lashing is excluded by evidence. The difference of the governing element does no harm, because that is based on the view that illa itself is the governing element. The second is that it returns to all if the whole is directed toward one purpose, as in: "I have made my house a waqf for my paternal uncles, and I have dedicated my orchard to my maternal uncles, and I have made my water-supply a charity for my neighbours, except if they travel," and otherwise it is for the last only, as in: "Honour the scholars, and keep your house as a waqf for your relatives, and free your slaves, except the wicked among them." The third: if the coordination is by waw, it returns to all; or by fa' or thumma, it returns to the last. This is the view of Ibn al-Hajib. The fourth: it is specific to the last, and Abu Hayyan chose this. The fifth: if the governing element is one, it applies to all; if it differs, it applies to the last, because differing items cannot be carried into one exception. This is the view of al-Bahabadhi, and it is based on the view that the governing element of the exception is the preceding verbs and not illa. Now, the words of some imply that if one made the exception from "the family of Lut," it would follow that his wife was either not destroyed or not guilty, and this is a gross error, because the exception from "the family of Lut," if we say it is one, is by consideration of the ruling against them of salvation and non-destruction, or by non-guilt and righteousness. Then "except his wife" would be a woman who is ruled to be destroyed or guilty. What guides you to this is what al-Radi mentioned concerning cases where the exception is multiplied and each subsequent item can be excepted from what it follows, as in: "The Meccans came to me, except Quraysh, except the Banu Hashim, except the Banu 'Aqil." He said: In a positive sentence in this case, for each odd item, only the accusative as an exception is permitted, because it is from a positive sentence. The analogy would be that for each even item the substitution (badal) and the accusative as exception are permitted, because it is not positive and the item excepted from is mentioned. In the case of odd and even items that are not positive, the situation is the reverse of this. This is based on the view of the majority that an exception from a negative is an affirmation, and from an affirmation is a negation, in contrast to al-Kisa'i, who said: The excluded item is silent concerning the negation or the affirmation of the ruling for it, and there is no indication in the sentence of either. The affirmation in the statement of monotheism is derived from the custom of the Law. Just as this question was disputed among the grammarians, it was disputed among the leading mujtahid scholars, and the verification of this belongs in its proper place.

Ibn al-Munir chose that "except the family of Lut" is an exception from "a guilty people," on the basis that it is disjunct. He said: This is preferable and more plausible, because in excepting them from the pronoun referring to a people who are denying, there is a remoteness, since the function of the exception is to remove what, were it not for the exception, would have entered into the ruling of the first. Here, entry is impossible with indefiniteness, and for this reason you rarely find an indefinite noun excepted from except in a negative context, because then it generalizes, so entry is realized were it not for the exception. For this reason, "I saw a people except Zayd" is not good, but "I did not see anyone except Zayd" is good. The end of his words. It has been answered that this is not like "I saw a people except Zayd," but rather like "I saw a people who did wrong, except Zayd," for the description identifies them and makes them as if they were limited. Al-Suyuti, in Hama' al-Hawami, said:

"An indefinite noun may not be excepted in an affirmative sentence unless it conveys a benefit. So one does not say: 'A people came except a man,' or 'Men stood except Zayd,' because there is no benefit. But if it conveys a benefit, it is permitted, as in: 'He remained among them a thousand years, except fifty years' (Q 29:14), and: 'Men who were in your house stood, except a man.'"

The people here mean the inhabitants of the town, as is explicitly stated in another verse, so they are in meaning limited. The scrupulous scholar relates from al-Sakkaki that he stated at the end of the section on inference in his book that excepting from a non-limited group is permitted by metaphor. Yet some of the usuli scholars also permitted excepting from an indefinite noun in an affirmative sentence and stated the matter without qualification. Indeed, what is explicitly stated in many grammar books is like what is in al-Hama'.

Some claimed that the exception should be from the explicit noun and that the pronoun is disjunct. This was justified on the ground that the pronoun in the description is the very item described, qualified by the description. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that some learned persons raised this, together with several questions, in prose and verse, to al-Kamal Ibn al-Humam, and did not mention that he answered them. The answer to what is claimed here has already been alluded to. As for the answer to the rest of what he found difficult and was asked about by al-Kamal, examining the question suffices, since it is something to be marvelled at. For this reason al-Shihab said: I think that Ibn al-Humam only kept silent about answering that because its refutation is obvious, and it should not come from one adorned with the ornament of excellence. Yes, every calculation that suggests itself to the mind is remote, namely that the exception is from the explicit noun. But al-Radi (stated) that if two or more items come together, each of which could be excepted from both, then there is a distinction. Either they differ in meaning or they do not. If they differ and it is possible for them to share in

[Page 66]

That exception is not far-fetched: both (nouns) share it, as in *ma barra abun wa-ibnun illa Zaydan*, meaning "Zayd is a righteous father and a righteous son." If sharing is not possible, as in *fadala ibnun aban illa Zaydan* (a son surpassed a father except Zayd), or if the exception is distant, as in *ma daraba ahadun ahadan illa Zaydan*, then the usual rule is that the doer differs from the one acted upon. We then examine. If it is clearly determined that the excepted noun belongs to one of the two and not the other, it is an exception from that one, and it follows it directly, as in *ma fada wasiyyun nabiyyan illa Aliyyan* (the executor did not surpass the Prophet except Ali), may God ennoble his face. If it may belong to each of the two, then if the excepted noun comes after both, it is an exception from the last one, as in *ma fadala ibnun aban illa Zaydan* and likewise *ma fadala aban ibnun illa Zaydun*, because restricting it to the nearer one is preferable, since its reference to both is impossible. If it comes before both together, then if one of the two is in the nominative, either in form or in meaning, the exception is from that one, because its position is after the verb; it is as if the exception directly follows it, as in *ma fadala illa Zaydan aban ibnun* or *min ibnin*. If neither is in the nominative, the first is more appropriate for it because it is nearer, as in *ma faddaltu illa Zaydan wahidan ala ahadin*, and a governing element is assumed for the latter. If it comes between the two, the one before it has the stronger claim, because the basic position of the excepted noun is after the noun it excepts from, as in *ma fadala aban illa Zaydun ibnun*, and a governing element is likewise assumed for the latter. If the two do not differ in meaning, they share it. If the governing elements differ, as in *ma daraba ahadun wa-ma qatala illa Khalidan*, [it is an exception from the second] because the doer of *qatala* is a pronoun referring to *ahad*. End of quotation.
