﴿When the messengers came to the family of Lut﴾ This begins the explanation of the destruction of the criminals and the deliverance of the family of Lut. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun indicates that their coming was for the purpose of carrying out what they had been sent with regarding that. The intended meaning is not the very beginning of their coming, but rather their general presence among the family of Lut. For what is related of him, peace be upon him, in the words of the Exalted, ﴿He said, "Surely you are a people unknown [to me]."﴾ he said only after the *al-latya wa-l-latti* (repeated and various efforts), when his stratagems were exhausted and his excuses failed him, and when, in bearing the hardships and enduring the plots from his people, who intended harm to them, he did not witness from the messengers the customary help and support, in what they bring and what they leave, as he struggled to rescue them. This was a denunciation of their abandonment and their failure to support him in such distress that befell him because of them, since they, peace be upon them, were not directly with him in the means of defense and resistance, until it compelled him to say ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a strong support.﴾ as detailed in Surah Hud. It was not that he, peace be upon him, said this at the beginning of their arrival to him, in the sense of "You are a people whom I do not recognize and from whom I recoil, so I fear you will visit me with evil," as has been said. How could that be, when their answer, related in the words of the Exalted,

﴿When the messengers came to the family of Lut﴾ This begins the explanation of the destruction of the criminals and the deliverance of the family of Lut. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun indicates that their coming was for the purpose of carrying out what they had been sent with regarding that. The intended meaning is not the very beginning of their coming, but rather their general presence among the family of Lut. For what is related of him, peace be upon him, in the words of the Exalted, ﴿He said, "Surely you are a people unknown [to me]."﴾ he said only after the *al-latya wa-l-latti* (repeated and various efforts), when his stratagems were exhausted and his excuses failed him, and when, in bearing the hardships and enduring the plots from his people, who intended harm to them, he did not witness from the messengers the customary help and support, in what they bring and what they leave, as he struggled to rescue them. This was a denunciation of their abandonment and their failure to support him in such distress that befell him because of them, since they, peace be upon them, were not directly with him in the means of defense and resistance, until it compelled him to say ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a strong support.﴾ as detailed in Surah Hud. It was not that he, peace be upon him, said this at the beginning of their arrival to him, in the sense of "You are a people whom I do not recognize and from whom I recoil, so I fear you will visit me with evil," as has been said. How could that be, when their answer, related in the words of the Exalted,

﴿They said, "Rather, We have brought you that about which they used to doubt."﴾ That is, [We have brought] the punishment with which you used to threaten them, so they doubted it, disbelieved it, and called you a liar concerning it. They had already peeled the staff (an idiom for having made the matter plain) and had made the clarity of the matter evident to him, peace be upon him. So how could distress and tightness of chest afflict him after that? This was said by al-'Allamah Abu al-Su'ud, and it is a reasonable statement. The particle *bal* (بل), meaning "rather," has been taken as an *idrab* (a turning away from one matter to another) from what he, peace be upon him, supposed about their abandonment of support for him. The meaning is:
[p. 68]
"We did not forsake you, nor did We leave you between yourself and them. Rather, We have brought you the punishment that will destroy them, the punishment about which they used to call you a liar when you threatened them with it."

Others, after explaining his words, peace be upon him, "[what] you have heard" (بِما سَمِعْتَ), have taken it as an *idrab* away from the cause of the fear mentioned, with the meaning: "We have not come to you with that for which We showed displeasure. Rather, We have brought you that in which is your joy, your delight, and the cooling of your eyes against your enemy, namely the punishment with which you used to threaten them and they used to call you a liar." They did not say "with their punishment" (بِعَذابِهِمْ) even though the purpose is achieved, so that the statement would contain reassurance in two respects: the certainty of their punishment and the certainty of his truthfulness, peace be upon him. In this there is a reminder of what he used to endure from them of denial. It has been said: He, peace be upon him, alluded to his fear and aversion by [their] being "unknown" (مُنْكَرُونَ), so they answered him, peace be upon him, with an allusion that is better and better still. In my view, there is no impediment to reading the statement as an allusion according to what we have quoted from al-'Allamah as well. Perhaps the placing of this exchange before what took place between him and the people of the city of argument (المُجادَلَة) was, as he said, for the sake of hastening to mention the glad tidings to Lot, peace be upon him, of the destruction of his wicked people and the deliverance of his family, immediately after the mention of the glad tidings to Abraham, peace be upon him, concerning them both. Since that required explaining how deliverance was accomplished and the order of its beginnings, it was indicated in summary, and then the people's action and what was done to them was mentioned. He did not mind the change in the chronological order, trusting in its observance in another place. The attribution of bringing the punishment to him, peace be upon him, although it descends upon the people, is by way of delegating the matter to him, as if they had come to him with it and entrusted its affair to him, so that he might send it upon them as he used to threaten them. Thus the *ba'* (ب) is for transitivity (*ta'diyah*), and it is permitted that it be for accompaniment (*mulabasah*). Both possibilities are also allowed for the *ba'* in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And We have come to you with the truth﴾, that is, with the established, certain matter about which there is no room for doubt or uncertainty, which is their punishment. He expressed it thus to affirm the negation of doubt concerning it. It is also permitted that "the truth" (بِالحَقِّ) refers to the report of the coming of the aforementioned punishment.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ is an emphasis of it. That is: We have come to you in what We said, with the true report, i.e., one that corresponds to reality, and indeed We are truthful in that report or in every report. Thus it serves as evidence of their truthfulness in it. According to the first reading, it is emphasis upon emphasis. Among people there is one who permitted that the *ba'* be for accompaniment, and made the prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the object pronoun. The state of this is not hidden.

﴿They said, "Rather, We have brought you that about which they used to doubt."﴾ That is, [We have brought] the punishment with which you used to threaten them, so they doubted it, disbelieved it, and called you a liar concerning it. They had already peeled the staff (an idiom for having made the matter plain) and had made the clarity of the matter evident to him, peace be upon him. So how could distress and tightness of chest afflict him after that? This was said by al-'Allamah Abu al-Su'ud, and it is a reasonable statement. The particle *bal* (بل), meaning "rather," has been taken as an *idrab* (a turning away from one matter to another) from what he, peace be upon him, supposed about their abandonment of support for him. The meaning is:
[p. 68]
"We did not forsake you, nor did We leave you between yourself and them. Rather, We have brought you the punishment that will destroy them, the punishment about which they used to call you a liar when you threatened them with it."

Others, after explaining his words, peace be upon him, "[what] you have heard" (بِما سَمِعْتَ), have taken it as an *idrab* away from the cause of the fear mentioned, with the meaning: "We have not come to you with that for which We showed displeasure. Rather, We have brought you that in which is your joy, your delight, and the cooling of your eyes against your enemy, namely the punishment with which you used to threaten them and they used to call you a liar." They did not say "with their punishment" (بِعَذابِهِمْ) even though the purpose is achieved, so that the statement would contain reassurance in two respects: the certainty of their punishment and the certainty of his truthfulness, peace be upon him. In this there is a reminder of what he used to endure from them of denial. It has been said: He, peace be upon him, alluded to his fear and aversion by [their] being "unknown" (مُنْكَرُونَ), so they answered him, peace be upon him, with an allusion that is better and better still. In my view, there is no impediment to reading the statement as an allusion according to what we have quoted from al-'Allamah as well. Perhaps the placing of this exchange before what took place between him and the people of the city of argument (المُجادَلَة) was, as he said, for the sake of hastening to mention the glad tidings to Lot, peace be upon him, of the destruction of his wicked people and the deliverance of his family, immediately after the mention of the glad tidings to Abraham, peace be upon him, concerning them both. Since that required explaining how deliverance was accomplished and the order of its beginnings, it was indicated in summary, and then the people's action and what was done to them was mentioned. He did not mind the change in the chronological order, trusting in its observance in another place. The attribution of bringing the punishment to him, peace be upon him, although it descends upon the people, is by way of delegating the matter to him, as if they had come to him with it and entrusted its affair to him, so that he might send it upon them as he used to threaten them. Thus the *ba'* (ب) is for transitivity (*ta'diyah*), and it is permitted that it be for accompaniment (*mulabasah*). Both possibilities are also allowed for the *ba'* in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And We have come to you with the truth﴾, that is, with the established, certain matter about which there is no room for doubt or uncertainty, which is their punishment. He expressed it thus to affirm the negation of doubt concerning it. It is also permitted that "the truth" (بِالحَقِّ) refers to the report of the coming of the aforementioned punishment.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ is an emphasis of it. That is: We have come to you in what We said, with the true report, i.e., one that corresponds to reality, and indeed We are truthful in that report or in every report. Thus it serves as evidence of their truthfulness in it. According to the first reading, it is emphasis upon emphasis. Among people there is one who permitted that the *ba'* be for accompaniment, and made the prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the object pronoun. The state of this is not hidden.

﴿So travel with your family﴾: this begins the arrangement of the principles of salvation, i.e., "Go with them during the night." The two Hijazi readers (Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr) read it with waṣl (connected), taking it as from *sara* (to travel by night), not from *asra* as in the reading of the majority. Both mean the same, according to what Abu 'Ubayda held, namely travel at night. Al-Layth said: it is said *asra* for travelling at the beginning of the night and *sara* for travelling at its end. The author of *al-Iqlid* (Sahib al-Iqlid) related *fasar* from *sara*, and Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of *al-Lawami'* related it from al-Yamani. It is general in meaning. It was also said that it is specific to travel by day and is not a metathesis of *sara*.

﴿in a portion of the night﴾: in a part of it, or at its end. From this is his saying:

*Open the door and look at the stars: how many portions of a dark night are upon us?*

It was said: it is after some good part of it has passed. In the expression there is emphasis (ta'kid) or abstraction (tajrid), according to the reading of the community, as it is said; and according to the reading *sir*, none of that applies. There will be a sequel to this, God willing. Mundhir ibn Sa'id related that a group read *biqatha'* with a fatḥa on the ṭa'.

﴿and follow behind them﴾: and be upon their trail, driving them, pressing them on, and keeping watch over their conditions. Perhaps the preference for *ittiba'* (following) over *suq* (driving), although the latter is what is intended by the command, is for the sake of emphasis on this, since driving may be done by going ahead of some while lagging behind others, and it customarily entails neglect of the state of the one who lags behind. The prohibited looking back is by His saying: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, i.e., none of you (addressed to you), [p. 69] and of them ﴿anyone﴾, who would see what is behind him of terror that he cannot bear, or who would be struck by the punishment. So the looking back is in its literal sense. It is also permissible that the meaning be: let none of you turn aside or lag behind for some purpose, lest he be struck by what strikes the wrongdoers. Thus looking back is metaphorical, because turning toward a thing entails loving it and not parting from it, so one lingers with it. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned that when God sent destruction upon his people and saved him and his family, in answer to his supplication against them, and he went out as an emigrant, he could not avoid striving in thanking God and perpetuating His remembrance and clearing his mind for that. So he was commanded to send them ahead, so that his heart would not be occupied with what it had left behind, and so that he would be watching over them and their conditions, so no glance from them would escape him, out of modesty on his part, nor any other slip in that terrifying and dreaded situation. And so that none of them would lag behind for some purpose and be struck by the punishment, and so that his journey would be that of the fugitive who goes ahead of his herd and escapes with it. They were forbidden to look back so that they would not see what was descending on their people and grow tender toward them, and so that they would prepare their souls for emigration and make them content to leave their dwellings, and go forward without looking back at what lies behind them, like one who grieves at parting from his homeland, who keeps twisting his neck toward it, as he said:

*I turned toward the tribe until I found myself, and I was weary of listening, neck and throat.*

Or the prohibition against looking back is made a metaphor (kinayah) for continuing the journey and abandoning delay and stopping, because whoever looks back must necessarily pause for at least a brief moment. End. The editor (al-Mudaqqiq) said: the summary of this is that the benefit of the command and the prohibition is that he, upon him be prayer and peace, should emigrate in a manner that enables him and his family to devote themselves to the remembrance of God, Exalted, and to be wholly free for His thanks. And in this there is, together with that, guidance to what is more conducive to resolve in journeying, and the etiquette of travel, and what is incumbent upon the leader and the led in it, and an alert to the manner of the true journey, and that it is more deserving of cutting off obstacles and putting aside attachments, and more deserving [...] and an indication that wholehearted turning toward God, Exalted, is sincerity. So to God, Exalted, belongs the excellence of the Revelation and its subtleties, which cannot be counted. End. You know that the benefit being emigration in a manner with which one can devote oneself to the remembrance of God, Exalted, and be free for His thanks is not obvious, as is not hidden. Perhaps for this reason some abridgers of his book omitted it. The reason God, glory be to Him, did not exempt the woman from travelling by night or looking back is that He was content with what was mentioned in another place. And the like of this is not novel in the Revelation.

﴿and go where you are commanded﴾: it was said: to where God, Exalted, commands you to go, and it is Syria according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. It was said: Egypt. It was said: al-Urdunn (Jordan). It was said: a place of deliverance not specified. So *imdu* (go) is transitive to *haythu* (where), and *tu'marun* (you are commanded) to the omitted pronoun by extension (ittisa'). It was objected that this is accepted for the transitivity of *tu'marun* to *haythu*, since its complement, the preposition *bi*, is omitted, the original being *tu'marun bihi* (you are commanded with it, i.e., with its going), so it was connected directly. But as for the transitivity of *imdu* to *haythu*, there is no extension in it, rather it is in its original state, since it is one of the indefinite adverbs, unless what was mentioned is taken as taghlib (predominance). It was answered: the connection of *haythu* to the verb here is not the connection of adverbiality, so that the transitivity of the verb to it directly would be appropriate, since it is an indefinite adverb, for it is a non-explicit direct object, as in *sirtu ila al-Kufa* (I travelled to Kufa). The grammarians have stated that it may be used with a verb, so the omitted element is not in *bal ila* (rather, to), so there is no problem. End. What is mentioned in the books of Arabic grammar is that the original use of *haythu* is as a place adverb, and it occurs for time rarely according to al-Akhfash, as in his saying:

*For the youth is intellect by which he lives, where (when) his leg guides his foot.*

He meant "when it guides." It is rarely used except as an adverb, and its being governed by *bi* is rare, in his saying:

*He was among us at the place where he unfastens the waist-wrap,*

and by *ila*, in his saying:

*To where Umm Qashm cast her saddle,*

and by *fi*, in his saying:

*So he became, in the place where we met their fugitive, freed and bound-handed and bleeding from the nose.*

[p. 70] Ibn Malik said: its inflection is rare, and among its occurrences unaccompanied by adverbiality is his saying:

*Indeed, where he who you are guardian of settles, a sanctuary in which there is honour and security.*

So *haythu* is the subject of *inna*. Abu Hayyan said: this is an error, because its being the subject of *inna* is a derivative of its being a subject (mubtada'), and this is never heard in that at all. Rather the subject of *inna* in the verse is *hima* (sanctuary), and *haythu* is the predicate, because it is an adverb. The correct view is that it is not inflected, so it is not a doer (fa'il), nor a direct object (maf'ul bihi), nor a subject (mubtada'). End. Ibn Hisham transmitted from al-Farisi its occurrence as a direct object, and on it he based His saying, exalted be He: ﴿God knows best where He places His message﴾. He mentioned that it may be put in the genitive by *min* and other particles, and that it does not occur as the subject of *inna*, contrary to Ibn Malik. Al-Zajjaj claimed that it is a relative pronoun. From what we have mentioned the state of its inflection becomes clear. The objection to what the answerer mentioned is that although the problem of transitivity is removed by it, it is nonetheless incorrect, because they have explicitly stated that a sentence annexed to it does not have a pronoun returning from it to the annexed noun. Najm al-A'imma said: know that an adverb annexed to a sentence, since it is an adverb of the verbal noun contained in the sentence, may not have a pronoun from the sentence returning to it. So one does not say *yawma qadima Zayd fihi* (the day Zayd arrived in it), because the link that is required has been achieved by annexing the adverb to the sentence and making it an adverb of its content, so it is as if you said: "the day of Zayd's arrival in it." End. And *haythu*, according to what they have mentioned, generally requires annexation to a sentence, and its being a verbal sentence is more common. Its annexation to a single noun is rare, as in:

*White blades, where the turbans are wound,* and *where Suhayl rises,* and this is not analogized by other than al-Kisa'i. Less common than this is its not being annexed explicitly, by being annexed to an omitted noun with *ma* substituted for it, as in his saying:

*When a breeze, from where it blows, wafts toward him.* That is, from where it blew. Here it is annexed to the sentence after it, so how can the pronoun in *yu'marun* be taken as returning to it? Some have stated that *haythu* cannot have a pronoun return to it. What is in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit) is that it is an indefinite place adverb, to which *imdu* is transitive directly, as you say: *qa'adtu haythu qa'ada Zayd* (I sat where Zayd sat). The apparent view is that the verb's connection to it, as the answerer said, is not the connection of adverbiality. So perhaps this is based on implying a verb suitable for the adverb to be connected to, such as *al-hulul* (dwelling), *al-tawattun* (settling), or others. It was related from some of them that *haythu* here is a time adverb, i.e., "go at the time you are commanded," and the command meant is what preceded in His saying, exalted be He: "So travel with your family in a portion of the night." It was rejected that on this view it should have been *umirtum* (you were commanded) rather than *tu'marun*, and moreover that it involves using *haythu* in its less common meaning without any reason. The apparent sense of the words of some eminent scholars is that the present tense is used in place of the past according to the meaning indicated first, which requires that a command to proceed to a place has preceded. If so, the form of the present tense is to evoke the scene, and the choice of "proceed to that" rather than "reach it and join it" is to signal the importance of deliverance and to observe the appropriateness between it and what preceded concerning those who remained behind.

﴿And We decreed﴾, that is, We revealed to him that matter, decreed and established. Qada (decreeing) here carries the sense of awha (revealing), which is why it takes the same complement with ila (to). The included meaning (tadmin, lexical embedding, where one verb is used in the sense of another) is treated as a circumstantial (hal), as we have pointed out, which is one of the two well-known views on tadmin. That matter is vague (mubham), and it is explained by ﴿that the last of these people will be cut off﴾. It is in apposition (badal) to it, according to al-Akhfash. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be an apposition to "the matter" if it is taken as an explanation (bayan) of it and not as an apposition. According to al-Farra', "that" is in the sense of dropping the preposition ba' (with), meaning "bi-anna dabira..." (that the last of...). Perhaps what is pointed to by "that matter" is the command contained in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and proceed where you are commanded﴾. The ba' is for accompaniment (mulabasa), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial (hal), meaning: We revealed that matter, concerning the salvation of him and his family, accompanied by a description of the state of his criminal people, that their root would be cut off. This is good, but it is not free from remoteness. Zayd ibn Ali and al-A'mash, may Allah have mercy on them, read "inna" with a kasra on the hamza. This is explained as a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What is that matter?" and the answer was given: "Indeed the last of..." Or it is in apposition, based on the view that revelation (wahy) carries the sense of saying (qawl). It is said that this is supported by the reading of Abd Allah: "And We said, indeed the last of..." This is a reading of interpretation (tafsir), not of the Qur'an, because it contradicts the written text of the Mushaf. Dabir means the last, and the intention is not the cutting off of their last one, but their complete destruction, so that not one of them remains. ﴿at dawn﴾, that is, entering into the morning, for the form af'ala is used to indicate entering into something, like atham (to accuse) and anjad (to aid). It comes from asbaha in its complete sense (tamma). It is a circumstantial (hal) of "these," and this is permissible because the noun in the construction is part of the whole. It has been said that a circumstantial may come from the second noun in an idafa (construct phrase) when the first noun is such; and the governing element is not the meaning of the idafa, contrary to some scholars. That it is the demonstrative noun is an error, because no one has said that the governed element of a circumstantial works in it. Abu Hayyan preferred that it is a circumstantial of the pronoun concealed in "cut off," which refers back to "dabir." This is permissible despite the difference in number (singular and plural), in consideration of meaning, because that refers to the meaning of "the last of these," so the circumstantial agrees with its governing noun in plurality.

Al-Farra' and Abu Ubayd estimated the phrase as "if they are entering the morning," just as you say: "You riding is better than you walking." It has been criticized: if this is an estimate of meaning, it is eloquent; but if it is an explanation of grammatical analysis (i'rab), there is no necessity for it, as is not hidden.

[p. 71]

﴿وجاءَ أهْلُ المَدِينَةِ﴾ This begins the narration of what the people did when they stood at the place of the guests, of the deed itself and its consequences, which were alluded to earlier in summary form. This came, in terms of sequence, before their knowledge of the guests' destruction, as you have heard. The conjunction *wa* (and) does not indicate order. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that this came after they knew of that, and that what proceeded from him, peace be upon him, in dialogue with them was out of concealment from them, giving them respite, and waiting for them. It is not hidden that the grief and constriction of his chest being a matter of concealment and respite is also something the sound nature rejects. By "the city" is meant Sodom, and by its people those wicked folk. Perhaps the reference to them in this way is to indicate their large number, along with what it implies of the extreme gravity of their deed, for it is fitting for the people of a city to honour the strangers who arrive at their city and to treat them well. Yet they turned away from this fitting conduct toward those whom they reckoned to be strangers arriving for the purpose of foul deeds, deeds which no one among the worlds had preceded them in. They came to the house of Lut, peace be upon him. ﴿يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾ meaning: rejoicing and glad, since it was said to them that with him, peace be upon him, there were guests, beardless youths of the utmost beauty and loveliness, so they became covetous. May God the Exalted curse them concerning this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 68:

﴿He said, "Indeed, these are my guests.﴾ Al-ḍayf (the guest), as we mentioned earlier in the original (al-aṣl), is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of ḍāfahu (he hosted him), and it is applied to the singular and the plural. For this reason it is valid to make it a predicate (khabar) for "hā'ulā'" (these). Its application to the angels, upon them be peace, is according to his (peace be upon him) belief, since they were in the guise of guests. It was also said: it is according to their (the angels') belief in that. The emphasis (al-ta'kīd) is not in response to their denial of it, but rather to affirm their connection to him and to show his care for them (upon them be peace) and his readiness to honor their rights and protect them from harm. For this reason he said: ﴿so do not disgrace me﴾, that is, in their presence, by harming them, so that they would know that I have no standing with you; or [it means]: do not disgrace me by disgracing my guest, for whoever is wronged regarding his guest has been wronged himself. It is said: "fadahtuhu fadḥan wa faḍīḥatan" (I disgraced him) when he revealed of his affair that which brings shame upon him; and it is said: "faḍaḥa al-ṣubḥu" (the dawn became exposed) when it became clear to the people.

﴿So fear God﴾ in your engaging in what would distress me, ﴿and do not disgrace me﴾, meaning: do not humiliate or demean me by assaulting those I have given protection. It is from the disgrace (khizy), in the sense of abasement and humiliation. Since their assault on them came after he had forbidden them from it with the words ﴿so do not shame me﴾, it had a greater effect on his side, peace be upon him, and brought more shame upon him. An assault on a guest before knowledge of him may be overlooked, but after knowledge and after opposing them by defending him and protecting him, that is the greatest shame.

He, peace be upon him, expressed what would befall him from their side after the aforementioned prohibition, because of their obstinacy and their open defiance of him, as disgrace, and his command to them to fear God Most High in that matter. It is also permissible that this be from khaza'a, which is modesty (haya'), meaning: do not make me feel shame before the people by your assaulting them. Some of them favored the first interpretation.

As for why he, peace be upon him, did not explicitly forbid that very abomination itself, it was said: because he knew that it would not benefit them. It was also said: out of consideration for the utmost courtesy toward his guests, since he did not state explicitly what would weigh heavily on their hearing and what their natures would recoil from, and a free man sees death as more pleasant in taste than that.

Some eminent scholars said: the meaning of ﴿fear God﴾ is to command them to fear Him, glorified is He, from committing the abomination. This was criticized on the grounds that it does not fit with its placement between the two prohibitions directly concerning him, peace be upon him.

Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Did we not forbid you from [sheltering] the worlds?"﴾ That is, from granting protection to any of them and from standing between us and him, or from hosting any of them. The hamza is for rebuke, and the waw, as many have said, is for conjunction with an implied clause, meaning: "Did we not warn you in advance and forbid you from that? For they used to molest every stranger with evil, and he, peace be upon him, would forbid them from that to the best of his ability and would come between them and those who confronted him. And they had already forbidden him from engaging in such things." So it is as if they said: "What you mention of disgrace and shame has come upon you only from your own side, not from ours, for had it not been for your interfering with what you were confronting, it would not have befallen you." And when he saw that they would not desist from what they were engaged in...

"He said, 'These are my daughters'—meaning the women of the people, or his own daughters in actuality. The discussion of this has already passed. The demonstrative (hā'ulā') is the subject (mubtada'), and (banātī, "my daughters") is its predicate (khabar), and there is an ellipsis in the speech, i.e., 'so marry them.' It is also permitted that (banātī) be a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (bayān), with the predicate omitted, i.e., 'they are purer for you,' as in the other verse. And it is permitted that (hā'ulā') be in the position of an accusative governed by an omitted verb, i.e., 'marry my daughters.' The first is the more evident.

﴿If you are going to act⁠﴾ expresses doubt about their acceptance of his words; it is as though he said: 'If you do what I tell you—and I do not think you will do it.' It has also been said: 'If you intend to satisfy desire in what Allah the Exalted has made lawful, rather than what He has forbidden.' The first interpretation, as in al-Kashshaf, is more apt.

In the Hawashi al-Shihabiyya it is stated that it is more fitting to the sense of doubt, and the practice of some of them indicates a preference for the second, it being said that it is what is immediately understood from the verb. On both interpretations the object is understood. It is permitted to treat the description as if it were intransitive. The answer to the condition is omitted, i.e., 'then it is better for you,' or 'then carry out that.'"

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 72:**

﴿Ö by your life﴾ is an oath by God, Exalted is He, by the life of our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, according to what the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Mardawayh and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, who said: "God did not create, produce or bring into being any soul more honored by Him than Muhammad (ﷺ). And I have not heard that God, Glorified is He, swore by the life of anyone other than him." He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿By your life﴾, etc.

It has also been said that it is an oath by the angels, peace be upon them, by the life of Lot, peace be upon him. This view, besides contradicting what has been transmitted (al-ma'thur), requires supplying a verb of speech, meaning: the angels said to Lot, peace be upon them: ﴿By your life﴾, etc. This is contrary to the basic principle, although the context of the story supports it and points to it. Therefore, the objection raised by the author of *al-Fara'id* that it is an unnecessary supposition does not stand. Yet if such a supposition were permitted, it would be possible to remove every text from its meaning by supplying something, and thus confidence in the meanings of the text would be lost.

Whichever view is taken, ﴿'amruka﴾ ("your life") is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is obligatorily omitted, meaning: "my oath" or "my swearing" or something similar. The word 'umr, with a fatha or a damma, means continued existence and life. However, they consistently used the fatha in oaths because of its frequent occurrence, so lightening it was appropriate. When the lam (of emphasis) enters it, the fatha is obligatorily retained and the predicate is omitted in the oath. Without the lam, it may be in the accusative or the nominative, and this is clear. It is a verbal noun (masdar) in a construct relation with its agent or its object. The insertion of the particle ba' (bi-) has been heard with it, and the predicate has been mentioned, but rarely.

It is mentioned that when it is stripped of the lam, it is not necessarily restricted to oaths; this is reported from al-Jawhari. Ibn Ya'ish said: it is only used for oaths as well. It occurs irregularly as *'amali*, and they counted it as an inversion (qalb).

Abu al-Haytham said:

The meaning of ﴿la'amruka﴾ is "your religion by which you build up," and it is explained as worship. He recited:

"O you who wed the Pleiades to Suhayl,
by your life (for God), how can the two meet?"

He meant "your worship of God, Exalted is He," for it is said, according to what is reported from Ibn al-A'rabi: 'amartu rabbi, meaning 'abadtuhu (I worshipped my Lord); and Fulan is 'amir li-rabbihi, meaning 'abid (a worshipper); and I left Fulan ya'muru rabbahu, meaning he worships his Lord. This is a rare usage.

There are several interpretations of the line. Sibawayh said regarding it: the original is 'ammartuka Allah ta'alා ta'miran, then the extra letters of the verbal noun were removed and it was placed in the position of the verb, construed with its first object. The meaning of 'amartuka is "I gave you life," by asking God, Exalted is He, to grant you life. Then, since the meaning of asking was implied in 'umr, it governed a second object, namely the Glorious Name. Accordingly, it is in the accusative in this view.

Al-Akhfash permitted its nominative case, so that it is the subject, meaning: "God, Glorified is He, granted you life." Al-Radi permitted that ﴿'amraka﴾ here be in the accusative as an object of an omitted verb, meaning: "I ask God, Exalted is He, for your life," and "I ask" takes two objects. Or the meaning may be: "I ask you by the right of your making God, Exalted is He, to live," that is, your belief in His continuance and eternity, Exalted is He. Then its accusative case is by omitting the particle of oath, as in "By God, I will surely act." It is a verbal noun with its extra letters removed, construed with its agent, and the Glorious Name is its object. There is no harm in construing 'umr with Him, Exalted is He, and it has come thus construed. A poet said:

"When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,
by God's life, their pleasure pleases me."

Al-A'sha said:

"And by the life of Him who made the months a sign,
from which the diminishing and completion of them are made clear."

Some have claimed that it is not permissible to say "la'umru Allah ta'ala" (by God's life, Exalted is He), because He, Glorified is He, is eternal and everlasting; and it seems they imagined that 'umr is only said of what has an end, which is not the case. Its construction with a first-person pronoun also occurs in their speech. Al-Nabigha said: "La'amri wa-ma 'umri 'alayya bi-hayyin" ("By my life, and my life is not easy for me").

Al-Nakha'i disliked this, because it is an oath by the life of the one swearing. I do not know the basis for this restriction, for in ﴿la'amruka﴾ there is an address to a person, an oath by the life of the one addressed. The ruling on swearing by other than God, Exalted is He, is established most thoroughly in its proper place.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, read ﴿'amruka﴾ without the lam, ﴿innahum la-fi sakratihim﴾, meaning: "they are indeed in their error," or "in the intensity of their lust which removed their minds and their discrimination between their wrong and the right by which they are guided," ﴿ya'mahun﴾, meaning: "they wander in bewilderment," so how would they hear counsel? The root of 'amah is blindness of insight, and it results in bewilderment; and on this basis it is explained so. The pronouns refer to the people of the city (Medina).

The use of the imperfect verb, in accordance with what is transmitted in the address, is to narrate a past state. It has also been said, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that the pronouns refer to the Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya and others found this unlikely, because it does not fit the preceding or the following context. For this reason it has been said that the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), and the clause ﴿ya'mahun﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase. It has been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive ﴿sakratihim﴾, with the governing element being "sakrah" or the sense of the construct relation. Its status is not hidden from you.

Al-Ashhab read "sukratihim" with a damma on the sin. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "sakaratihim" in the plural. Al-A'mash read "sukrihim" without a ta'. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of al-Jahdami, read "annahum" with a fatha on the hamza. Abu al-Baqa' said: this is on the assumption that the lam is extra. Similar is the reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, "alla innahum la-ya'kulun al-ta'am" ("Indeed they eat food") with a fatha, based on the view that the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') only accompanies the particle 'inna with a kasra on the hamza. The implied meaning in this reading is "la'amruka qasami 'ala annahum" ("By your life, my oath is that they..."). So understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 73:

Page 74

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, meaning a terrifying cry. The definite article is for the category (ta'rif li-l-jins). It is also said that it is the cry of Jibril, peace be upon him, so the definite article is for a specific referent (ta'rif li-l-'ahd). Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: "There is no indication in the verse for this specification; if it is established by a strong proof, then it may be held."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that he said concerning the verse: "The cry is like the thunderbolt (sa'iqa); every thing by which a people was destroyed is a thunderbolt and a cry." ﴿At sunrise﴾: entering the time of the sunrise. The al-Mudaqqiq said: The combination of ﴿in the morning﴾ and ﴿at sunrise﴾ is by way of the beginning and the end, such that the beginning of the punishment is at dawn and its end is at sunrise. The seizing by the cry means its overpowering them and its taking hold of them, and from this comes al-akhidh (the captive), the prisoner. You may also say: ﴿cut off﴾ in the sense of "it will soon cut off," and it ended. It is also said: "(at sunrise)" is a qualifying circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 74:

﴿So We turned it upside down﴾, i.e., the city, as is apparent. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers back to the towns (al-qura), even though they have not been previously mentioned. By "its highest part" is meant the surface of the earth and what is upon it, and this is the first object of "We made" (ja'ala), with "its lowest part" (wa-safilaha) being the second object of it. The discussion of this has already been given earlier. ﴿And We rained upon them﴾ in the midst of that ﴿stones﴾ ﴿of baked clay (sijjil)﴾, i.e., of clay that has become hardened into stone. According to the well-known view, sijjil is an arabicized form of the Persian "sang-gil" (sangk kal, i.e., stone and clay). Abu 'Ubayd and a group of scholars held that it is an Arabic word and that it is also pronounced "sijjin" with a nun, and they argued from the verse of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

"Blows which the heroes enjoined upon one another, sijjinan."

But this, as you see, is not conclusive. Al-Asma'i was asked about its meaning in the verse and said: "I will not explain it, since I used to hear it as a youth as 'sikhkhinan' with the letter kha (meaning 'hot'), i.e., 'heated'." "Sijjin" with the letter jim is also used. It has been said that it is derived from "al-sijill," which means "the book," i.e., clay upon which their names were written, or that God had written their punishment with it. The discussion of this has also already passed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 75:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾ — that is, in what has been mentioned of the story — ﴿are signs﴾ — indications by which the reality of the truth may be inferred — ﴿for those who discern﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "for those who look (carefully)." Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "for those who apply firasa (discernment)." Mujahid said: "for those who take heed." It has been said otherwise, and these meanings are close to one another. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan), it is said that tawassum (discerning) is a form of tafa''ul from wasm (mark), which is the sign by which something sought is inferred. Tha'lab said:

Tawassum is looking from the horn to the foot, and exhausting the aspects of recognition. The poet said:

"Whenever a tribe arrives at 'Ukaz, do they send to me their 'arif (headman) who discerns (yatawassam)?"

It is also mentioned that its origin is reflection and careful consideration, taken from wasm, which is the branding of a camel's hide or something else with a heated iron. It is said: "I discerned good in him (tawassamtu fihi khayran)," meaning that its signs appeared to me in him. 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

"I have discerned in you good, which I recognize, and Allah knows that my sight is steadfast."

The prepositional phrase (li-ayatin) is in the position of a qualifier, or it is related to it. This verse, according to al-Jalal al-Suyuti, is a basis for firasa (physiognomy). Al-Tirmidhi has narrated from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of the firasa of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah, the Exalted."

Then he recited the verse. Some Malikis used to judge by firasa in legal rulings, following the method of Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verses 76–77:**

﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, the destroyed city; and it was said: the towns (al-qura). ﴿Is on a road that remains﴾, that is, a established path that people travel and see its traces. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the signs (al-ayat); it was also said: it refers to the stones; and it was also said: it refers to the Blast (al-sayha), meaning: and indeed the Blast is in ambush (bi-mardad) for those who do the same deeds as they did, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾. (And muqim) was said to mean "known (ma'lum)," and it was said: "transgressing, constantly traversed (mu'tadin da'im al-suluk)." ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of the city or the towns, or in their being within the sight of people who witness them when they pass by them, ﴿is surely a sign﴾, a great one, ﴿for the believers﴾ in Allah, Exalted is He, and His Messenger ﷺ, for they are the ones who know that their evil conduct is what left their dwellings as desolate ruins; as for others, they attribute that to chance or to the astrological configurations. The singular "sign" after its plural earlier was said to be because what is observed here is only the remaining traces, not the entire story, as in what came before; and it was said: it is to indicate that for the believers one sign suffices.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 78:

﴿And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were wrongdoers﴾. They are the people of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). Al-Ayka (the Thicket) originally means a densely intertwined tree, and it is the singular of al-ayk. The poet said:

تَجْلُو بِقادِمَتِي حَمامَةُ أيْكَةٍ بَرْدًا أسِفُّ لَثاتَهُ بِالإثْمِدِ

[The dove of a thicket shows, with its primary feather, hail-white teeth, whose gums I sip with antimony.]

It is meant here as a ghaydah (a thicket), that is, a place of dense trees, based on what is narrated: these people used to dwell in the ghaydah, whose common trees were the al-dawm (doum palm), and it is said the al-sidr (lote tree). So God Most High sent Shu'ayb to them, but they denied him, and they were destroyed in a manner that you will hear, God willing, Most High. It is also said that it was a town in which they used to live. Its application to what has been mentioned is either by way of transmission (naql), or by naming the place after the state found in it, and then it became dominant over it until it became a proper name (ʿalam). The view that it is a proper name is supported by the fact that it was read as "Laykah" (ليكة) as a diptote (mamnu' al-sarf). 

(And "in" [إنْ]) according to the Basrans is the lightened form of the heavy one, its noun being an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the lam is the lam that distinguishes (al-lam al-fariqah). According to al-Farra', it is the negating "in," having no noun, and the lam is in the sense of "illa" (except). The one relied upon is the first, that is, "and indeed the matter was that those people were transgressing the limit."

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾, that is, We requited them with punishment for their earlier crime. The pronoun refers to the people of al-Aykah (the Thicket).

Al-Tabarsi claimed that the pronoun refers to them and to the people of Lut, but this is not correct. Numerous narrators report from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that He, exalted is His majesty, sent the heat upon them for seven days; no shade sheltered them from it and nothing could keep it away from them. Then He, glory be to Him, sent upon them a cloud, and they began seeking shelter in it, so He sent down upon them fire from it, and it consumed them. This is the punishment of the Day of the Canopy."

﴿And indeed they both﴾, that is, the two places of the people of Lut and the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both. Most scholars held this view. It was also said that the pronoun refers to al-Aykah and Madyan, and although the second is not mentioned here, the mention of the first points to it, since Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent to its people.

Ibn 'Asakir and others transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Madyan and the People of the Thicket are two nations to whom Allah, exalted, sent Shu'ayb, peace be upon him.'"

This view is not free from distance. Indeed, it has been said that the first view is also like this, because the description of the city of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, as ﴿a clear highway (imam mubin)﴾, that is, a clear road, repeats what was stated earlier about it, namely that it is ﴿on an enduring path (sabil muqim)﴾, as most exegetes hold. Joining the other place with it in the report does not remove the repetition regarding it. Perhaps for this reason some said: the pronoun returns to Lut and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, meaning: indeed they both are on a clear path of truth.

Al-Jubba'i said: the pronoun refers to the report of the destruction of the people of Lut and the report of the destruction of the people of Shu'ayb. The word imam (imam) is a name for that which is followed, and it has been applied to the road, to the Preserved Tablet, and to any tablet prepared for reading, and to a builder's measuring line. According to this view, it means the Preserved Tablet.

Mu'arrij said: imam means "book" in the dialect of Himyar. The statement that they are both in the Preserved Tablet indicates the prior decree of Allah, exalted, regarding the destruction of the two peoples, because of what He, glory be to Him, knew of their evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 80:

﴿And certainly the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers﴾ meaning Thamud, ﴿the messengers﴾ when they denied their messenger Salih, peace be upon him. For whoever denies one of the messengers of Allah, glorified is He, it is as if he has denied all of them, because their word is in agreement on monotheism and the fundamentals which do not differ with the difference of nations and eras. And it has been said: the intended meaning of "the messengers" is Salih, peace be upon him, and those with him among the believers, by way of taghlib (predominance) and treating the followers as messengers, as it has been said: "the Khubaybun" for Khubayb ibn al-Zubayr and his companions. And the poet said:

"It cut me off from supporting the two Khubaybs, my cutting
and the saying that each of them (the two) descended from the she-camel and her young one"

The position of a messenger, because he is like the one calling them to follow Salih, peace be upon him. So the plural in this sense has no basis at all in my view.

Al-Hijr is a valley between the Hijaz and al-Sham, where they used to dwell. Al-Raghib said: That which is surrounded by stones is called hijr, and by it the Hijr of the Ka'bah and the dwellings of Thamud were named. The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, forbade his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, as in Sahih al-Bukhari and others, from entering upon these people except while weeping, out of fear that there would befall them what befell them.

It is reported from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the people, in the year of the Battle of Tabuk, drew water from the wells from which Thamud used to drink, and kneaded dough with it, and set cooking pots with meat. So the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, commanded them to pour out the pots, and to feed the camels the dough, and he commanded them to draw water from the well which the she-camel used to come to.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 81:**

﴿And We gave them Our signs﴾: from the she-camel, her young one, her drinking, and her milk.

Some have mentioned that the she-camel had five signs: her emergence from the rock; the nearness of her offspring's birth at the time of her emergence; her great size, so that no camel resembled her; and the abundance of her milk, enough for all of them. It has also been said that their prophet, peace be upon him, had miracles other than those mentioned, and it does not harm us that they were not detailed. Yet, as a general claim, this is nothing. It has also been said that the "signs" are the rational proofs set up for them, which point to Him, glory be to Him, and which are scattered in the souls and the horizons, though this is far-fetched. It has further been said that they are the verses of the Book revealed to their prophet, peace be upon him.

It is objected to this that he, peace be upon him, had no transmitted Book. The answer may be that a Book does not necessarily have to be revealed to him literally; it is sufficient that it was with him, and he was commanded to act upon what is in it, and this is in the position of its being revealed to him. It may also be said that it was revealed repeatedly in actuality. The strength of the objection is not hidden. It has also been said that the "signs" may be taken to include what reached them of the signs of the messengers, peace be upon them all. And when it is valid to say that denying one of them is like denying all of them, why would it not be valid to say that what one of them brings of signs is as if all of them had brought it? This is open to examination. In sum, the apparent meaning is the first explanation.

﴿But they turned away from them﴾: not inclined to act upon what they require. The placing of the object before the verb is for the sake of a consideration that suits the rhyming endings of the verses (rhythmic closings, *ru'us al-ayy*).

And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, feeling secure ﴿from the descent of punishment upon them﴾. It was also said: [they felt secure] from death, because they were deceived by their long lives. It was also said: [they felt secure] from being destroyed, from thieves breaking into their homes, and from enemies forming factions against them, because of how strongly their houses were built.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The most sound view that appears to me on this matter is that they felt secure about the consequences of the Hereafter, so they did not act in accordance with it, but acted according to their sense of security." The placement of the statement ﴿So the Cry seized them at morning﴾ provides stronger support for the first view. In Surah al-Aʿraf, the words ﴿so the earthquake seized them﴾ occur. The two were reconciled by saying that the Cry leads to the earthquake, or that the Cry is a figurative expression (majaz, a non-literal usage) for it.

The restriction "at morning" has been raised as a difficulty, along with what is reported about the sequence of their circumstances after the prophet (peace be upon him) warned them of the descent of punishment: when it was the forenoon of the fourth day, they embalmed themselves with aloe and wrapped themselves in leather shrouds, and then a cry came to them from the sky, and their hearts were torn apart. This report implies that the Cry seized them after the forenoon, not at morning. It has been answered that if the report is authentic, then ﴿at morning﴾ should be understood as meaning that the Cry occurred during the day rather than at night, or the word "morning" was used for an extended period of time running up to the forenoon. It was also said that the verse and the report can be reconciled in a manner similar to how the two verses mentioned just before were reconciled. In this there is room for reflection, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 84:

﴿Then what they used to earn did not avail them﴾ — that is, it did not repel from them what had descended upon them — ﴿what they used to earn﴾: from carving out sturdy houses, or from that together with gathering wealth and equipment. ﴿But they fell prostrate, dead﴾ — "fa-ma" (then what): the first "ma" is negative, and it may also be interrogative; the second "ma" may be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya, a particle that turns the following clause into a verbal noun) and may be a relative pronoun (mawsula). Abu Hayyan preferred the latter, and its returning pronoun is elided, i.e., "the thing that they used to earn [by it]."

In al-Irshad it is stated that the "fa" (then) indicates the sequence of the non-avail specifically at the time the punishment descended, according to what they used to hope for, not the non-avail in an absolute sense, for that is a continuous matter. And in the verse there is from the accusations against them what is not hidden.

[Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 15, verse 85]

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾, that is, except as a creation clothed in truth and wisdom, such that it does not suit the continuance of corruption and the establishment of evils. Wisdom required the destruction of such people, to repel their corruption and to guide those who remain toward righteousness. ﴿And indeed the Hour is coming﴾, and there is no doubt that We will also take vengeance upon the likes of these people. The first sentence refers to their worldly punishment, and the second to their punishment in the Hereafter. In both sentences there is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) that is not hidden. The first includes an indication of the reason for the destruction of those people: that it is a matter which wisdom required. In *al-Tafsir al-Kabir* (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's commentary), regarding the arrangement of the verses, it is said: when He (exalted is He) mentioned the destruction of the disbelievers, it was as if it were said: how is that fitting for the Merciful? So He (glorified is He) answered that He only created creation so that they would be occupied with worship and obedience. So when they abandon it and turn away from it, wisdom requires their destruction and the purification of the earth.

The commentator (al-Razi) criticized this, saying that it is only correct according to the view of the Mu'tazilites (*al-Mu'tazila*, the rationalist school). He then mentioned another explanation of this: that the purpose of this story is to make the Prophet (ﷺ) patient in the face of the folly of his people. When he hears that the earlier nations treated their prophets (peace be upon them) with such corrupt treatment, it becomes easy for him (peace and blessings be upon him) to bear the folly of his people. Then, when He (exalted is He) explained the sending down of punishment upon the earlier nations who denied, He said to him (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed the Hour is coming﴾, and Allah (exalted is He) will take vengeance for you upon your enemies in it, and will requite you and them according to your good deeds and their evil deeds. For He (glorified is He) did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with justice and equity. So how is it fitting for His wisdom to neglect your affair?

To the permissibility of interpreting *al-haqq* (the truth) as *al-'adl* (justice) went Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud), who indicated that the *ba'* (in *bi-al-haqq*) is causal, and that the meaning is: We did not create that except by reason of justice and equity on the Day of Recompense for deeds. He mentioned that the second sentence points to this. Perhaps making each sentence refer to a separate matter, as we have indicated, is preferable.

Some of the Ash'aris (*al-Ash'ariyya*, followers of al-Ash'ari) used the first sentence as proof that the actions of servants in general are created by Him (exalted is He), since they are included in what lies between them. Some Mu'tazilites claimed that it refutes those who say this, because sinful acts are false, and if they were created by Him (glorified is He), they would be created by truth and falsehood, and what is falsehood is not created by truth. This is a statement devoid of verification.

﴿So forgive﴾, that is, turn away from the disbelievers who deny, ﴿with gracious forgiveness﴾, which is forgiveness that is free from reproach. This is what more than one narrator related from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) defined *al-safh* (forgiveness, pardon) itself as leaving off blame, and mentioned that it is more emphatic than *al-'afw* (pardon). In the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) with this there is an indication that he (peace be upon him) was able to take vengeance upon them. So it is as if it were said: turn away from them, bear their harm, do not hasten to take vengeance upon them, and deal with them in the manner of one who forgives and is forbearing. The sum of this is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to oppose them with a pleasing character, forbearance and deliberation, by warning them and calling them to Allah (exalted is He) before fighting, and then fighting them. According to this, the verse is not abrogated (*ghayr mansukha*, i.e., not subject to *naskh*, abrogation). But it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak that it is abrogated by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*), and it seems they went to the view that what is meant by it is tolerance toward them and leaving off fighting them. Al-'Allama al-Tibi (al-Tayyibi) preferred this latter view, saying: so that the conclusion of the stories comprises both consolation and the command to tolerance, and a transition to another topic, which is His (exalted is He) saying later: ﴿And indeed﴾ to its end. In it is the discussion of turning away from the splendour of the life of this world, which is among the greatest kinds of harm. But it is mentioned in *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) that what the arrangement requires is that His (exalted is He) saying: ﴿We did not create the heavens﴾ to its end is a combination of the two margins of *Mufassal al-Ayat* (the book of verse-explanations), the proof-based (*al-burhaniyya*) and the favour-based (*al-imtinaniyya*), summarized from them, with an added emphasis of restriction (*al-hasr*), so that the one who argues with it may present it to the opponents, and be consoled by it against the mockery of the deniers, and as a preparation for the refreshing of the mention of the purpose, that the Reminder is complete in the matter of guidance and sufficient for everything connected to it of the aim that is due its proper care. Then he said: From this it becomes clear that the verse is a conjunction upon ﴿We did not create﴾ etc., the conjunction of the particular upon the general, indicating that the most complete of blessings, the most worthy proof, the most worthy thing by which the thirst is quenched, and that whoever is given it is not harmed by the loss of anything other than it, and whoever seeks desire in other than it is left to his desire. End of quotation. So reflect.

[p. 78]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 86:

﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾, who brings you to the utmost perfection, ﴿is the Creator (al-Khallaq)﴾ of you, of them, and of all other things absolutely, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of your circumstances, their circumstances, and of everything. Nothing is hidden from Him, exalted is His majesty, of what has passed between you and them. So it is fitting that you entrust the matters to Him, that He may judge between you. Or, He is the One who created you and knew the details of your circumstances. Glorified is He, He knew that gracious forgiveness today is more beneficial than the sword being more beneficial. So this is a causal justification (ta'lil) for the command to forgive on both interpretations, as it has been said. Some meticulous scholars said: on the latter interpretation it is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the mentioned command, and on the former it is for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is surely coming﴾. Zayd ibn Ali, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, and Malik ibn Dinar recited "huwa al-Khaliq" (He is the Creator), and likewise it is in the codices (mushaf) of Ubayy and Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is suitable for both the few and the many. (Al-Khallaq) is specific to the many, and (al-Alim) is more fitting for it. It is, as has been said, more appropriate to what preceded it in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 87:

﴿And We have certainly given you seven﴾, that is, seven verses, and they are al-Fatihah (the Opening). This was related from Umar, Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Ja'far, Abu Abdullah, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with them all.

This was also related with a chain traced back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from the narrations of Ubayy and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both. It has also been said that the seven are seven surahs, namely the al-Tuwal (the long surahs). This was related from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. According to one narration, they are: al-Baqarah, Ali Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal and Bara'ah counted as one surah. In another version, Bara'ah is counted apart from al-Anfal as the seventh. In yet another, Yunus is counted instead of both of them. In another, al-Kahf is counted. It has also been said that the seven are the surahs beginning with "Ha Mim." It has further been said that they are seven of the scrolls (suhuf) sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them, in the sense that he (ﷺ) was given what contains seven of them, even if not in their exact wording, and these are the "sub'" (the sevens). From Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam: they are seven matters: command, prohibition, glad tidings, warning, the coining of parables, the enumeration of blessings, and the reports of nations. The soundest of these opinions is the first. Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi have transmitted it and traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Hayyan said: it is not appropriate to deviate from it; indeed, that is not permissible.

An objection is raised against the view that they are the long surahs: this surah is Meccan, whereas those seven are Medinan. This was related from al-Rabi'. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, Ibn Jarir and others have transmitted that he was told: "They say they are the long surahs," and he replied: "This verse was revealed, and none of the long surahs had yet been revealed." It is answered that what is meant by "giving" them is their sending down to the lowest heaven, and there is no difference in this between Medinan and Meccan revelation. It is objected that the apparent sense of "We have given you" (atayna-ka) rules this out. It has been said that this is the placing of what is expected in the position of what has occurred, for the purpose of bestowing favour, and there are many similar examples.

﴿from the oft-repeated (al-mathani)﴾ is an explanation of "seven." According to what he said in one place in al-Kashshaf, it is the plural of mathna, in the sense of "repeated" and "reiterated." It is also possible that it is the past participle form of the verb of the pattern mafa'ala, from the root of tathniyah (doubling), in the sense of repetition and recurrence, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿Then return your gaze twice (karratayn)﴾, meaning one repetition after another, and like the expression "labbayka wa sa'dayka" (here I am at your service, again and again). He intended, as in al-Kashf, that it is a plural to express the meaning of repetition and recurrence, just as the dual form was used for the same purpose. However, the use of the dual in this sense is more common, because it is the first degree of repetition. It is also possible that he meant that mathna in the sense of repetition and recurrence, just as the explicit dual has the same meaning in expressions such as ﴿karratayn﴾, and then it was pluralized for emphasis. His saying "from tathniyah" is a clarification of the meaning, since it is from thany in the sense of tathniyah. The first view is preferable when looking at the apparent wording, and the second when looking at the root. In another place he said: it is from tathniyah or from thana' (praise), and the singular form is mathnat or mathniyyah with a fathah on the mim, according to most of the copies. Otherwise, according to what the careful scholar (al-Mudaqqiq) said, the word is derived by its wording from thana' (praise) or thany, the plural of mathna of the pattern mafa'il, from either of them, either as a verbal noun pluralized when it became an adjective, or as a noun of place originally, transferred to the adjective for emphasis, like "ard ma'sadah" (a land full of lions). This is because the place of praise, in the second case, is figurative, and the one praised is likewise the place of folding. There is no difficulty in the principle of the 'atf (conjunction) that it may be transmitted from it and not invented from the beginning.

The application of this term to al-Fatihah is because its recitation is repeated in the prayer. This was related from al-Hasan and Abu Abdullah, may Allah have mercy on them both, and from al-Zajjaj, because it is doubled by what is recited after it from the Qur'an. It has also been said, and attributed to al-Hasan as well, that it is because it was revealed twice: once in Mecca and once in Medina. It was objected that it was already called by this name before its second revelation, since the surah, as you have heard more than once, is Meccan. It has also been said that this is because many of its words are repeated, such as al-Rahman and al-Rahim, "iyyaka" (You alone), "al-sirat" (the path), and "alayhim" (upon them). It has been said that it is because it contains praise of Allah Most High. Both views are as you see. It has also been said, and attributed to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, that the term "mathani" is applied to al-Fatihah because Allah, glory be to Him, set it apart and reserved it for this nation, so He did not give it to others. This reservation was also related regarding other surahs, and it was said regarding them that this is because its recitation is repeated, or its words or stories or admonitions are repeated, or because it contains praise of Him, exalted be His majesty, as He deserves, or because it is praised for its eloquence and inimitability, or because it brings praise upon the one who recites it. From Abu Zayd al-Balkhi: the term "mathani" is applied to it because it turns the people of evil away from their evil. So reflect.

It is also permitted that by "mathani" is meant the entire Qur'an, and Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted this from Abu Malik. The discussion of the justification for applying it to the Qur'an, along with the difference between the singular and plural forms, will come, God willing. It is also permitted that by it is meant all the books of Allah, Most High, and in that case "min" (from) is partitive; on the first view it is explanatory.

﴿and the Glorious Qur'an﴾ is in the accusative and is conjoined to "seven" (sab'an). If by them is meant the verses, the surahs, or the seven matters related from Ziyad, then this is conjunction of the whole to a part, by taking "the Qur'an" to mean the entire collection between the two covers (al-Daftayn), or conjunction of the general to the specific, by taking it to mean the common meaning shared by the whole and the part. In this there is an indication of the distinction of the specific, to the extent that it seems to be other than it, as in the reverse case. If by them is meant the sevens, then it is conjunction of one attribute to another, as in the verse: "To the king, the lord, and the son of the hero..." on the basis that the Qur'an in itself is the sevens; that is, "We have given you what is called the seven oft-repeated and the Glorious Qur'an." Some have chosen to interpret "the Glorious Qur'an," like "the seven oft-repeated," as al-Fatihah, based on what al-Bukhari transmitted from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin (All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds) is the seven oft-repeated and the Glorious Qur'an which I have been given.'"

In al-Kashf, the view that these two are al-Fatihah is more fitting to the context, because of what has passed regarding the restriction of "the Book and a clear Qur'an" to the surah, and it is more accurate with respect to the reality, since at that time the Prophet (ﷺ) had not yet been given the whole of it. End of quotation. The matter of conjunction is clear from what precedes it.

A group recited "wal-Qur'ani" with the genitive, as a conjunction to "al-mathani." Whoever held that the waw is inserted (muqhamah) and that the sense is "seven of the oft-repeated Qur'an" was far from correct.

[Page 79]

[Page 80]

﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾: do not raise your gaze with the longing of one who desires, nor let your look linger ﴿upon what We have given enjoyment to﴾ of the adornments and finery of this world, ﴿as pairs among them﴾: kinds of the disbelievers, the Jews, Christians and polytheists. It was also said: men along with their wives. The prohibition was addressed to him (ﷺ), and it does not imply actually engaging in the act or drawing near to it. It was also said that it is addressed to his community, although the address is to him, upon him be prayers and peace. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the verse: a man was forbidden from wishing for the wealth of his companion. Indeed, after the revelation of the verse, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became extremely cautious regarding what it contains. Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir that "he (ﷺ) passed by camels belonging to a tribe called the Banu al-Mulawwih or the Banu al-Mustaliq, which had grown fat in their urine and dung. He covered himself with his garment and passed on without looking at them, in obedience to His saying: ﴿Do not extend your eyes…﴾ the verse." Such an act is counted among the blocking of the means (sadd al-dhara'i', blocking the means that lead to what is forbidden).

Some scholars supported the first view with this, and with the apparent indication of the context. Its sum, together with what precedes it, is: ﴿We have given you the great blessing﴾, and every blessing, however great, is contemptible in comparison to it. So you should be content with that and not desire the enjoyments of this world. From this is derived his (ﷺ) saying: "He is not of us who does not chant (yataghanna) the Qur'an," on the basis that yataghanna is from al-ghina (richness), in the form of the short vowel (maqsur), like yastaghni, and not the long vowel (mamdud). This is supported by the authentic hadith about horses: "As for the one that is a covering for him, it is the man who tied it out of contentment and chastity" (tagħannīan wa-ta'affufan).

And from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever has been given the Qur'an, and then sees that someone else has been given more of this world than he has been given, has belittled something great and magnified something small." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated something with the same meaning from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna. Al-'Iraqi said: "The report is related, but I have not found its narration from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, in any of the books of hadith."

Some people mentioned, regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse, that seven caravans came to him from Busra and Adhri'at on a single day, belonging to Qurayza and al-Nadir, carrying various kinds of wheat, perfume and jewels. The Muslims said: "If these were ours, we would have strengthened ourselves with them and spent them in the way of Allah, the Exalted." So the verse was revealed. It is as though He, glorified is He, were saying: "We have given you seven things that are better than seven caravans." This was narrated from al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl. It has been criticized as weak, or not authentic, because the surah is Meccan, while Qurayza and al-Nadir were in Medina, so how could this be said? It is as you see. It is true that it is narrated that he (ﷺ) came to Adhri'at with seven caravans belonging to the Jews of Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, containing etc., but this is not well known. They have said that his (ﷺ) travel to Syria was not known. The report of the revelation was used as a supporting point for the view that the prohibition is directed at the chief of those addressed, upon him be prayers and peace, like the prohibition in His saying: (And do not grieve over them) since they did not believe. The Prophet (ﷺ) wished that everyone sent to him would believe, and the continued disbelief of the disbelievers was hard upon him, upon him be prayers and peace, because of his great compassion. For this reason it was said to him: (And do not grieve over them). It seems that the first sentence refers to the prohibition against looking at their wealth, and this sentence refers to the prohibition against turning toward them. The meaning is not "do not grieve over them because they are the ones enjoying that," for enjoying it is not a basis for grief over them. And the meaning "do not grieve over their enjoyment of it" requires an omitted noun, and what that involves of departing from the apparent meaning without any need for it is not hidden.

﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾: this is a kinaya (allusion or figurative expression) for humility toward them and gentleness with them. The origin of this is that when a bird wants to gather its chick to itself, it spreads its wings over it. The two wings of a son of Adam are his two sides.

﴿And say: Indeed I am the plain warner﴾: that is, the one who warns, who makes clear the coming down of Allah's punishment and His vengeance that inspires fear, for those who do not believe.
