﴿As We sent down [the Scripture] upon those who divided it﴾. It has been said that this is connected to His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We have certainly given you﴾ and so on, on the basis that it occupies an accusative position as a descriptive modifier (نعت, *na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (مصدر, *masdar*) of "آتَيْنا" (*ataynā*, "We gave"). The meaning is: "We gave you seven of the *mathani* (المثاني, the oft-repeated) with a giving like Our sending down (كإنزالنا, *ka-inzālinā*), [Our] sending down (أنزلنا, *anzalnā*)," and it has the sense of "We sent down to you that [Scripture] with a sending down like Our sending down upon the People of the Book."

Those who have made the Qur'an into parts (ʿiḍīn): that is, they divided it into truth and falsehood, saying out of obstinacy and enmity, "Some of it agrees with the Torah and the Gospel, and some of it is false and contradicts them both." The interpretation of "those who divide it" (al-muqtasimīn) as the People of the Book is narrated from al-Ḥasan and others. In *al-Durr al-Manthur*, al-Bukhari, Saʿd ibn Manṣur, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said regarding the verse: "They are the People of the Book. They divided it into parts, believing in some of it and disbelieving in some of it." This is also reported as a prophetic statement (marfūʿ). al-Tabarani, in *al-Awsat*, transmitted from al-Habr (a title for Ibn ʿAbbas) who said: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'What about the saying of Allah, ﴿As We sent down upon the dividers﴾?' He (ﷺ) said, 'The Jews and the Christians.' He said, '﴿Who have made the Qur'an into parts﴾. What are "parts"?' He (ﷺ) said, 'They believed in some of it and disbelieved in some of it.'"

Or they divided it for themselves in mockery of it. It is narrated from ʿIkrimah that some of them would say, "Sūrat al-Baqara is mine," and others would say, "Sūrat Āl ʿImrān is mine," and so on.

It is also permissible that "those who divide" refers to the People of the Book, and that "the Qur'an" is taken in its linguistic sense, i.e., "what is read" (al-maqrūʾ) from their scriptures. That is, those who divided what they read from their books, distorted it, acknowledged some of it and denied some of it.

The placement of the words ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾ etc. between the connected element and what it relates to has been interpreted as relating to the extension of what is the purpose of the discourse, namely consolation. This view of connection has been criticised on the grounds that it lowers the rank of this context, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was given what no one before or after him was given like it. Taking the Qur'an in its linguistic sense also has its problems.

It has been said that it is connected to the saying of Allah, ﴿And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner"﴾, because it carries the force of a command to warn, as if it were said: "Warn the Quraysh of the like of what We sent down as punishment upon the dividers," meaning the Jews. This is what befell the Banu Qurayẓa and the Banu al-Naḍīr, by treating the expected as if it had occurred. And so it did occur. This has been criticised on the grounds that the thing compared to, the punishment that is the object of the warning, should be known at the time of revelation, and this is not the case, so the comparison becomes pointless. Treating the expected as though it had occurred has an impressive place within inimitability, but only when it coincides with a context that calls for it, as in the saying of Allah, ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ and its like. Moreover, restricting "the dividing" to the Jews merely because the punishment mentioned is specific to them, despite the Christians sharing with them in the dividing that follows from agreement and disagreement, and in the sense of dividing as distortion, which encompasses both scriptures, is an unwarranted restriction. Indeed, restricting the punishment mentioned to them while it is one of the results of the dividing is restriction without a restrictor.

It is also permissible that "the dividers" refers to a group of the Quraysh, who were twelve. Ibn al-Sa'ib said they were sixteen men: Ḥanẓala ibn Abi Sufyan, ʿUtba and Shayba, the sons of Rabīʿa, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hisham, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid, Qays ibn al-Fākih, Zuhayr ibn Umayya, Hilal ibn ʿAbd al-Aswad, al-Sa'ib ibn Ṣayfi, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥarith, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, Zamʿa ibn al-Ḥajjāj, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Aws ibn al-Mughira. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira sent them during the season of the pilgrimage to stand at the entrances of the roads to Mecca in order to deter people from believing in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They spread out at those entrances. Some would say, "Do not be deceived by the one who came out, for he is a sorcerer." Another would say, "He is a liar." Another would say, "He is a poet." And other such nonsense. So Allah destroyed them on the Day of Badr, and before that by calamities.

The word "those who" (alladhīna) may be taken as an object of "warn" (al-nadhīr), with "as" (kamā) as its second object. The meaning then is: warn the ʿiḍīn, those who divide the Qur'an into sorcery, poetry and fables, as We sent down upon the muqtasimīn, those who divided the entrances to Mecca and spoke nonsense like their nonsense.

[p. 82]

It has been criticised that, along with its other problems, this view shares with what came before the fact that the punishment compared to the warning punishment was not known to those being warned as having occurred. Moreover, there is no reason to restrict the description of dividing into parts to those warned and to exclude the dividers from among them, since they were examples for them in this. Their description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as a sorcerer, a poet and a liar follows from their description of the Qur'an in such terms, and this is nothing other than the dividing into parts. Nor is there reason to exclude them from the scope of the warning. Furthermore, the punishment that befell them was not so severe that the punishment of others should be compared to it, nor was it specific to them, but was general to both groups and others. Also, some of those counted among the warned, according to one view, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-Aswad and others, died before the destruction of most of the dividers on the Day of Badr. Nor is there any reason to place the second object before the first, as you see.

It has also been said that it is an attribute of the object of "those who," which has been placed in its position after being omitted, and that the dividers (al-muqtasimūn) are those sitting at the entrances of the roads, as has been clarified. That is: a warner of a punishment like the punishment We sent down upon the dividers.

It has also been criticised that, along with what has passed, this view requires that "as We sent down" be part of the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ), and this is not appropriate for him. It has been defended by saying that it is like when one of the king's close attendants says, "We have commanded such-and-such," while the one commanding is the king, as mentioned before, not far off; or that it is a quotation of the saying of Allah. There is in this a degree of strain that is not hidden. Furthermore, this view involves making the qualifying attribute work on the object, which is not permissible.

It was answered that the Kufans permit this, and the one who holds this view built his speech upon that. Or that what is meant by "object" is the non-explicit object, and its estimated form is "with a punishment," and this does not prevent the attribute from governing it. It has been said that the dividers, on the assumption that the phrase is an attribute, are the group who conspired together to ambush Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him), and Allah destroyed them. The "dividing" here means "sharing in a plot." There is no difficulty with the comparison, because their punishment is a certain matter that the Mighty Qur'an has spoken of, so it is correct for it to be the thing compared to the punishment of warning. The relative pronoun is either the first object of "warn," or of what it indicates from "warn."

It has also been criticised that, setting aside the disagreement or obscurity surrounding the objecthood, this view means there is no benefit in mentioning the description "dividing into parts" within the relative clause, or the description "dividing" in the sense mentioned, within the second object. This is because that mention serves only to indicate that the relative clause and the attribute are the cause of the judgment established for the relative pronoun and the qualified noun. Therefore there is no point of similarity on which the comparison of their punishment with their punishment rests, since the ʿiḍīn have no connection to the conspiring to ambush, which was the cause of the destruction of those others, while those others have no connection to the dividing into parts, which was the cause of the destruction of these. There is no relation between the two causes, either conceptually or in existence, that would justify one occurring on one side and the other on the other side. The agreement of the two groups on general wrongdoing, understood from agreement on evil, is not the same as agreement on the specific evil of ambush, which is indicated by "conspiring." The "dividing" the entrances indicates this, not the dividing into parts. Making the relative pronoun the subject, so that its predicate is the oath clause, is not fitting for the eloquence of the revelation and the greatness of its noble status. [End of quotation.]

This approach is narrated from Ibn Zayd. In a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, transmitted by al-Bayhaqi and Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Dalāʾil*, something of this sort is implied. From here it has been said that the objection to its unfittingness is denied. Some who accept it say that it is permissible for the relative pronoun to be an attribute of "the dividers," with those men intended, and the meaning of "making them into parts" is their judgment that it is fabricated and their denial of it. Here the Qur'an is intended in its linguistic sense, so it returns to a description of them as denying their own scripture and turning away from belief in it and acting upon what is in it. This agrees with the saying of Allah concerning them and their people, ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them﴾, on the basis that the signs are the signs of the book revealed to their prophet (peace be upon him), as was said earlier. If you refuse this on the basis of what you heard there, we are committed to the relative pronoun being an object, and we say: the benefit of mentioning the two descriptions in the way mentioned is to indicate the gravity of the matter of denial, and that it is, in its causal role for the punishment, like the dividing to kill the Prophet. We accept what this implies of the greater heinousness of that dividing, because it can only result from denial and increased enmity toward the Prophet. But there is discussion of this.

It has been said that what makes it correct for one of the two descriptions to be on one side and the other on the other side is that denial, in the view of the deniers, leads to nullifying the matter of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and extinguishing his light, and this is its final cause. The dividing mentioned is of the same kind. But this is as you see.

Abu al-Baqa' said, and I wish he had not said it: "As We sent down" is connected to the saying of Allah, ﴿We gave some of them enjoyment in pairs﴾, and it is in the position of an accusative as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, meaning: We gave them enjoyment as We sent down, and the meaning is: We bestowed favour upon some of them as We punished some of them.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others mentioned that it may mean: "Say, I am the clear warner, as We have indeed sent down in the books that you will come as a warner to the dividers," that is, the People of the Book. What is meant, as has been said, is that the "ma" in "kamā" is a relative pronoun, and the similarity implied by the "kaf" is conformity. This together with what is in its scope is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the object of "say." That is: say this statement in the state of it being as We sent down to the People of the Two Books, i.e., conforming to that. On this view it is most suitable to take the dividing as distortion, so that describing them with it becomes an allusion to their distortion and concealment of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). You know that this has a remoteness to it, but it is more fitting than some of what was mentioned before. Close to this is what has been said: the meaning is "And We have indeed given you the seven oft-repeated (verses) as a giving that conforms to the giving which We sent down to the People of the Two Books, and informed them of it in their books." There is much to say about this.

As for making the "kāf" superfluous, with the meaning "I am the clear warner of what We sent down," its matter is independent of needing to be pointed out.

Al-ʿAllāma Abu al-Suʿud, after relating several opinions and then commenting on them, said: "The closest of the opinions mentioned is that ﴿as We sent down﴾ is connected to the saying of Allah, ﴿And We have indeed given you﴾, etc., that the dividers are the People of the Two Books, that the relative pronoun with its relative clause is a qualifying attribute explaining the manner of their dividing, and that the place of the kāf is accusative as a verbal noun." The talk of the sublimity of the context being above comparison is among the evident points of noble reflection. [End of quotation.]

[p. 83]

The meaning is: "Indeed, We have given you the seven oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an, a giving similar to the sending down of the two Books upon their people." The commentary does not mention what was sent down to those two Books, because the purpose is to show the similarity between the two givings, not between what each is connected to. It departs from applying to the comparison's subject what is in the comparison's referent, which would be to say, "as We gave to those who divided [the Qur'an] (al-muqtasimin), as stated in His words: ﴿those whom We gave the Book﴾, etc." This is done to draw attention to the distance between the two givings, for the first is by way of honour and favour, so how far apart they are from the second. That this (the People of the Book) is the referent of the comparison does not detract from it, since this is only because it is accepted among them. The first's existence is prior to the second in time, not because of any excellence inherent in its own nature. A parallel to this is what has been said about the Abrahamic prayers. There is thus in the comparison no indication that the referent is superior to the subject, let alone any implication that what is connected to the first is what is connected to the second.

They are mentioned under the heading of "division" (iqtisam) to deny that they truly possessed this quality, given the existence of what negates it, namely the mentioned sending down, and to notify that it was incumbent upon them to believe in all of it, in accordance with their belief in what was sent down to them, by the rule of shared cause and unity in the reality which is the absolute revelation.

The placing of His words ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾, etc., between these is for its complete connection to what is the aim: explaining the state of what was given to the Prophet (ﷺ).

He first explained the exalted rank and elevated station of the Prophet (ﷺ), to such an extent that it warrants his contentment with his position and his self-sufficiency with it over anything else. Then he was forbidden from turning to the splendour of the worldly life. Allah, glorified is He, expressed the giving of it to its people with "enjoyment", which indicates that its disappearance from them is imminent. Then [he was forbidden] from grief over the non-belief of those absorbed in it. He was commanded to care for the believers and to be content with them over others, and to show his standing with the obligations of the message and the ceremonies of warning, as detailed throughout what was given of the Great Qur'an.

Then he returned [page 84] to the manner of its giving, in a way that incorporated what removes the doubts of the deniers and draws them down from obstinacy, by explaining its shared character with what they have no doubt is a true revelation. So reflect. And Allah, the Exalted, has with Him the knowledge of the Book.

This is speech that clearly bears the marks of verification.

In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), after quoting most of these views, [Abu Hayyan] says: "These are contrived views and interpretations. What appears to me is that when Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) not to grieve over those who did not believe, and commanded him (ﷺ) to lower his wing to the believers, He commanded him (ﷺ) to inform the believers and others that he is the clear warner, lest the believers think that, since he was commanded (ﷺ) to lower his wing for them, they were released from the duty of warning. So he was commanded (ﷺ) to say to them: ﴿Indeed I am the clear warner﴾ to you and to others, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾. The kaf (ك) is then an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and the estimate is: 'And say a word like what We sent down upon the divisioners, that you are a warner to them.' So the statement to the believers regarding warning is like the statement to the disbelieving divisioners, lest it be thought that your warning to the disbelievers opposes your warning to the believers; rather, you are in the description of warning to them in one station, warning the believer as you warn the disbeliever, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿I am only a warner and a bringer of good news to a people who believe﴾." End of quotation, word for word. As you see, it is weak in wording and meaning. Allah, the Exalted, knows best what He intends, and with Him is the knowledge of the Book.

ʿIḍīn (عِضِينَ) is the plural of ʿiḍah (عِضَة), and its origin is ʿiḍawah (عِضَوَة), with the ʿayn vowelled with kasra and the ḍād with fatha, meaning a part. So it is defective in its final radical, from ʿaḍḍāhu (عَضّاهُ) with shadda, meaning he made it into limbs (aʿḍa') and parts (ajzā'). The meaning is: they made the Qur'an into parts.

It has also been said: "ʿaḍah" in the dialect of Quraysh means sorcery, so they say to a male sorcerer ʿāḍih (عاضِهٌ) and to a female sorceress ʿāḍihah (عاضِهَةٌ). In a hadith narrated by Ibn ʿAdi in al-Kamil and Abu Yaʿla in his Musnad: "May Allah, the Exalted, curse the ʿāḍihah and the musta'ḍihah." He (ﷺ) meant the sorceress and the one who has sorcery practised for her, that is, the one who uses the sorcery of another. On this view, it is derived from ʿaḍahtuhu (عَضَهْتُهُ), and the omitted final radical is a hāʾ, as in shafah (شَفَة, lip) and shāh (شاة, sheep), on the view that their origin is shafahah and shāhah, as evidenced by their plurals shifāh and shiyāh and their diminutives shufayhah and shuwayhah.

From al-Kisa'i it is reported that it is from ʿaḍihahu ʿaḍhan and ʿaḍīhah, meaning he slandered him with falsehood. It is said: the taking of ʿaḍah in the sense of sorcery derives from this, because falsehood has no basis, and sorcery is the imagining of something that has no reality. Al-Farra' held that it is from al-ʿiḍāh (عِضاه), a tree that harms like thorns. Some scholars preferred the first view.

The sound masculine plural is used to compensate for what was omitted from it, like ʿazīn (عَزِينَ) and sinīn (سِنِينَ). Otherwise, by rule it should not take the masculine sound plural, since it is not rational and its singular form has changed. Similar cases are many and regular. Some Arabs bind it to the yāʾ and make the i'rab (grammatical case inflection) fall on the nūn, saying ʿiḍīnaka, like sinīnaka. This dialect is common among Tamim and Asad.

In expressing the division of the Qur'an by ta'diyah (التَّعْضِيَة), which is the separating of the limbs of a living being, a process that entails the removal of its life and the nullifying of its name, rather than mere division and separation, which may occur in things that partition does not harm, [the verse] is emphasising the ugliness of what they did to the Great Qur'an.

[Page 85]

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾, meaning: on the Day of Resurrection We will surely question all categories of disbelievers, the dividers (al-Muqtasimin) and others, with a questioning of rebuke and reproach, ﴿about what they used to do﴾ in the world, in speech, action and omission. This includes what was mentioned of the dividing and the making of the Qur'an into parts, either by entering it primarily, or it means: We will requite them for that. Under either interpretation, there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So on that Day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾, because what is meant here, as we have indicated, is the affirmation of the questioning of rebuke and reproach, or of requital, on the basis that questioning is a metaphor for it. There, the negation is of the questioning for information, because He, exalted is He, knows all their deeds. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas. The Imam (al-Razi) weakened this view, saying: there is no sense in restricting the negation of the questioning for information to the Day of Resurrection, because that kind of questioning is impossible for Him at every time.

It is answered that it is based on their assumption, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will come forth before Allah all together﴾. For it will become manifest to them on that Day that He, glorified is He, nothing is hidden from Him, so He has no need for asking for information. It was said: what is meant is that there is no questioning on that Day from Him, exalted is He, nor from anyone else, unlike the world, where He may ask others. This was refuted by saying that His statement, "because He, glorified is He, knows all their deeds," rejects it.

Many have chosen, in combining the two, that the negation is with respect to some situations and the affirmation with respect to others, and the full discussion of that will come. Some have inferred that the pronoun in ﴿We will surely question them﴾ refers to ﴿the dividers, who made the Qur'an into parts﴾ because of proximity. It is also permissible that it refers to everyone, believer and disbeliever, because of a preceding indication of that in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And say: Indeed I am the clear warner﴾, and that the particle is general, as is apparent.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Abu al-Aliyah that he said about the verse: He will question all the servants on the Day of Resurrection about two things: about what they worshipped, and about what they answered the Messengers with.

Al-Tirmidhi and a group narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "They will be questioned about the word: There is no god but Allah." It was narrated by al-Bukhari in his History, and by al-Tirmidhi by another route from Anas as a statement of his own (mawquf). It is also narrated from Ibn Umar and Mujahid. The meaning, according to al-Bahr, is: they will be questioned about fulfilling "There is no god but Allah" and about affirming its utterance through deeds. As for the fa' (the particle "fa"), it was said it is for the sequencing of the threat upon their deeds, some of which were mentioned. It was said: it is for giving the reason for the prohibition and command before it. It was claimed that it is the fa' that enters upon the predicate of a relative clause, as in your saying: "The one who comes to me, then for him is a dirham," based on the view that (alladhina) is the subject. You have known the state of that.

In the mention of the attribute of Lordship, with His pronoun attached to him, upon him be blessings and peace, there is what is not hidden of showing kindness toward him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

[Page 85]

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾, meaning: on the Day of Resurrection We will surely question all categories of disbelievers, the dividers (al-Muqtasimin) and others, with a questioning of rebuke and reproach, ﴿about what they used to do﴾ in the world, in speech, action and omission. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Abu al-Aliyah that he said about the verse: He will question all the servants on the Day of Resurrection about two things: about what they worshipped, and about what they answered the Messengers with.

Al-Tirmidhi and a group narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "They will be questioned about the word: There is no god but Allah." It was narrated by al-Bukhari in his History, and by al-Tirmidhi by another route from Anas as a statement of his own (mawquf). It is also narrated from Ibn Umar and Mujahid. The meaning, according to al-Bahr, is: they will be questioned about fulfilling "There is no god but Allah" and about affirming its utterance through deeds. As for the fa' (the particle "fa"), it was said it is for the sequencing of the threat upon their deeds, some of which were mentioned. It was said: it is for giving the reason for the prohibition and command before it. It was claimed that it is the fa' that enters upon the predicate of a relative clause, as in your saying: "The one who comes to me, then for him is a dirham," based on the view that (alladhina) is the subject. You have known the state of that.

In the mention of the attribute of Lordship, with His pronoun attached to him, upon him be blessings and peace, there is what is not hidden of showing kindness toward him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾. Al-Kalbi said: that is, make it manifest and declare it openly. It is said: "ṣadaʿa bil-ḥujjah" (he stated the proof openly) when one speaks it aloud, and for this reason the dawn is called ṣadīʿ (the one that splits open) because of its becoming manifest.

It is also permitted that it be an imperative from ṣadʿ al-zujājah (splitting the glass), which means separating its parts. That is: separate truth from falsehood. Its root meaning, as it has been said, is clarification and distinction. The «الباء» (bāʾ, "with") in the first sense is a ṣilah (a redundant, merely connecting particle), and in the second sense it is sababiyyah (causal, indicating means). As for «ما» (mā), it is permitted that it be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with an omitted returning pronoun (ʿāʾid), meaning: "by that which you are commanded." The governing preposition was then deleted, so the verb reached the pronoun directly, becoming "tu'maruhu" ("you are commanded it"), and then it was deleted. Perhaps the one who said this did not consider deleting it while it is in the genitive case (majrūr), because the condition for deleting it was absent. This is based on the view that deleting a returning pronoun that is in the genitive requires that it be governed by the same preposition that governs the relative pronoun, in form, meaning, and attachment. It has also been said that the meaning is: "proclaim what you are commanded to proclaim," so the second bāʾ was deleted, then the third, then the definite article (lām al-taʿrīf), then the noun in the construct (al-muḍāf), then the pronoun (hāʾ). This is an affectation with no need for it, and it nearly causes a headache.

The intended meaning of «ما يُؤْمَرُ بِهِ» (what he is commanded) is the sacred laws (sharāʾiʿ) in general. The statement of Mujahid, as transmitted from him by Ibn Abi Hatim, that the meaning is "recite the Qur'an aloud in prayer," by its apparent sense restricts the meaning, and there is no need for that either, as is not hidden. More evident than this is what has been transmitted from Ibn Zayd: that what is meant by «بِما تُؤْمَرُ» is the Qur'an that was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he would convey it to them. It is also possible that it is a maṣdariyyah (verbal-noun particle), meaning: "proclaim with your being commanded," which is what al-Zamakhshari meant by his saying: "i.e., with your command, a verbal noun derived from the passive form." Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying that this is based on the view of those who permit that the verbal noun be understood as «أنْ» plus a passive verb, whereas the correct view is that this is not permitted. It was answered that the disagreement concerns whether a pure verbal noun may be解 resolved into a maṣdariyyah particle plus a passive verb. As for whether a passive verb may be joined to a maṣdariyyah particle, that is not the point of dispute. If his objection to al-Zamakhshari's interpretation as "command" was that he should have said "being commanded," then that is another matter, and it is easy. Furthermore, the eloquence of this verse is not hidden.

Abu ʿUbayda said: [it is] "ʿan ruʾyat mā fī al-Qurʾān minhā" (away from seeing what is in the Qur'an of them). It is reported that some Arabs heard a reciter recite it and prostrated, and when asked about it he said: "I prostrated because of the eloquence of this speech." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained hidden, as has been reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, before the revelation of that. When it was revealed, he and his companions went out, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾: that is, do not pay attention to what they say, and do not be concerned about them. Therefore the verse is not abrogated (mansūkhah). It has also been said that it is among the verses of truce (muhādanah), which were abrogated by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf). This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (Nāsikh), from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers.﴾ Against you, or against you and the Qur'an, as related from Ibn 'Abbas: [it means] their suppression and destruction.

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi and Abu Nu'aym both in al-Dala'il, and Ibn Mardawayh, with a good chain (sanad), reported: "The mockers were al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Harith ibn 'Utayl al-Sahmi, and al-'As ibn Wa'il. Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and complained of them to him. He showed him al-Walid, and Jibril, peace be upon him, pointed to his eye-vein (akhall). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You have done nothing.' He said: 'I have sufficed you against him.' Then he showed him al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he pointed to his eyes. He said: 'You have done nothing.' He said: 'I have sufficed you against him.' Then he showed him al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and he pointed to his head. He said: 'You have done nothing.' He said: 'I have sufficed you against him.' Then he showed him al-Harith, and he pointed to his belly. He said: 'You have done nothing.' He said: 'I have sufficed you against him.' Then he showed him al-'As ibn Wa'il, and he pointed to the sole of his foot. He said: 'You have done nothing.' He said: 'I have sufficed you against him.' As for al-Walid, he passed by a man from Khuza'a who was feathering arrows, and [an arrow] struck his eye-vein and severed it. As for al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, he alighted under a samura tree and began saying: 'O my sons, will you not ward off from me? I am destroyed! I am being stabbed with thorns in my eye.' They began saying: 'We see nothing.' He remained so until both his eyes went blind. As for al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, sores broke out on his head and he died of them. As for al-Harith, the yellow water (dropsy) seized his belly until his excrement came out of his mouth, and he died of it. As for al-'As, he rode to al-Ta'if and lay down upon a shabraqa (a thorny plant), and a thorn entered the sole of his foot and killed him."

al-Kirmani, in his commentary on al-Bukhari, said: The mockers are the seven who inflicted harm while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying, as came in the hadith of al-Bukhari, and they are: 'Amr ibn Hisham, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, Umayya ibn Khalaf, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and 'Imara ibn al-Walid. In al-A'lam by al-Suhayli, [it is stated] that they were thrown into the well of Badr, and he counted them differently from what was mentioned. In al-Durr al-Manthur and elsewhere there are many differing reports regarding their number, their names, and the manner of their destruction. al-Sha'bi counted among them Habbar ibn al-Aswad. al-Bahr criticised this, saying that Habbar embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest and traveled to Madina, so counting him is a mistake. This is certain if his, peace be upon him, sufficing against them was by destruction, as is apparent. The Imam mentioned something similar to what we have related of the differing reports, then said: "There is no need for any of that. What is known is that they were a group possessing strength and power, for such people are the ones who are able to commit this kind of folly in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with his exalted rank and great station." The Qur'an indicates that Allah, glorified is He, annihilated them, destroyed them entirely, and removed their plotting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 96:

﴿Those who set up with Allah another deity﴾. That is, they took a deity whom they worship alongside Him, exalted is He. The use of the present tense (ṣīghat al-istiqbāl) is to bring the past state vividly to mind. In describing them with this, there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a lessening of the gravity of the matter for him, peace be upon him, by indicating that they did not limit themselves to mocking him (ﷺ), but dared to commit the great sin which is associating partners with Him, glory be to Him. ﴿But they will come to know﴾ what they do and what they leave undone. And in this there is a warning that is not hidden.

In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan) it is said that this is a warning to them of recompense for their mockery and their polytheism in the Hereafter, just as they were recompensed in this world.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 97:

﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾ of the words of polytheism and mockery. The sentence is adorned with emphasis (ta'kid) to convey the certainty of the consolation (tasliyah) it contains. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') conveys the continuity of the knowledge, in accordance with the continuity of its object, through the continuity of what necessitates it, namely the utterances of the disbelievers.

﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾: Turn to your Lord for relief from the constriction of your breast, by glorifying Him while joined with His praise. That is, say: "Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Allah." Or: "Exalt Him above what they say, praising Him for having guided you to the truth." Here *tasbih* (glorification) and *hamd* (praise) carry their linguistic meanings, as they do on the first reading, while in the customary sense they refer to the utterance of those two phrases. Mentioning the title of *rububiyyah* (lordship) together with the pronoun referring to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, shows a kindness toward him that is not hidden, and it indicates the reason for the command mentioned, namely the matter stated above. ﴿And be among those who prostrate﴾: that is, among those who pray. This is an expression of the whole by a part. According to what some have held, this part is the best of the parts of prayer, based on the authentic saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "The closest a servant comes to his Lord is when he is prostrating."

This is not a place of prostration, contrary to some scholars. In his being commanded with what has been mentioned, there is guidance for him toward what removes the distress he feels, as if it were said: "Do that, and your Lord will remove from you the distress and oppression you feel in your breast." For greater emphasis on the matter of prayer, the command to it has been given, as you see, differing from the preceding command in this specific manner. In this there is an encouragement to prayer that is not hidden. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, whenever a matter grieved him, would turn to prayer. And it is authentically related: "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me of your world, and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer."

Some have mentioned that in the verse there is an indication of encouragement to perform it in congregation. And that the absence of restricting the prostration with any phrase such as "to Him" or "to your Lord" indicates that it is something that hardly comes to mind to perform for other than Him, the Exalted, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 15, verse 99:

﴿And worship your Lord﴾: persist in the worship of Him, glorified is He, in which you are engaged. It has been said: the use of the apparent name "your Lord" (al-'unwan al-salif) just above is an emphasis on what preceded it, namely the manifestation of kindness toward him (ﷺ) and the indication of the reason for the command to worship. ﴿Until there comes to you the certainty (al-yaqin)﴾: that is, death, as related from Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. It was called this because it is certain to overtake every living being. The attribution of "coming" to it indicates that it is directed toward the living and seeks to reach him. The meaning is: persist in worship for as long as you are alive, without neglecting it for a moment. Ibn Bahr said: the certainty is the victory over the disbelievers which Allah, exalted is He, promised to His Messenger (ﷺ). Whatever it is, the intended meaning is not what some of the heretics (mulhidin) claimed, those things which they call unveiling (al-kashf) and witnessing (al-shuhud). They said: when the servant attains that, the obligation of worship falls from him, and worship is only for those who are veiled. Indeed, by this they have exited the religion and left the bond of Islam and the community of the Muslims.

Some trustworthy scholars mentioned that this command came after the Night Journey (al-Isra') and the ascent to the heaven. Do you think that the dawn of unveiling and witnessing did not become clear to him that night, and that the great generosity and bounty did not bestow upon him the certainty? God is greatest! No one in whose heart is an atom's weight of faith, or a mustard seed's worth of intellect by which he is included among mankind, would dare to say that. Moreover, the Messenger (ﷺ), for as long as he lived, continued to observe the rites of worship and to bear the burdens of obligation, without deviating from the right path by the slightest measure. Shall it then be said that the certainty did not come to him, peace be upon him, until he died, and that therefore he remained in the hardships of obligation until he met the Lord of the worlds? I do not think anyone would conceive of that in his heart, even if he had long wandered in the wildernesses of error and it became manifest.

Yes, some noble scholars, in commenting on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We certainly know﴾ etc., mentioned words that contain something of what the Sufis (al-Sufiyya) mention, but it is far, by many stages, from the aim of those base people. In al-Kashshaf: after He, exalted is He, had demolished the foundations of the ignorance of the disbelievers, and had thundered and lightened with what He showed of His action toward those who spoke like those wicked ones, that statement, by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We certainly know﴾, emphasized this with the utmost emphasis, coming from a station of extreme displeasure and majesty, in order to relieve His beloved, upon him be peace, to the greatest extent of relief. Then He guided to what is higher than that, by which He qualified him for intimate conversation, companion to companion. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾, an indication of turning to Him wholly, of complete detachment from other than Him, and of adornment with the attributes of one who turns to Him with good acceptance and need. For that is what glorification and praise require of one who understands them. Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And be among the prostrators﴾, a proof of the nearness implied in it, for prostration is the utmost of humility and need, and it is the manifestation of annihilation (al-fana'), even of oneself, and the partner of subsistence (al-baqa') with the One whose command is by its five (prayers). His saying, exalted is His majesty, ﴿And worship your Lord﴾ etc., its outward meaning is apparent, and its inner meaning points to the fact that journeying toward Allah, exalted is He, does not end, and that the witnessing in which one settles never fully occurs. So there is no overwhelming calamity except that above it is a greater calamity.

When I become hidden, it appears, and when it appears, it hides me.

And from the tongue of this station: ﴿My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾. End of the quotation. It is not hidden from what many of the exegetes mentioned: the correspondence of the end of this surah to its beginning, and that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And We certainly know﴾ etc., is in response to ﴿And they say: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best and is most wise.
* * *
From the way of allusion (al-isharah) in what preceded of the verses: what they said, summarized as follows, regarding ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, meaning: inform them that I forgive the passing thoughts of the hearts of the knowers after they perceive the places of their occurrence and make up for what is required of them, and I show them mercy with kinds of overflowing bounties, and I bring them to the highest unveilings and witnessings. ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾: it is the punishment of veiling and of being expelled from the door.

Ibn 'Ata' said: this verse is guidance for him (ﷺ) on how to guide, as if it were said: keep My servants between fear and hope, so that for them the path of uprightness in obedience may be sound. For whoever is overcome by hope neglects it, and whoever is overcome by fear makes them despair. Some of them mentioned that in it is an indication of preferring the side of fear over hope, because He, glorified is He, applied the two attributes of mercy to Himself, while punishment was not applied in that same manner. You know that what is mentioned in many books is that a person should be balanced between hope and fear, except at the time of death, when his hope should be greater than his fear. On this matter there is a long discussion, to be sought in its proper place.

﴿By your life, they are in their intoxication, wandering blindly﴾. Al-Nawawi said: that is, by your life, which was singled out from among all the worlds. Al-Qurashi said: this is an oath by the life of the Beloved (ﷺ).

He, glorified is He, swore by it only because it was by Him, exalted is He. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern (al-mutawassimin)﴾, that is, those who perceive by insight (al-mutafarrisin). They mentioned that insight (al-firasa) has degrees. Some of it is attained by the eye of the outward; some by what the ears of the knowers perceive of what Truth speaks through the tongues of creation; some by what appears in the form of the one who perceives, from the forms of the Truth's action, glorified is He, and His making speak and His bringing into being for him, until all the hairs of his body speak with different tongues, so that he sees and hears from his own outward self what indicates the occurrence of unseen matters; some by the senses of the inner self, where by their subtlety they find the first beginnings of the unseen through the sparkling; some by the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara) through what appears in it of longing and agitation, and that is the secret of His love, for when Allah, exalted is He, wishes to open the unseen, He casts into the self impressions from its valley, either pleasing, so that it longs for them, or displeasing, so that it is repelled; and no one knows that except one whose nature is divine (rabbani al-sifa). Some of it is attained by the heart, either by inspiration (al-ilham) or by unveiling. Some of it is attained by the intellect, and that is what falls upon it of the weighty descent of unseen revelation. Some of it is attained by the spirit (al-ruh), with or without an intermediary. Some of it is attained by the eye of the secret (al-sirr) and its hearing. And some of it is attained in the secret of the secret: the appearance of the brides of the destinies of the unseen, intertwined with divine, lordly, spiritual forms; so he sees the action of the Essence in the Attributes and hears the Attributes, in the manner of speech and address, from the Essence without any intermediary. There is the utmost end of unveiling and insight.

Al-Junayd, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about insight and said: they are divine signs that appear in the secrets of the knowers, so their tongues speak of that, and thus they hit the Truth. They have other expressions on this as well.

﴿So turn away with a gracious turning away﴾.

'Amr ibn Dinar related from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, from his father 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: the gracious turning away is a turning away with no rebuke in it, and no rancor after it, along with a return to what was before the involvement in opposition. It was also said: the gracious turning away is consoling the offender by removing his shame and treating the place of the pains of regret in his heart.

﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated (al-mathani)﴾. These are the seven attributes, namely life, knowledge, power, will, sight, hearing and speech. The meaning of their being "oft-repeated" is that their affirmation for him (ﷺ) was repeated and reiterated. So for him, upon him be peace, they were first in the station of the existence of the heart and its being formed with his character and qualified with his attributes, and second in the station of subsistence through the true existence (al-wujud al-haqqani). It was also said: the meaning of their being oft-repeated is that they are the secondary attributes established in His Essence, glorified is He, and their offspring.

And it has come in the hadith: "The servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him; and when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, and his sight with which he sees," etc. ﴿And the Great Qur'an﴾: and it is, according to them, the Essence that comprises all the Attributes.

﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to kinds of them﴾, etc. Some of them said regarding this: the Truth, glorified is He, was jealous for him, upon him be peace, that he should look with approval upon anything of the created world and direct his gaze to it. He wanted from him (ﷺ) that his times should be devoted to Him, his states restricted to Him, and his precious breaths held in trust with Him. The Messenger (ﷺ) was as He willed from him, glorified is He; therefore in the highest station it occurred: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾, ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and be among the prostrators﴾, ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾. What has passed from al-Kashshaf of what is contained in it is sufficient for whoever wishes an allusion from those seeking guidance.

This, and I ask Allah, glorified is He, to protect us from the evil of destiny, and to bestow upon us success in what He loves and is pleased with, by the sanctity of the Prophet (ﷺ), his family and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them all. What has passed in the interpretation of the Book of Allah, exalted is He, is by the pen.
